en: In the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva Precepts, although extensive, is rooted in the three trainings; and although the categories of precepts are numerous, they are subsumed within the three clusters (*triskandha*). What are these three clusters?

They are precisely what are called the precept of restraining from misconduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). This...
The three clusters (triskandha) fully embody all practices of the *pāramitās*;

it is by means of this that Buddhas of the past and future attain realization, and it is from this that the Great Vehicle and the Lesser Vehicle arise for the cultivation of self-benefit and the benefit of others—nothing transcends this.
Does not the Sūtra say: "This is the original source of all Buddhas, the fundamental root of practicing the Bodhisattva path"? It further says: "The multitude..."

To receive the Buddha-precepts upon birth and immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas—wherein one’s status is identical to that of Great Enlightenment—is this not the proof that one is truly a child of the Buddhas?
Therefore, on the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal, Vairocana is the Lord who expounds the teaching;
on the thousand petals, Kāśyapa is the Master who recites it. You should know that they have been transmitted from one to another in succession so that it shall never be interrupted.
The *Prātimokṣa* of the Western Regions consists of as many as one hundred thousand verses and sixty-one chapters,
whereas that practiced here in this land is merely the single chapter on the "Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground" recited by the Dharma Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Although they differ in their breadth and brevity, it is like raising a single main rope so that all the meshes of the net unfold, or tasting a single drop [to know the flavor of the whole].
The entire tide has been fully understood; what is "this" and what is "that"? There is nothing lacking and nothing remaining.

Formerly, the Chan Master Xuetang, the General Superintendent of Jianghuai and Fujian, dwelt securely in *dhyāna* and entered deeply into *prajñā*. Furthermore, by means of the *Prātimokṣa*, he encompassed all who were fortunate to encounter him.
The Sage Yuan unified the empire, merging the systems of chariots and books;

yet, fearing that the texts of the *Vinaya* would not circulate widely, he had them carved upon woodblocks for distribution throughout lands as numerous as motes of dust, so that all sentient beings, as numerous as motes of dust, might universally see and hear them.
Through the precepts, concentration arises; through concentration, wisdom arises. Thus the three trainings increase and the three virtues are perfected, extending to the end of the future.
Regarding the one called the Master of Instruction, Xuedang: his mother declined to accept the title "Xuedang.
Throughout her life, she delighted in associating with renowned scholars and gentlemen, never regarding matters of life and death or personal hardship as obstacles.

Her magnanimity in providing for the poor and her fondness for charity were so expansive that they surpassed what others could achieve; these qualities are evident in the poems and writings of various worthy sages.
I have carefully examined both sets of words and am deeply moved by the imperial decree;
now that you have further granted me land in the south, your favor is even more profound. Thus, I shall carve this scripture to circulate it throughout the ten directions.
Thus, with these words, he looked up to pray for the longevity of Nan-shan.
Written in the sixth month of the second year of the Dade era by Wu-wei Weida, abbot of Zhongwu Kunshan Dongchan Monastery.
Handing incense, I respectfully preface this *Brahmajāla Sūtra Bodhisattva Precepts Preface*.
Formerly, the Way of the Master (Confucius) was transmitted to Zisi; Zisi transmitted it to Mencius. After Mencius, [the lineage] did not...
Having received his transmission, the Way of Shoufeng was passed on to Xuetang. Why is it that after Xuetang, one seeks to broaden this transmission?
Shoufeng was one who mastered both Confucianism and Buddhism and was fully equipped in both Chan and doctrinal teachings;
he was a distant descendant of Henan Fazhao and the legitimate son of Qianxi Faxiang, receiving the orthodox transmission of Yuanzhao and inheriting the lineage of Langya.
Throughout his life, his poetic compositions were as refined as the golden wind and the precious moon;
he lectured on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the *Yuanjue jing*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and whenever he annotated the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, he applied himself with earnest diligence.

He wished to have these carved into printing blocks to ensure their wide circulation, yet now that his karmic conditions for transformation have ended and his spirit has passed into nirvana, this aspiration remains unfulfilled. Now, the General Administrator Xuetang Da...
The Upādhyāya dwells as the foremost among his disciples and is honored by kings and nobles;
he follows the Way of the Teacher without deviation and succeeds to the Dharma of the Teacher with perfect likeness.

Thus, observing his observance of the precepts, there is the merit of preventing evil and inciting goodness within the seeds of thought; it is therefore called "restraint" (saṃvara), which restrains evil and promotes goodness.

He caused the practice of precepts to spread and evil to be extinguished; carving this into woodblocks in the present age to complete his father’s unfinished work may be called filial piety in the way of a son.
Does not the Sūtra say, "The name of filial piety is precept"? This is precisely what that refers to.

Xuetai was the eighteenth-generation descendant of Linji; he propagated the winds of the school and presided over ten great monasteries, all of which he enlarged and honored with new halls and buildings.
He extensively established fields and gardens, cast Buddha images, constructed scriptural treasuries, and provided meals for tens of thousands of monks, performing infinite kinds of supreme causes.

Although he twice received imperial edicts commanding him to assume the authority over the monastic community, he steadfastly declined to go, preferring to remain in quiet seclusion; consequently, he was moved by divine inspiration.
By Imperial Decree, five thousand mu of land were bestowed; Xuetang, through various meritorious deeds,
prays for the prolongation of Your Majesty’s sagely longevity to repay this profound grace.
"May the Empress Dowager enjoy health and peace for ten million years;

may His Imperial Highness the Prince of Jin enjoy wealth and honor for eight thousand springs; and may the high ministers both within and without share in abundant and lasting felicity—this is the aspiration of this Xuetang.
Kaitai, retired from office, respectfully transcribed this from his grandfather, the śramaṇa Wufeng Yansuo Puxiu.
Having purified myself through ritual bathing and fasting, I respectfully compose this preface to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra Bodhisattva Precepts*.
To begin with, all sentient beings constantly take the three types of mental action and the four types of verbal action as the root of their karmic creation; these are the most eminent...
All *sattvas* take the ten thousand practices of the six *pāramitās* as the cause for attaining Buddhahood.

I, the Great Bhagavān, out of compassion for the bhikṣus of the final dharma age—who are gradually moving further from the Buddha—have established these teachings ever more profoundly. I have instructed Ānanda:
"You have often heard me, within the *Vinaya*, proclaim the three definitive meanings of cultivation and practice; namely, 'to gather the mind' is..."
Precepts give rise to concentration; concentration gives rise to wisdom. These are called the Threefold Training in the Outflows-free (anāsrava-śikṣā).

First, one must refrain from sexual misconduct; next, one must refrain from killing; and furthermore, one must refrain from stealing. Sexual misconduct, killing, and stealing are known as the karma of the three poisons.
If these are not permanently severed, how can one cultivate and realize unsurpassed bodhi? If one does not refrain from sexual misconduct, one will certainly fall into the realm of Māra.
Even if one practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to the utmost, it is like steaming sand and gravel to make rice—it can never be eaten as food.

If one does not refrain from killing, one will surely fall into the realm of spirits; by taking the lives of sentient beings, one commits a root offense and enters the great hells with no hope of escape for a long time.
Therefore, the Buddha said that on the ground of a *brāhmaṇa*, grass and vegetables do not grow; I have instead permitted the bhikṣus to eat the five [vegetables].

Regarding pure meat: how can it be otherwise? After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings while claiming to be disciples of the Śākya, pure bhikṣus, or bodhisattvas, are like those walking on a forked path who do not even tread upon living grass, much less pluck it with their hands.

If one does not refrain from stealing, one will surely fall into the wrong paths; if one wishes to cultivate samādhi, which fundamentally issues from transcending worldly toil, a thieving mind will not permit it.

To remove these defilements, one must not, during the final dharma period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, slander bhikṣus who have left the household life and possess the precepts, claiming they follow the path of the Hīnayāna;
for by such delusive doubts, immeasurable sentient beings will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The three types of great precepts mentioned above were all expounded from the golden mouth of the former Buddhas and World-Honored Ones in the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Pure and luminous, or obscured and dark—what I have thus spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

If there are bhikṣus who practice the holy life and uphold the holy precepts—whether the five precepts, the ten precepts, the four hundred bodhisattva precepts, the two hundred and fifty bhikṣu precepts, or the five hundred bhikṣuṇī precepts—in regard to these...
Regarding the precepts, there is only the matter of transgression; according to what one has violated, one falls into the evil realms. Mencius said:
"The gentleman, in his relation to birds and beasts, cannot bear to see them alive and then witness their death, nor can he bear to hear their cries and then eat their flesh.
Therefore, the gentleman keeps the kitchen at a distance. Master Dongpo’s *Record of the Hall of Great Compassion* states:

To observe the fasts and precepts, to uphold the Vinaya, to lecture upon and recite its scriptures, and to honor and adorn the stupas and temples—these are the things by which the Buddha taught people day and night.

Yet some among his followers believe that observing the fasts and precepts and upholding the Vinaya are inferior to being "mindless," that lecturing upon and discussing the scriptures is inferior to being "speechless," and that honoring and adorning the stupas and temples is inferior to "non-action" (*wuwei*). Thus they remain satiated [with their own views].
To indulge merely in eating, wandering, and pleasure is to deceive the Buddha on a grand scale.
The Imperial Historian Huang of the Shangu Valley once composed a text of vows; now, before the Buddha, I make this great vow:

from this day forth until the end of the future world, I shall no longer engage in lustful desire, no longer eat meat, and no longer drink wine. Should I ever again indulge in lustful desire, may I fall [into hell].
Those who dwell in the fiery pits of hell—even if they eat meat—shall fall into hell and swallow glowing iron balls;
even if they drink wine—they shall fall into hell and drink molten copper for immeasurable kalpas.
Because all sentient beings drink wine, eat meat, engage in lustful debauchery, and commit killing, I shall undergo these sufferings on their behalf. Furthermore, he spoke this verse of certainty:

"Those who cannot cease from wine, cannot abstain from meat, do not sever their greedy desires, and lack contentment—even if they align themselves with the Buddha’s wisdom and insight—will surely enter hell.
How true these words are! Examining the intent of the sages and worthies of a thousand ages is equivalent to observing the deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Now, the Abbot Xuetang Chan Master has given rise to the bodhicitta.
Giving rise to the mind of great compassion, the adamantine firm mind, and the inconceivable mind of noble merit,
he subsequently established Tianqing Chan Temple in the capital; renovated Kaithai Chan Temple, Fayuan Chan Temple in Luoyang,
Dajue Chan Temple in Zhengzhou, Fazang Chan Temple in Fengzhou, and Kainbao Hui’an Chan Temple in Bianliang.
The ten great renowned monasteries— including Chan Temple, Langya Chan Temple in Chuzhou, Shengjue Chan Temple in Tongzhou,
Linji Chan Temple in Daming, and Jinghui Luohan Chan Temple in Songyin— all bear the seals of imperial favor.
By imperial decree, by the august edict of the Empress Dowager,

and by the command of the Prince of Jin, all matters of protection— such as the enlargement and exaltation of temple halls, the establishment of fields and gardens, and the casting of statues— were carried out.
Having established Buddha images, compiled the Tripitaka, and provided alms to tens of thousands of monks,

his various merits and infinite superior causes moved the Imperial Decree to specially grant him five thousand *mu* of land; subsequently, he traveled to Jiangnan to print twenty sets of the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*).

He carved twelve halls of Buddha altars and woodblocks for various sutras and dharanis within the Tsang region; he newly engraved the illustrated transformation tableaux and commentaries for the Fifty-three Visits of Sudhana,
as well as the Brahma’s Net Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra, intending to continue the legacy of the Tathagata at the end of his era.
The lifespan of the Dharma still fulfills the heart’s aspiration for the Peak of Longevity;

because this sutra is so honored and sublime, within the Palace of Hundred Million *koṭi* of Purple-Golden Vajra Radiance in the Lotus Flower Treasury World, the Buddha Vairocana spoke to the thousand Buddhas within the thousand flowers, and those thousand Buddhas spoke to the hundred million *koṭi* Śākyamunis, saying:
"O thousand Buddhas, listen attentively as I briefly explain the hundred [teachings]."
From the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground" within the Dharma-gate of Ineffable Teachings as Numerous as the Sands of a Thousand Ganges Rivers:
The Vajra Jewel Precept of the Radiance of the One Precept is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all Bodhisattvas, and the treasury of precepts within the Buddha-dharma—the Prātimokṣa.
Should one commit the ten grave pārājika offenses or the forty-eight minor offenses...
Whether stained by offenses or like the sun and moon, like a jeweled necklace or a mote of dust, the assembly of Bodhisattvas attains perfect enlightenment through the precepts.
When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Therefore, the supreme merit of this giving and these precepts pervades ten billion four-continent worlds, ten billion palaces of the sun and moon, and ten billion Mount Sumerus.
In billions of Jambudvīpas— inexpressible, immeasurable, inexhaustible, and endless— the Emperor and Prince of Jin receive the great grace of this almsgiving as their supreme recompense;
below, for all within the realm under heaven, the *poṣadha* is spread, so that even the most base creatures and the moving world are moistened by its benefits.
Having departed from the retributive suffering of the four modes of birth and attained liberation through seeing and hearing, he realized the extraordinary merit of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
may His Majesty enjoy a long life of hundreds of millions of years,
and may the Prince of Jin ascend to the sagely calculation of eight thousand autumns.
May the Empress Dowager and the Empress doubly receive celestial blessings; may the Crown Prince and the Grandson all ascend to the realm of longevity;
and may the internal and external ministers enjoy benefit, joy, peace, and tranquility. Written on the full moon of the seventh month in the second year of the Dàdé era by the former Censor-in-Chief.
Guo Tianxi, having washed his hands and burned incense,
respectfully prefaces this commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra Bodhisattva Precepts*.
This is the Commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* together with its preface.
Preface by the Śramaṇa Huìyīn, Abbot of Bǎoyìng Monastery, who lectured on the sutras and transmitted the precepts at Luòyuàn:

As for the gateway to extinguishing the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses and attaining Buddhahood, none is more essential than the "Chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground" from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.

Those who merely understand the words of the Master may all receive this precept. Thus, the World-Honored One intended for those of later generations with wisdom and faith to accept it with a firm mind and protect it;

even if they were coerced by the suffering of fire, iron, spears, blades, or being carved and incised, they would never relent in their resolve to transgress it. Therefore, the opening words of this sutra are direct and compassionate.

The commentary on the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is extensive; fearing that readers might become weary of its vastness, I have collected the various meanings and annotated them directly upon the original text so that those who peruse it may easily achieve understanding.

If one reveres these precepts and relies upon them—thereby perfecting purity, attaining cool serenity, adorning wisdom and concentration, and realizing unsurpassed enlightenment—it can truly be called wisdom.

At this time, on the full moon day of the late summer month in the third year of the Shaosheng era, the cyclical year being Bingzi, [was written] the Preface to the Bodhisattva Precepts of the Brahmajāla Sūtra.

"Brahmā's Net" (Fannwang) refers to the *dhvaja-jāla* (banner-net); it signifies that the Brahmā King, leading the various hosts of Brahmās as his preceding and following attendants, [manifested this net].

There was a great jeweled banner, its top draped with a net of the seven treasures, which had come from afar to the Buddha’s dwelling to offer worship, listen to the Dharma, and request the turning of the wheel of the Dharma.
Because the Buddha observed this banner and its net and took them as a metaphor, he preached this sutra titled the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.

Regarding the metaphors, there are both general and specific types; the general metaphor illustrates the distinctions between the sentient world (*sattvaloka*) and the physical world (*bhājanaloka*), as well as how the Buddha’s teachings reach and transform them.

This also differs from the separate analogies for the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*). First, the analogy of the protective fence illustrates the restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*):

the three karmas are without flaw, just as a net protects trees so that birds and filth do not invade. Second, the analogy of the tree illustrates the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*):

various virtues are nurtured and grow, just as a tree receives the net and produces flowers and fruit. Third, the analogy of the tree illustrates the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*): the two benefits are universal, just as a tree provides shade and fruit for all.

"Round as a spread net" refers to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, which describes fish leaping from the river onto the bank; "sūtra" (*jing*) means a teaching, specifically this scripture that serves as the "net of Brahmā.
"Bodhisattva" is the full term for *bodhisattva*; in Chinese, it is translated as "Awakened Being" (*jue youqing*).

"Awakened" (*jue*) refers to the fruit sought, and "being" (*youqing*) refers to the sentient beings to be saved. Named according to what is sought and what is saved, it is abbreviated as "Bodhisattva."
"Precepts" (*śīla*) refers to the undertaking and training in the Threefold Pure Precepts; its nature consists of the capacity to prevent evil and incite goodness within the seeds of volition.
It is also called "restraint" (*saṃvara*), because it restrains good so that it may be practiced and stops evil so that it may be extinguished.

It is also called "prohibition" (*niyama*), because it prohibits and guards the three types of action from committing any evil. "Sequence" (*krama*) means cause and beginning; it sets forth the virtues of the teaching.
The gradual origins of the establishment of the ritual procedures (as detailed at length).
All you sons of the Buddha, join your palms with a sincere mind and listen as I now wish to recite the Preface to the Great Precepts of all Buddhas.

"Various" does not refer to one [group] alone; it encompasses both the laity and the ordained, as well as the assembly of men and the assembly of women. "Buddha-sons" refers precisely to the aforementioned fourfold assembly;
because they receive the Buddha's precepts and practice them to succeed to the Buddha’s position, they are called Buddha-sons.

"With palms joined, listen with a sincere heart" means that listening to and receiving the Buddha's precepts is the cause for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, one must not treat this lightly, but should instead reverently join the palms and listen.
Focus your mind with the utmost concentration and listen attentively to what I shall say. That which I now wish to proclaim is the introduction composed by me;
it is my intention to expound upon the Great Precepts of the Buddhas.

As for these, they were first received at the time of their initial resolve by the Buddhas of the past—those who are near, such as the Seven Buddhas, and those who are distant, reaching back to the infinite past. If one considers the moment of their first aspiration, this is when they were originally upheld.

This precept extends directly until the attainment of Buddhahood; the initial formulation of this Great Precept at the time of becoming a Buddha is precisely the prologue of this sutra, which serves as the prologue to the Great Precepts of all Buddhas.
The assembly gathers.
On the night of the recitation of the precepts, the fourfold assembly gathers and listens in silence.
The Dharma Master recites the precepts; listen attentively, with careful composure and stillness.
One knows for oneself that one has committed an offense.
Without having attained the path of knowledge of others' minds or the divine eye, one knows the offenses committed by others;
that is, one knows that they may have committed an offense after going forth, or that they will certainly commit one later, or that they have previously committed a transgression.
One must perform repentance.
One must indeed perform repentance; in Sanskrit this is called *kṣamā*, which here means "to repent" or "to disclose.
It refers to disclosing one's own committed offenses before the assembly.
Repentance brings peace and happiness.
If a person suffers from illness due to past evil karma, once they have repented, the suffering of the disease will be cured, and thus they attain peace and happiness.
Furthermore, because one who has violated the precepts experiences mental and physical unease and suffers from remorse day and night, through repentance they attain peace.
If one does not repent of these transgressions, the retribution will become increasingly grave.
Because one continues to commit offenses day after day and night after night, they gradually increase, just as water droplets accumulate.
Those who are free from offense remain silent.
Knowing themselves to be free from offense, they do not further speak to recount their names or offenses.
Because they remain silent, it should be known that the assembly is pure.
One must truly know for oneself that one is without fault before remaining silent; thus it is called "silence.
Now, to remain silent whether one is guilty or innocent is a profound deception.
Venerable sirs!
Because the two assemblies of the ordained possess the purity of the precepts and advance in great practice to seek great enlightenment,
they have the virtue and learning of great masters;
this is not the case for upāsakas, upāsikās, and others.
The two assemblies of householders who possess the five precepts and so forth:
listen attentively;
listen with careful discernment.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa:
the Buddha himself left home at twenty-nine, practiced asceticism for six years, attained enlightenment at thirty-five,
and entered parinirvāṇa at eighty-five.
During the period of the Semblance Dharma—

when the True Dharma lasts for one thousand years and the Semblance Dharma lasts for another thousand years— and at the time this preface was composed, which falls within that Semblance Dharma period—
one should revere and honor the Prātimokṣa.
"Should" (ying) means to accord with; "ought" (dang) means what is required or necessary; "follow" (zun) means to receive and practice in accordance with.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, monks have no other reliance; if they do not receive and uphold these precepts, they will have nowhere to turn for refuge—this is why it is said so.
The *prātimokṣa* is precisely this precept; this is the citation and explanation of its name.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *prātimokṣa*, which in Chinese means "individual liberation precept.
This refers to the ten grave precepts mentioned below, through which one is individually liberated by abandoning and turning away from all evils.
When upholding these precepts,
what are the meritorious benefits?
It is like encountering light in the darkness.
Before upholding these precepts, one is shrouded by delusion and clear wisdom does not arise, remaining perpetually like darkness;
once these precepts are upheld, wisdom gradually increases, as if encountering light.
It is like a poor person obtaining treasure.
Before one upholds the precepts, one is like a destitute person who lacks the wealth of wisdom—the true jewel of the Dharma.
Once this precept is upheld, it becomes one of the seven noble riches and a treasure of supramundane Dharma-wealth.
It is like a sick person recovering from illness;
by upholding this precept, the disease of the afflictions is eliminated, resulting in peace and recovery.
It is like a prisoner being released from jail.
Because taking up the precepts as a cause will lead one out of the prison of the triple world, it is like a long-distance traveler finding a way home.
Not yet having taken these precepts is like leaving one's home and wandering far away upon the perilous paths of birth and death; now, one resolves to take them up.
The precepts are like the first stage of a journey; by not resting day after day, one will gradually and before long arrive at the home of nirvāṇa.
You should know that these are the Great Teacher for all of you.
By means of the five aforementioned metaphors, this precept is illustrated; only then can it be understood that one should rely upon it for study and practice.
Because it advances and pursues [the goal] with rules and instructions to guide all things so that they may give rise to correct understanding, the precepts are called the "Original Teacher.
This is no different from when the Buddha dwelt in the world;
during his lifetime, the Buddha would always recite these precepts every half-month, and the sons of the Buddha followed them accordingly.
Because the Buddha’s daily conduct and the established rules are in perfect accord, it is said that there is no difference between them.
It is difficult for a sense of dread to arise;
though the three miserable realms involve extreme suffering, their minds feel no weariness or fear, desiring only the causes of evil while failing to contemplate its consequences.
A virtuous mind is difficult to arouse.

Whenever a virtuous mind arises, it accords with principle and benefits others; yet now, my mind is devoid of fear and anxiety, thinking solely and exclusively of attaining peace and happiness for myself, while disregarding the suffering of others.
Therefore, the Sūtra—the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—says:
"Do not treat even a small offense lightly, thinking it will bring no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel."
Do not despise even a minor offense, for like small water gradually accumulating to become a great body of water, so too do minor offenses, if not repented, accumulate to become great offenses.

When water fills it, a vessel is said to be full; when offenses reach their limit, one is said to have "completed the vessel. To have completed the vessel means that the karma for the three miserable realms has reached its full measure.
One commits a transgression in a single kṣaṇa;
because at the moment of committing the offense one quickly gives rise to the intention,
the calamity falls upon one in the Avīci Hell.

The shadow of karma pursues the form and cannot be escaped; it drags one toward the destination of rebirth. This is stated with reference to the most grievous cases, yet it applies to other hells as well.
Once one loses this human body, ten thousand kalpas may pass before it is regained.

Furthermore, due to the gravity [of their karma], they cannot regain a human body for ten thousand kalpas; moreover, "ten thousand kalpas" is a conventional expression for ten million kalpas, meaning that as long as their karma is not exhausted, they remain within [samsara].
Even in the prime of youth, physical beauty does not endure.
Because even the full bloom of youth and vigor cannot remain for long,
it is like a galloping horse;
this metaphor illustrates that the impermanence of ethical discipline is as swift as a running horse, passing away in a mere instant.
Human life is impermanent, passing more swiftly than mountain streams;
the rapid flow of mountain waters is surpassed even further by the impermanence of human life.
Though one may exist this very day, it is difficult to guarantee survival until tomorrow.
The above two metaphors explain the principle that impermanence is swift: in reality, one cannot guarantee that the exhalation will be followed by an inhalation;
once the exhalation does not return, one’s life-span is abandoned. O assembly!
The great assembly in this gathering was each and every one single-minded;
every individual focused their mind exclusively and without distraction, cultivating progress in every thought-moment.
Diligently cultivate vigor;
that is, exert the mind and mental factors to prevent evil, give rise to goodness, and bring all wholesome deeds to completion.
Be careful not to be indolent.
The mind that is constantly negligent, lacking virtue, and indolent, causes all wholesome qualities to decline and all unwholesome states to increase;
such laziness is the essential nature of indolence.
Sleep causes the body and mind to lack mastery; its function is to obstruct contemplation. When sleep covers the mind, all wholesome states cease, and the mind is left to run wild.
Impermanence is close at hand; while your task remains unfinished, do not covet sensory objects or allow your mind to run wild.
At night, you must restrain the mind.
Whenever the hour of night arrives, you should collect and record the mind, ensuring it does not become distracted by grasping at external objects.
Maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
Whenever the hour of midnight arrives, let your mind constantly dwell upon observing and reflecting on the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
do not let the time pass in vain.
A human body is difficult to obtain, the Buddhas are difficult to encounter, the True Dharma is difficult to hear, and the Sangha is difficult to meet;
if one’s mind harbors no such reflections, it may be called a life lived in vain—like returning empty-handed from a mountain of jewels, with nothing for oneself to sustain.
It is merely a futile exertion;
indulging in forms and craving sounds, one vainly establishes these practices and undergoes exhausting toil that ultimately yields no benefit or salvation,
leading to deep regret in later generations.

If one does not cultivate goodness while alive, one will fall into the three miserable realms at death; through ten thousand deaths and a thousand births, one shall personally undergo profound and heavy sorrow and regret.
Since no one can take one’s suffering upon themselves, it is said that [worldly efforts] are merely a source of weariness, leading to deep remorse in future lives.
Each and every member of the assembly should, with single-mindedness and careful attention, train in accordance with the Dharma by relying upon these precepts;
this is what you should learn. This exhortation to the great assembly is that you should learn with one mind, following the teaching and practicing it in accordance with it;
you must certainly cultivate and study these Great Bodhisattva Precepts. The extensive version consists of one hundred and twelve fascicles and sixty-one chapters, translated by Kumārajīva.

When the Duke (Fu Jian) was specifically reciting the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Single-Minded Ground" which briefly clarifies the characteristics of the precepts, it was during the reign of Yao Xing,
when more than five thousand sections of sutras and śāstras were being translated and transmitted. Finally, this sutra was translated within the Xiaoyao Garden in the third year of the Hongshi era.
Venerable sirs, the spring season consists of one period of four months:
from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month; from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month is the summer season;
and from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month is the winter season.
Half a month has passed;
one month has passed; two months have passed; one and a half months have passed;
two and a half months have passed; three months have passed; four months have passed; two months [have passed].
Half has already passed;
with one night remaining, there is three months and a half left.
Three months remain; two months remain; one month remains; two and a half months remain.
One month and a half have passed; fifteen days remain.

Old age and death are drawing near, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish. Venerable ones, upāsakas, and upāsikās, for the sake of attaining the Way, you must single-mindedly seek diligence with vigor.
Why is this? It is because all Buddhas, through single-minded and diligent seeking, attained it.
If one can attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how much more so other wholesome dharmas?

Each of you, while hearing [the Dharma] and being strong and healthy, should strive with diligence to cultivate the good; why not seek the Path? How can you wait until old age? What joy is there in this?
This day has already passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly; like a fish in shallow water, what joy is there in this?
"Is the Saṃgha assembled?
"The Saṃgha is assembled.
"Are they in concord?"
The assembly is harmonious.
Those who have not received full ordination should depart.
If someone answers that those who have not received the precepts have already departed, or if there is no answer, it means this assembly contains no one who is unordained.
Regarding the precepts:
if there are bhikṣus who have not arrived, one should announce their *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purification).
If someone answers, "The bhikṣus who have not arrived have already announced their *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*," then if no one answers, [one should proceed].
"In this assembly, there is no one who speaks of desire.
What shall the harmonious Saṃgha now perform?
He replied, "The formal act (*karmavācanā*) for reciting the precepts."

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today is the fifteenth day; the Saṃgha shall recite the Prātimokṣa. If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, grant its consent that we shall recite the Prātimokṣa in assembly.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Question: "Is the formal motion completed? Answer: "It is completed."

The assembly should listen with a single mind: the precepts purify the body and speech; they restrain the mind and give rise to right mindfulness; through much hearing, true wisdom is born. Thus, the precepts are the foundation;
the precepts are the wondrous treasury of the Dharma; they are also the wealth for transcending the world.

The precepts are a great vessel capable of crossing the ocean of birth and death; the precepts are a pool of coolness for bathing away all afflictions and fevers; the precepts are the art of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It subdues and eliminates evil poisons; it takes the precepts as its ultimate companion, enabling one to cross perilous and evil paths.

The precepts are the gateway to the nectar of immortality, traversed by all the noble ones. One who upholds the precepts does not become arrogant in mind, remaining single-mindedly diligent and free from negligence.

They do not grasp at the characteristics of right precepts, nor do they harbor thoughts of wrong views. This is called pure precept-keeping, praised by all Buddhas; one who upholds the precepts has no regret in their heart.
One's aspirations are likewise fulfilled: the precepts serve as the moat of the Dharma-city, capable of warding off the thieves of affliction;

the precepts serve as a valiant general, able to crush and subdue the hosts of Māra’s armies; the precepts serve as a wish-fulfilling gem, able to bestow treasures upon merchants; the precepts serve as a sublime tower for sporting within various *samādhis*;
and upholding the precepts serves as level ground, with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) serving as the dwelling that can give rise to the light of wisdom.

Attaining the power of concentration and wisdom through progressive illumination, adorning the myriad practices until the Way of Buddhahood is fully realized—all this has the precepts as its very foundation.
Therefore, the wise person with a steadfast mind guards the precepts; they would rather lose their own body and life than ever violate them.
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas, for I now wish to proclaim the precepts.
The assembly should listen with a single mind: even regarding minor offenses, one’s heart should feel great dread. When there is an offense, repent with a single mind;
thereafter, do not commit it again. The horse of the mind gallops down evil paths; its heedlessness is difficult to restrain.

The Buddha taught that the diligent practice of the precepts is like a sharp bridle and rein. Those who can faithfully accept the teachings and precepts spoken by the Buddha’s own mouth are people whose "horses" are well-tamed.
One who can destroy the army of afflictions, yet neither accepts instructions nor delights in the precepts, is a person whose horse is untamed;

such a person sinks into the army of birth and death. If a person guards the precepts as a yak loves its tail, binding the mind with heedfulness like a monkey placed in chains, and constantly exerts diligence day and night to seek true wisdom, then such a person is within the Buddha-dharma.
One can attain a pure livelihood.

Venerable sirs, today, on the fifteenth day of either the waxing or waning moon, we perform the *poṣadha*. You laymen (*upāsaka*), laywomen (*upāsikā*), and those who have received the bodhisattva precepts should listen with single-minded attention.
Those who have committed an offense should confess it; those without offense should remain silent. By remaining silent, you shall be [known to be] pure.
"Venerable sirs, you have been informed that you are pure and fit to receive the Upāsaka, Upāsikā, and Bodhisattva precepts.
Having completed the introduction to the Bodhisattva precepts, I now ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard?"
Thus it was asked three times.
Since the Venerable Ones are pure in this matter and remain silent, let it be so held.
From the Brahmajāla Sūtra of Rocana.
This is called "Fulfilment and Purity.

The Buddha taught that the *Śāstra* (treatise) is the Buddha himself; thus, by harmonizing the teaching with the capacity of the recipient, the principle is revealed through what is spoken, and the name "Brahmajāla" (The Brahma Net) is manifested.
The *Sūtra* states that this is the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound as explained by Vairocana Buddha.
"Mind" refers to the fifty mental states, such as faith and so forth, or fifty-four mental states; according to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are fifty-five mental states.
The stages (*bhūmi*).

Prior to the various stages, they are collectively termed the Stage of Practice through Resolute Belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) is termed the Stage of the Pure Mind (*vimalā-bhūmi*);

and from the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) upward, they are termed the Stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*). The preceding mind is exclusively the causal stage, while it also extends to the fruit of Buddhahood.
The Dharma.
There is nothing that is not a sublime path.
The Gate.
The sages and saints travel through them in common;
the categories and types differ. The mind-ground is the dharma-gate, and the dharma-gate of the mind-ground is the chapter—this is the mind-ground.
The "Dharmapada Chapter" (Famenpin) refers to that which is taught; it is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound based on the speaker.
Regarding the "Bodhisattva Precept Text" (Pusa jieben):

"Precepts" (*śīla*) are the very essence (*mūla*) of the Bodhisattva; thus, it is the "Precept-Essence. Furthermore, these are the "Essence" (*mūla*) of all Buddhas; this "Essence" refers to the fundamental source (*mūlamūla*). "Buddha-Bodhi" [refers to the awakening of the Buddha].
The merits of the Bodhisattva arise from this precept.
At that time—
“at that time” meaning precisely then— he, Śāntamati, shall correctly proclaim and transmit this precept within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu).
At the time of Śākyamuni,
Vairocana Buddha is precisely the second-tier *parabhogika* (other-enjoyment) Buddha who acts as the teaching master capable of preaching.
"For this great assembly" refers,
by distant indication, to the three stages of worthiness prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and all ordinary beings.
It briefly opens up, from among hundreds of thousands of *Ganges-sand* numbers of ineffable Dharma-gates.
This extensive precept code contains such a vast number [of items].
The "mind-ground" is like the tip of a single hair;
now, this single chapter on the "mind-ground" is like the tip of that hair within the aforementioned extensive number, thereby manifesting its extreme brevity.
All Buddhas of the past have already spoken of this; all Buddhas of the future shall speak of it; and all Buddhas of the present are now speaking of it.
All Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time—those who have studied, those who will study, and those who are currently studying—have likewise done so.
This demonstrates the realization [of its truth]. Since all Buddhas of the three periods have spoken of these precepts in common, those who study them hereafter shall see [them as such].
The wise who seek self-improvement have a basis for their progress; thus their efforts are not in vain.
I have already practiced this mind-ground for a hundred kalpas.
This is what Śākyamuni, conforming to the world, calls me when he points to his own original body—having cultivated this from the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment.
The precepts lead directly to Buddhahood, truly requiring three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, though for brevity we speak of a hundred stages of mind;
these are the dharmas to be cultivated, while Vairocana is the fruit to be sought. I am named Vairocana.
This emanated Śākyamuni refers to his own original body as Vairocana. "You Buddhas" refers to the thousand Śākyamunis;
this is based on the gate of the emanated conduct of all Buddhas, wherein the Vairocana Buddha atop the thousand-petaled lotus addresses the thousand Śākyamunis.
The hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis shall transmit what I have spoken,
causing the transformation Buddhas to pass down the precepts of the Mind-Ground Dharma Gate that I, as the Sambhogakāya Vairocana, have personally realized and taught.
Chapter.
[I bestow] a small portion of all things upon all sentient beings.
It is called the "Path" because it provides instruction on the fifty-five mental states for those in the three preceding stages of worthiness,
and because it causes one to cultivate and perfect unsurpassed enlightenment within the third stage.

At that time, the Lotus Flower-Pedestal Treasury World (Padmagarbhalokadhātu) was precisely situated at the second level of the transformation-manifesting stage arising from the Truth; it represents the flower-seat upon which the Buddha of Other-Enjoyment (parasaṃbhogakāya) sits,
and its name, "Treasury of the Pedestal," signifies that it contains within it a thousand worlds.
The majestic celestial light is also called the world-system of majestic celestial light.
Upon the lion throne, it is thus named.
Upon the lion throne,
Vairocana Buddha emits rays of light;

as the Buddha transmits the Buddha-precepts, he first emits many rays of light to symbolize that the pure precepts are without flaw, that the various protections and defenses are manifold, and that they are capable of eliminating all defilements.
The Buddha of Delusive Darkness addressed the Buddha upon the Thousand-Petaled Lotus:
"I now address this Great Transformation Buddha of a thousand feet in height upon this thousand-petaled lotus."
He took with him the chapter on the Dharma-gate of my Mind-ground and departed.
"To depart" means to leave; he caused the transmission of the Dharma to return to his own realm of transformation, where he proceeded further and further.
Thereupon, he again manifested as a thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred million Śākyamunis.

This succession of transmissions, concerning the phases of establishing the teachings and the phases of practicing and transforming others, is explained in various ways—approximately by one thousand Śākyamunis or even by a hundred billion Śākyamunis.
In reality, the sounds of the Dharma spoken by them all manifest from the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) within one's own enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*);
furthermore, these do not arise apart from the seeds of sound that emerge from the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the immaculate consciousness (*amalavijñāna*).
Furthermore, for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall now explain in sequence the chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Superior Mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*).
This is taught according to the sequence of the fifty-five preceding minds, and because one practices them in sequence within the three stages (*bhūmi*) as well.
"You all should receive, uphold, read, and recite this with single-minded devotion and practice accordingly.
Tell the Buddhas, great and small, and all sentient beings to each receive and uphold,
and each practice this chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground."
At that time— namely,
when Vairocana had finished transmitting [the teachings] and the Buddha upon the Thousand-Petaled Lotus had completed receiving the Dharma—
the Buddha upon the Thousand-Petaled Lotus...
Upon each flower in the thousandfold world-system are a thousand great transformation Buddhas;
there are a hundred billion Śākyamunis,
and within each of the thousand great world-systems are a hundred billion minor transformation Buddhas.
They rose from their majestic lion thrones in the Lotus Treasury World,
and rising from the second level of the land of other-enjoyment,
they each withdrew to their own realms.
The transformation Buddhas, both great and small, each withdrew.
"Raising the body" means emitting light;
it signifies that all the Buddhas emitted light from every part of their bodies, hence the term "raising. Thus, each Buddha emitted light from his entire body.
The light all transforms into immeasurable Buddhas;
because within the light of each Buddha there are likewise transformed immeasurable Buddhas,
they simultaneously manifest immeasurable flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white.

Each of the Buddhas used flowers of four colors to make offerings to the Buddha; thus, the Buddhas making offerings to the Buddha was for the purpose of transforming those of lower stations and causing those who revere the Dharma to hold the person in high esteem.
Having made offerings to Vairocana Buddha and out of reverence for the Original Teacher,
they have completed the upholding of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as previously expounded.
In truth, one first receives the Dharma and only thereafter makes offerings to the person;

having completed the offerings, one says "the reception is finished," because the purpose of making offerings is solely to repay the kindness of receiving the Dharma, and it is only when the repayment of that kindness is complete that it is called "finished."
"Each and every one.
This refers to the fact that there are not merely one thousand Śākyamunis, nor even a hundred billion Śākyamunis, but rather many distinct ones.
From this Lotus Treasury World, they vanish.
In this manner, the various large and small transformation Buddhas each vanish from their respective lands of other-enjoyment and arrive here.
Having vanished, they enter the Samādhi of the Body-Nature’s Flower-Light (*t'i-hsing hsü-k'ung hua-kuang san-mei*).

This is the name of the meditative concentration entered by the Buddha; it is a state of concentration capable of gathering the mind and sustaining meritorious virtues, just as empty space contains all things.
By attaining the samādhi that is entirely without obstruction, one is able to give rise to wisdom;
wisdom can expound the Dharma, and through its practice, obstacles are severed and principle is realized—like a flower bearing fruit, or like light dispelling darkness.
They returned to their original source worlds.
Thus, these thousand Buddhas and hundreds of billions of Buddhas each departed from their respective native lands,
proceeded to the Lotus Treasury World to hear this Mind-Ground Precept, and then returned to the lands where they had originally manifested.

"Under the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa" signifies the meaning of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) proceeding to its seat to attain Buddhahood; it is complete with the eight phases [of a Buddha's life]:
birth in the royal palace, renunciation, ascetic practice, attainment of the Way, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entry into nirvana.
He emerged from the Samādhi of the Body-Nature’s Flower-Light of Space.
He asked: "The Buddha's mind is always in meditative concentration; for what reason did you previously say he 'entered' concentration and now say he has 'emerged'? He replied:

"If it were the Buddha's actual body, it would indeed be constantly in concentration; however, this refers to the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya), which manifests the appearance of entering and emerging."
Having emerged [from samādhi], he then sat upon the Vajra Throne of Thousandfold Radiance (Vajra-sahasraraśmi-rāja-pīṭha). This is precisely the Vajra Throne beneath the Bodhi tree;

it is not mentioned by that name in other places because those [teachings] were intended for those of inferior capacity, whereas this is intended for those of superior Mahāyāna capacity. Having emerged from samādhi, he ascended [the throne] immediately without waiting for further entreaty.

The Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne then expounds the Great Dharma. If one considers those of inferior faculties, it refers to the throne upon which he preaches the Dharma after manifesting the Eight Phases of Enlightenment;

this symbolizes the throne of the Dharma-King who, having attained Buddhahood and preached the Dharma, radiates a thousand rays of light, and is thus the "King of Thousand Rays" and the "Throne of the King of Thousand Rays."
And as for the Hall of Sublime Light:
because the Buddha sat within that hall intending to preach the Sublime Dharma and first emitted a subtle and wondrous light, the two locations— the King’s Seat and the Hall of Light—
are explained together as the Dharma-gate of the First Assembly.
It speaks of ten world-oceans;
that is, within a single world-system in one direction among the ten directions, there is a Buddha-land.
This first assembly’s teaching of the Dharma refers to each of the ten directions, wherein one *paranirmita-vashavartin* (enjoyment) Buddha-land is described for each respective direction.
Because this land is vast and expansive— surpassing the minor defiled lands prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) where not a single lower rank exists— it is further called an "ocean.
He then rose from his seat,
rising from the previously mentioned Vajra-Thousand-Rays-King Seat.
"Arrived.
It means "reached.
The palace of Śakra.
This refers to the heaven where the Lord of the Thirty-three Devas resides.
It speaks of the ten abodes (*bhūmi*).
One dwells in non-retrogression only upon reaching the seventh abode; if one enters the stage of non-retrogression, it is called "dwelling" in a single abode, which collectively encompasses all ten.

1. The Stage of Initial Resolve (*Prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*): Because one generates the bodhicitta upon seeing the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. 2. The Stage of Refining the Ground (*Caryāpratipatti-vihāra*):

Because one polishes and refines the mind to eliminate its defilements, and because one feels compassion for all sentient beings, seeking their benefit and happiness. 3. The Stage of Cultivation (*Caryā-prayoga-vihāra*):
One observes one’s own body as consisting of the six elements and five faculties, which perish moment by moment; one cultivates this contemplation of suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

1. The Stage of Practice (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*): It is so named because one practices by means of eliminating the grasping at a self; it is called "dwelling in the noble birth" because one’s practice is identical to that of the Buddhas, as one receives the Buddha’s spiritual essence and enters the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

2. The Stage of Endowment with the Five Expedient Means (*pañca-upāya-saṃbhāra-vihāra*): It is so named because one is able to benefit oneself and others, providing welfare and peace to all sentient beings.
3. The Stage of the Rightly Directed Mind (*samyak-citta-vihāra*): It is so named because, upon hearing praise or slander of the Buddha, the mind remains steadfast and unwavering.
8. The Stage of Non-retrogression through Movement (*cala-avaivartika-vihāra*): Because the mind is certain not to regress regardless of whether a Buddha exists or does not exist.

9. The Stage of the Youthful Prince (*kumārabhūta-vihāra*): Because there is no failure in the three karmas; one gives rise to the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-abhikṣṇa-karaṇīya*), and since one’s true practice is without fault, nothing can destroy it.

10. The Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*): Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one tames sentient beings; preaching well according to their capacities, one perfectly accords with them to bring them to maturity.

The ritual succession is not in vain; therefore, through the diligent study of the ten consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) and the ten wisdoms (*jñāna*), one’s transformative and beneficial meritorious deeds reach completion.
This signifies the manifestation of a perfected person, like a great king of a nation who delegates all state affairs to his crown prince and performs the formal display of consecration.

Thus, below this, one who possesses the full status and maintains right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness), abiding in the principle of the *dharmadhātu*, is designated as [the Bodhisattva of the Tenth Stage].
He dwells there.
Furthermore, he rises from his seat and goes to the Yāma Heaven.
[The name] Suyāma should properly be translated as "Division of Joy," because they experience joy according to their respective portions at various times.
The Ten Practices are taught.
This is the third assembly, wherein the Buddha expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices: 1. The Practice of Joy:

Rejoicing in giving both internal and external things without stinginess, able to gladden oneself and others because there is no resentment or malice. 2. The Practice of Benefiting Others: Skillfully protecting the three... [text fragment ends]
First, the practice of accumulation, because it is able to benefit all sentient beings;

second, the practice of non-contradiction, because when performing the two types of beneficial conduct, one can accord with the minds of others through the root of being respectful and conscientious without contradiction;

fourth, the inexhaustible practice, because through the cultivation of diligence, the mind does not retreat or become distracted, remaining equal throughout the three periods of time until the end of the future, and penetrating the ten directions.
5. The Practice of Dispelling Delusion: Because one thoroughly understands the karmic conditions of birth and death, the mind is not deluded.
6. The Practice of Skillful Vision: Because one observes all sentient beings in every moment of thought without attachment. 7. The Practice of Non-Attachment:
Because one skillfully cultivates supreme practices, does not stagnate in emptiness or existence, and realizes that conditioned phenomena have no real nature. 8. The Practice of Difficult Attainment.
9. Because they constantly gather superior roots of goodness through great vows, practicing only for the benefit of others without seeking their own results;

10. Because they practice the ten wholesome dharmas with deep-rooted nature, conforming to principle, benefiting beings, and being skilled in transformation; 11. Because they practice truthfulness, ensuring that their words correspond to their deeds and that what they do is established as true.
Within this stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), the profound mind increases and excels, delighting in the cultivation of all things.
Because they constitute the practices of a bodhisattva, they are established as the names of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*).
Furthermore, rising from his seat, he went to the fourth heaven;
counting downward from the desire realm, it is called Tuṣita in the Sanskrit language—*Tuṣita* is not the formal term, which is correctly *Dṛṣṭānta*.
This is called "Contentment" because the gods of that heaven know contentment regarding their desires and pleasures;
thus, the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are taught.
This is the fourth assembly, wherein the Buddha expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications. Wisdom illuminates the ultimate truth and does not abide [in it].
Turning [the merit] with the mind set on great compassion to save all beings is called the dedication toward the single characteristic of rescuing and protecting sentient beings.

Because one can rescue and protect sentient beings through the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and because by means of great wisdom one further leaves behind the notion of a "sentient being," one is able to pull them from suffering and deliver them by destroying the darkness of delusion.
Second is the indestructible dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*): having faith and orientation toward the Three Jewels and the precepts, one attains [this state].

1. Because of the four kinds of indestructible faith; 2. Because of learning the dedication of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, dedicating in accordance with what the Buddhas of the three periods of time have performed; 3.

Because of the dedication reaching all places, for the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of goodness brings benefit to boundless beings, universally benefiting the entire Dharma-realm, and because his practices and vows are limitless; 4. Because of the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit, as the mind is ever...
Sixth, because one’s bodily conduct while in meditative concentration benefits sentient beings without a moment’s pause,

one equally dedicates all roots of goodness toward the manifestation of the eight phases of attaining enlightenment and the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to transform and benefit living beings. Seventh,
one equally accords with all sentient beings through dedication by abiding in a non-discriminative mind, free from notions of enemy or friend, male or female, and so forth.

Therefore, one constantly uses this mind to practice transformation for the benefit of others; this is the eighth dedication, the dedication of the eight marks of reality (*aṣṭa-tattva-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*), because it is able to decisively investigate both principle and phenomena without error, and because its practice is authentic and does not transcend the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The ninth is the dedication of liberation free from bondage and attachment, because all practices and vows are universally cultivated, and one proceeds toward the state that is contrary to obstacles and defilements.
Because it is directed toward True Suchness (*tathatā*), these ten kinds of boundless dedications to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) enable one to act as a Dharma-master who guides sentient beings.
Being free from marks (*animitta*), these practices are as vast as the Dharma-realm;

by constantly dedicating these practices to the three spheres, one instructs beings through the Dharma so that they may harmonize their three karmas, control their six sense faculties, and eliminate the various afflictions and obstacles of sentient beings.
Within this tenth dedication, the four stages of application (*prayoga*) are subsumed under the collective name "Superior Sage" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
Because the great compassionate mind increases and excels, one universally dedicates all roots of goodness to rescue and protect suffering sentient beings.
Thus, the names of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* differ slightly from these; fearing prolixity, they are not detailed here.
Again, rising from his seat, he went to the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*).

There, because he delights in the mental pleasure of personally enjoying various things— such as the correct term "Delighting in Emanations" (*nirmāṇarati*) and the happiness of emanating pleasures for oneself— he returned to enjoy them.
It speaks of the ten dhyānas.

This is the fifth assembly, wherein the Buddha expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Dhyānas. In the Sanskrit language, *dhyāna* is sometimes called *dhyanana*, which is translated here as "meditative concentration" (*zhènglù*).
First is the pure dhyāna of those who have left the household life; second is the pure [dhyāna] of drawing near to virtuous friends.
1. Meditation on the three types of *āraṇya* dwellings; 2. Meditation on being free from frivolous discourse and worldly clamor;

3. Meditation on the pliancy of body and mind; 4. Meditation on wisdom that is tranquil toward all sounds; 5. Meditation on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*);

6. Meditation on being free from attachment to flavors and the defilements of afflictions (*kleśamala*); 7. Meditation on supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), clarity, and purity; 8. Meditation on internal knowledge of directions.

He then sported in supernormal powers and pure meditative concentrations; because he contemplated these ten dharma-gates with tranquility and focused his mind single-pointedly, they are called the Ten Meditations (*daśadhyāna*).
Thereupon, he rose from his seat and proceeded to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

The full name is the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin). It is called the tenth stage because [the bodhisattvas there] are able to exercise mastery over all five sensory objects emanated by others for their own enjoyment.
Thus, it is designated as the tenth stage.
This is the sixth assembly, the Dharma-gate of the Ten Bhūmis taught by the Buddha: 1. The First Bhūmi, the Joyous (*Pramuditā*):

Because one first attains the nature of the noble ones, fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness, and is able to benefit both oneself and others, one gives rise to great joy. 2. The Second Bhūmi, the Stainless (*Vimalā*):

Because one possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and remains far removed from the defilements of afflictions that could give rise to even subtle transgressions. 3. The Third Bhūmi, the Radiant (*Prabhākārī*).
The fourth is the Ground of Refulgent Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*), because these six dharmas of total retention (*dhāraṇī*) are able to emit the light of boundless sublime wisdom.

The fifth is the Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*), because by abiding in the most excellent factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the flames of wisdom burn away the fuel of afflictions, causing the flames of wisdom to increase.

The sixth is the Ground of Manifesting Reality (*Abhimukhī*), because the aspects of the two types of knowledge—of the ultimate and the conventional—are joined like the budding of teeth, making their union extremely difficult to achieve.

Sixth, because the most excellent non-conceptual *prajñā*, induced by the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*), is now present while abiding in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Seventh, because one reaches the limit of effortful application within the signless (*animitta*) while abiding in the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), thereby transcending the mundane and the paths of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Eighth, because non-conceptual wisdom flows spontaneously and continuously in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), such that the signs, functions, and afflictions do not [arise].

Because it is capable of movement, the ninth stage, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*), achieves the subtle and wondrous four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is able to preach the Dharma skillfully throughout the ten directions;
because the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā*), is like a great cloud of Dharma-wisdom that contains the waters of manifold virtues,
obscuring the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) that fills the space of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, they arrive at the first dhyāna—
namely, the first dhyāna—
and therein expound the ten vajras.
This is the seventh assembly, in which the Buddha expounds the ten Vajra Dharma-gates: (1) the mind that awakens to all phenomena;
(2) the mind that transforms and delivers sentient beings; (3) the mind that adorns the world-realm; (4) the mind that dedicates roots of goodness;
(5) the mind that serves the Great Master; (6) the mind that realizes all phenomena in reality; (7) the mind that extensively practices patience; (8) the mind of long duration...
The ninth is the mind of fulfilling one's own practice; the tenth is the mind of fulfilling the wishes of others.
Because these ten minds are firm and indestructible like a vajra, they are established under this name. Thus it is concluded.
Furthermore, one arrives at the second dhyāna,
the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration,
wherein ten types of patience (*kṣānti*) are taught.
This eighth assembly expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Patiences: first, the patience of the single sound; second, the patience of conformity;
third, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; fourth, the patience of being like an illusion; fifth, the patience of being like a mirage; sixth, the patience of being like a dream;

seventh, the patience of being like an echo; eighth, the patience of being like a shadow; ninth, the patience of being like a transformation; and tenth, the patience of being like space. These ten patiences are all realized through noble wisdom.
The name "patience" (kṣānti) is established because it signifies the sealing and understanding of all phenomena, the severing of defilements, and the realization of purity.
Furthermore, one reaches the third dhyāna,
which is the stage of sublime bliss free from joy.
The Ten Vows are now expounded;
this is the Dharma-gate of the Ten Vows from the Ninth Assembly:

(1) the vow for infinite roots of goodness, (2) the vow for the increase of dharma-love, (3) the vow for the increase of close attendance, (4) the vow for the attainment of great supernormal powers, and (5) the vow for the self-realization of correct wisdom.
The first vow is to cause others to understand; the second is to uphold the true Dharma; the third is to extensively benefit all sentient beings;
the fourth is to shoulder the burden of sentient beings; the fifth is to practice according to reality.
By the power of these ten great vows, one is able to sustain all gateways of practice without exception, and thus they are called "vows."
He further proceeded to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara within the fourth dhyāna.
In full, his name is Maheśvara-deva; this is translated as "Mahā-Īśvara Deva" (Great Sovereign God).
This deity is the king of the fourth dhyāna and the lord of the Sahā world-system; because he governs all the devas, he possesses great [power].
Because the palace is manifested through transformation in accordance with my person, it is said that my original source is the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*).
I am indeed Śākyamuni; the source of the preaching of the precepts flows from this Lotus Treasury World down to this place.
Vairocana Buddha,
the Teacher who is able to preach,
[preaches] the chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground which is being taught.
This is the dharma-gate that has been explained. The meaning of the "mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*) has already been clarified previously.
The remaining billions of Śākyamunis are likewise thus—without duality and without distinction—as described in the "Chapter on the Worthy Eon" (*Bhadrakalpika-parivarta*).
The preceding section of the sutra has clarified that within one great trichiliocosm,
ten billion Śākyamunis each expound the dharma-gates of the first ten assemblies; now, this section distinguishes the remaining cases by analogy,
showing that within each of the other nine hundred and ninety-nine great trichiliocosms, there are likewise ten billion Śākyamunis, each expounding the ten assemblies.
The Dharma gate is identical to the preceding matter; therefore, it is described thus.
At that time, it was when the initial manifestation of the transformed marks occurred.
Śākyamuni Buddha is precisely one of these Buddhas from the Zhou period;
he first appeared coming from the east of the Lotus Treasury World.
From the thousand-petaled lotus throne of the second level of the Buddha’s enjoyment for others,
he came to this Jambudvīpa continent and entered the palace of the Heavenly King.
This is the palace inhabited by the Heavenly King Vaśavartin, the sixth heaven of the desire realm.

Having explained the *Māra-parivarta-sūtra*, [it should be noted that] in the Sanskrit language, *māra* means "obstruction" or "disturbance," because it prevents virtuous deeds from being accomplished; thus, when the Buddha was about to achieve [enlightenment],...
The Way first subdues them, after which the Demon King undergoes transformation; among the sons and subjects of the demons, there are none who do not submit and follow.
This is the Transformation Buddha subduing the true Māras.

As for those who say that the true subjugation of Māras occurs when one attains the Self-Enjoyment Body upon the Great Jewel Flower King Throne, they refer to that [subjugation]; as for the subjugation of Māras beneath the tree, it refers to this [Transformation Buddha].
The manifested Buddha who appears as Māra is also a manifested Buddha; first he subdues Māra, and subsequently he manifests the eight phases of attaining enlightenment.
His descent into Jambudvīpa in the south is the manifestation of this small transformation-body Buddha in that state.
As for the country of Kāśī:
among the sixteen great kingdoms, five hundred medium-sized kingdoms, and one hundred thousand small kingdoms within Jambudvīpa,
this country of Kāśī is counted among the great kingdoms.
The mother’s name was Māyā,
which here means "Great Artifice. This Great Bodhisattva, having attained great wisdom and vows, realized that worldly phenomena are like illusions and vowed to become the mother of a Buddha.
My father’s name was Śuddhodana;
he was the father through whom Śākyamuni manifested his birth.
My name is Siddhārtha.

He was endowed with perfect virtue; in the Sanskrit language he is called Sarvārthasiddha, which means "One who has Accomplished All Aims," signifying the complete perfection of both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
At the age of seven, he left the household life.
This is the appearance of one who has left the household life.
He attained enlightenment at thirty;

according to the Hīnayāna, he left the household life at nineteen and attained enlightenment at thirty, while according to the Mahāyāna, he left the household life at twenty-nine and [attained enlightenment] at thirty.
Fifth, upon attaining enlightenment,
I was titled Śākyamuni;
this is translated as "The Able One" (Néng rén).
Muni: This is translated as "Silent Quiescence," because both the wisdom that realizes it and the principle realized by that wisdom are free from all clamor and affliction.
Thus, the Buddha [attained enlightenment] at the site of the path of quiescent extinction.
That is to say, beneath the Bodhi tree, upon the diamond throne—the place where the Buddha attained the Way—it is called the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Because arising and ceasing have been extinguished, it is termed "quiescent extinction.
He sat upon the Diamond Flower-Light King Throne.
When the Buddha sat upon the Vajrāsana and was about to preach the Dharma, he first rained down flowers and emitted light,
reaching as far as the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara. This is because,
having risen from the Vajrāsana, he transcended the intervening space and arrived at the palace of Īśvara.
Among these, that which was taught in the sequence of the ten dwelling places summarizes the dharma-gates of the ten assemblies by citing its two extremes.
At that time, the Buddha beheld the net-bannered staff of the Great Brahma Heaven Kings.
The kings of the four dhyānas, each leading their retinues and carrying precious banners, came to where the Buddha was.
They then spoke for his sake that the immeasurable worlds are like the mesh of a net;
the realms of sentient and non-sentient beings are each distinct from one another.
Each and every world is distinct and different in immeasurable ways;
within each great trichiliocosm, there are likewise ten billion sets of four great continents.
The gateway of the Buddha’s teaching is also like this.

The teachings spoken by the Buddha pervade the great trichiliocosm; because they can encompass all who possess the nature of the Mahāyāna, they properly cover the Mahāyāna while simultaneously covering the other vehicles.
I have now come to this world for this purpose.
"Śākyamuni" refers to the land he himself transformed.
"Eight thousand times. "Times" (fǎn) means returning;
it carries the sense of coming and going. When the roots [of beings] have matured, he comes to transform them; when the conditions for transformation are exhausted, he returns. Return after return.
The figure of eight thousand is merely an approximate large number and is not necessarily fixed.
This is for the sake of this Sahā world;
"Sahā" here is translated as "Endurance," meaning that within this world, amidst the extreme evils of the five turbidities, one must endure manifold sufferings.
He sat upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne,
attained Buddhahood upon taking his seat,
and proceeded as far as the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara.
He traveled back and forth, proclaiming the Dharma gates of the ten assemblies;
therein, among the entire great assembly,
there was a small portion of all [beings].
The brief exposition on the Mind-Ground is concluded.
This is according to the Mahāyāna precepts of the Mind-Ground.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] descended from the Palace of the Heavenly King to Jambudvīpa, beneath the Bodhi tree.
As previously stated in the *Māra-parivarta-sūtra*, from the time [the Buddha] descended until he attained Buddhahood,
this was for the sake of ordinary beings on the stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, it refers to the stage of ordinary beings.
For all sentient beings who are ordinary persons shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—
ordinary persons who, due to their lack of wisdom, are each mired in delusion—
I shall now speak from within the mind-ground of the original Vairocana Buddha, concerning the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
This precept flows forth from within the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*).
It is the single precept that is constantly recited;
for the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha has constantly recited and brought forth this one Great Vehicle precept.
Radiance. The essence of radiance is pure and free from the darkness of ignorance through the precepts. Vajra.
The nature of the precepts is firm adherence; they can shatter afflictions just as a vajra can destroy all things.
This is the "precious precept.
These precepts are as valuable as worldly treasures and are also counted among the seven noble riches.
This is the source of all Buddhas;
when the Buddhas of the ten directions first resolve their minds on enlightenment, they uphold this precept and thereby attain Buddhahood.
It is the source of all Bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all enter the higher stages by means of this precept.
It is the seed of the Buddha-nature;
the seeds of the four wisdoms are the very essence of the Buddha-body, and it is also through this precept that the seeds of the Buddha-nature gradually increase.
One attains Buddhahood by long-term realization of the principle.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
this refers to the entirety of the Buddha-nature of principle and a small portion of the Buddha-nature of practice.
All consciousnesses consist of form and mind:
"mind" refers to the seventh consciousness; "consciousness" refers to the preceding six; "form" refers to the five sense organs and their physical bases;
and "mind" refers to the eighth consciousness. Only when these are combined are they termed a "sentient being."
These are sentient beings and minds;
by distinguishing them from insentient objects, those who possess sentience may receive the precepts,
all of which enter into the Buddha-nature precepts.
This precept is the nature for attaining Buddhahood, not true suchness (*tathatā*). It is incorrect to say that one receives the Buddha-nature precept;
it must be understood as such. When, when.
