This is because the world is not uniform at all times;
there is always a cause.
This precept is the constant and determinate cause for attaining Buddhahood.
"Chang-chang" (When-when).
This refers to the fruit realized, which is realized stage by stage throughout the ten stages; hence it is called "Chang-chang.
Furthermore, because cause and effect are discussed in conjunction, it is called "Chang-chang."
The eternally abiding Dharma-body is so called because it is free from the transitions of the four marks; furthermore, by taking the observance of the three precepts as the cause,
one realizes the three Dharma-bodies which remain quiescent, continuous, and uninterrupted— therefore, it is termed "the ever-actualizing."
Thus, this refers collectively to the ten precepts and the ten *prātimokṣa* rules.
The ten fundamental types emerge from the world;
these precepts flow forth from within the self-realized portion of one's own enjoyment-body and pervade the entire world.
This is the Dharma-realm.
Precepts are themselves the Dharma; the Dharma is able to prevent what is non-Dharma.
This is that which all sentient beings of the three periods of time uphold upon their heads.
Wear this volume upon your head.
Receive and uphold it;
grasp its essential meaning and be careful not to let it be forgotten, but always keep it in mind.
"I shall now, for the sake of this great assembly—
the three classes of worthy ones prior to the stage of 'pointing to the ground'—
speak again."
It has been taught eight thousand times previously, and because it is taught now as well, it is called "repeated teaching. However, in comparison with the prose section (*gadya*),
there is no repetition regarding the principle of the ten precepts or the chapter on the ten inexhaustible treasuries of precepts (*daśākṣayakaraṇḍaka-śīla*).
Because it categorizes the ten precepts, it is called a "Chapter" (*varga*); because it encompasses and gives rise to meritorious qualities, it is called a "Treasury" (*piṭaka*).
These precepts give rise to the three bodies, the four wisdoms, and one hundred and forty kinds of uncommon qualities.
This is the fundamental source of the precepts for all sentient beings.
Because one attains ultimate Buddhahood by upholding these precepts and thereby brings forth the Five Vehicles,
these precepts are likewise their very source.
Inherently pure; the nature of precepts is free from defilement, fundamentally pure and without flaw.
I, now Vairocana—

I am Śākyamuni, who accords with worldly convention; the one currently indicated as the second level of the *parasaṃbhogakāya* Buddha is the Rūpaśānta Buddha, upon whom my minor transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) relies.
He sits upon a lotus pedestal;
this pedestal is the very seat formed by a thousand-petaled lotus.
Upon the circumference of these thousand petals...
Upon the thousand flower petals surrounding the flower throne,
there further appear one thousand Śākyamunis;
upon each individual petal appears a great transformation Śākyamuni Buddha one thousand *zhang* in height, manifesting by virtue of the thousand petals.
A thousand Śākyas.
One flower [covers] ten billion lands; in each land is one Śākya.
Before [each], there are a thousand-petaled flowers; upon each flower is a Great Śākya King. Within one great trichiliocosm, there are...
There are ten billion minor Śākyas, each ruling over one of the four great continents.
Each sits beneath a Bodhi tree and simultaneously attains the Way of Buddhahood,
all together beneath the Bodhi tree on the Vajra Seat within the Southern Continent of their respective lands, inside Central India.
At the same time each day, there were no before or after; they all attained the Way of Buddhahood simultaneously.
In this manner, he counted them on his fingers by the hundreds, thousands, and billions.
Because the transformation Buddhas manifest upon the body of Vairocana himself,
there are the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis.
The manifested Buddhas each receive the multitudes as numerous as motes of dust,
leading them by spiritual power to the assembly of the Three Sages.
All have come to my presence;

Śākyamuni and the assembly have all come to the abode of Samantabhadra. Having heard the Bodhicitta Precepts, whenever one beholds a manifested Samantabhadra, listen as I recite the Buddha’s precepts.
"Listen as I recite the precepts of all Buddhas," or "Śākyamuni, command the assembly to listen as I recite the precepts spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha.
Thus, the gate of ambrosia shall open.
Precepts are like nectar that removes the heat of afflictions; "opening" means to understand, for they dissolve all the bonds of the enemies of affliction.
At that time, [there were] hundreds of billions...
This was when he had previously gone to the abode of Śākyamuni to receive and complete the instruction on the precepts;
he then returned to his original site of enlightenment,
the place where all the Śākyas originally attained the Way.
Each sat beneath a Bodhi tree in their respective native lands under those trees,
reciting the precepts of my original teacher.
The Buddha attained the precepts through the precepts and thus took Śākyamuni as his original teacher;
furthermore, since Śākyamuni received and transmitted them from Vairocana, Śākyamuni recites the precepts that his original teacher, Vairocana, recited.
The ten grave precepts and forty-eight rules for recitation—
both the grave and light, as well as the fundamental prohibitions—
are precepts like the sun and the moon.
It manifests the virtue of the precepts; it can dispel the darkness of ignorance and eliminate the feverish afflictions of suffering.

Like a jeweled necklace, the jewel of the precepts adorns the body, causing one's good reputation to spread swiftly, inspiring humans and devas in the near term, and ultimately bringing about the sublime reward of Buddhahood in the distant future.
Furthermore, while ornaments such as necklaces may be beautiful when worn by the young and handsome, they are not beautiful when worn by the elderly or decrepit;
yet the ornament of the pearl of precepts is beautiful upon all alike.
Through this, the multitude of subtle-dust bodhisattvas attain perfect enlightenment.
This clarifies that throughout the entire extent of the Dharma-realm, there is not a single bodhisattva who attains Buddhahood without relying on these precepts.
This was recited by Rocana; I, too, recite it in this same way.
This cites the exhortation of the Sages to ordinary beings: if even the Buddhas recite this, how could ordinary beings not recite it? By upholding these precepts, one suddenly attains Buddhahood.
You, newly initiated bodhisattvas...
Śākyamuni addressed the Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness (śaikṣa), who are termed "new learners" relative to those on the grounds (bhūmi).

He exhorted them to receive and uphold the precepts as a practice for their own benefit; for if one does not personally practice them, one cannot exhort others, nor can one transform them through the shared practice of samānārthatā.
"Having received and upheld these precepts, transmit them to all sentient beings"—
these two lines clarify the practice of benefiting others.
Listen attentively as I recite them correctly.
"Right" means "proper. The Buddha commanded us to listen attentively as I recite these precepts; they are indeed most proper and essential.
Within the Buddha-dharma, the Vinaya-piṭaka is contained within the Tripiṭaka taught by the Buddha; this is the Vinaya-piṭaka.
*Prātimokṣa* is a designation for the *pratimokṣa-śīla* (the discipline of individual liberation), as will be explained below;
let the assembly believe it with a sincere mind.
He exhorts the assembly of the three types of worthy ones to believe his words, saying:
"You shall become Buddhas.
When he causes them to believe that they shall become Buddhas, they receive and uphold the precepts; therefore, they will certainly become Buddhas.
I am one who has already attained Buddhahood;
you should also believe that I became a Buddha after having received these precepts.
Always maintain such faith.

Because one constantly recollects [the precepts] in every thought-moment regarding what is to be accomplished and what has already been accomplished, and because the mind does not waver, the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) is fully perfected.

Through the two aforementioned factors of faith and ethical discipline, [the other perfections] are brought to fulfillment; conversely, this reveals that without faith, this ethical discipline cannot exist.
All those who possess a mind,
all those who possess the lineage of the Mahāyāna, and all those who possess the bodhicitta of the four wisdoms,
should all receive the Buddha-precepts.

"Comprehensive inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) means recording and gathering together. This refers to the fact that although there are four types of wisdom, those who possess the bodhicitta are collectively recorded and gathered within these Buddha-precepts.

Although one must first generate the resolve (*cittotpāda*) to be fit to receive the precepts, those who possess the spiritual disposition (*gotra*) must ultimately and inevitably generate this resolve.
When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts,
those who possess the Buddha-nature will, upon encountering superior conditions, certainly receive the Buddha’s precepts and immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Having already received the precepts, one enters the ocean of the Buddhas' Dharma; because this is subsumed within the stage of cause, it is not the stage of fruition.
This stage is identical to that of Great Enlightenment.

Having received the precepts with the initial resolve, one is immediately equal to the Great Awakened One; because the initial reception of the precepts is identical, it is said that their "status" is the same.
This does not mean they share the status of a Buddha.
They are truly the children of all Buddhas.
Because they receive the Buddha’s precepts and are born from the Buddha’s oral teachings, they succeed to the Buddha’s position and are called true sons.

The great assembly all reveres them as the Buddha tells the three groups of worthy ones: "By means of the precepts one attains Buddhahood; the essential requirement is a mind of profound gravity and deep reverence."
"You are worthy to hear and receive.

Listen with a sincere heart as I recite the Buddha's words and the Buddha's precepts; this is no small matter, but requires that you apply yourself to the utmost, with focused and careful attention, free from distraction."
At that time,
when the Buddha was about to manifest his transformative marks, Śākyamuni Buddha—
In each of the four great continents, there is one minor transformation Buddha.
This refers to the period immediately after [the Buddha] first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment;
it is the time when the transformation body has just completed its initial realization of the Way.
The Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa was first established when,

after attaining enlightenment, the Buddha first contemplated the causes for his own realization of Buddhahood and found them to be rooted in the observance of this precept; thus, as soon as he had attained it,
he established this precept, which differs from the Hīnayāna approach where the rule is only formulated upon the occurrence of an offense.
Be filial and obedient to one's parents.
Since parents possess the grace of giving birth and raising one, thereby providing the vessel for cultivating the Way, one must be filial and obedient.

For those currently living, provide them with offerings to the utmost of one's ability and encourage them to resolve upon the mind of the Way; for those who have passed away, let their precepts and virtues serve as a hidden support, ensuring they all attain liberation.
Suffering.
Regarding the teacher-monks:
it is because the teacher-monks possess the virtue of instructing and guiding that they enable one to realize the fruits of the Way; all of this is due to the instruction of one's original teacher.
The power of the Three Jewels has the grace of providing deliverance.
Filial piety and obedience are the dharma of the ultimate Way.
Because the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is that which is ultimately realized, one asks: "True Suchness is without marks; how can there be filial piety?
The answer is: "Now, to cause one to leave behind transgressions and harmonize with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is called filial piety."
Filial piety is called the precepts.

Since one must be filial toward one’s parents, teachers, monks, and the Three Jewels, one must necessarily cultivate goodness; because goodness does not contravene principle, it constitutes the observance of the precepts.
Therefore, filial piety is named the precepts.

It is also called "restraint" (*saṃvara*), which is a specific name for precepts (*śīla*). Restraint means to cause the good to be practiced and to cause evil to be ceased; the very essence of ceasing evil and cultivating good is precept itself.
The Buddha immediately emitted immeasurable light from his mouth.

Because the capacities of the assembly were vast, he emitted many rays of light; the emission of light from the mouth signifies that those who uphold the Mahāyāna precepts with determination will certainly attain Buddhahood.
At that time— that is,
at the very moment of the teaching and the moment the Buddha’s mouth emitted light—
there was an assembly of ten million billion followers.
Since all those who have a karmic connection with the Buddha and are capable of hearing the precepts have gathered here, this serves as a general indication of their total number.
As for "the bodhisattvas," this specifically refers to those among the aforementioned hundred trillion who practice the two benefits (self-benefit and benefit for others).
The eighteen Brahmās:
this refers collectively to the three heavens of the first dhyāna, the four heavens of the second dhyāna, and the nine heavens of the third dhyāna, with the Brahmā Kings as their leaders.
The six deva kings of the desire realm.
The six heavens of the desire realm together with their devaputras,
and the sixteen great kings;
for among humans in Jambudvīpa, within the five regions of India, there are sixteen great kings.
Join your palms and listen with a sincere heart.
As the great assembly above wishes to hear the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna, they have all joined their palms and listen with a sincere heart to receive it.
"Buddha" refers specifically to Śākyamuni; one recites the name of all Buddhas.
Throughout the two periods of past and present, extending throughout the ten directions and numbering more than the sands of the Ganges,
the Mahāyāna precepts are, in brief,
the ten grave rules and forty-eight minor rules; in detail, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Buddha told them:
"Regarding the words of the compilation, the Bodhisattvas said: 'From this day forward, every half-month, we shall [recite]...'"
Regarding "neither increasing nor decreasing": in terms of persons, it signifies being neither weary nor forgetful. As for the representation of the Dharma:

the dark fortnight (the waning moon) represents the gradual darkening from light until its exhaustion, which signifies that once the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is completed, evil karma is extinguished.

The bright fortnight (the waxing moon) represents the gradual movement from darkness toward light until its fullness, which signifies that once repentance is completed, wholesome karma becomes perfect and complete.
The Buddha himself recited it.
Having reflected upon this precept by which he himself attained Buddhahood, he now raises it for his own recitation with the intention of benefiting others by encouraging them to recite it as well.
The Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas:
the Buddhas of the three periods of time collectively uphold and recite them; because the Buddha recites the Buddha-precepts, he exhorts future generations, for the Dharma is itself the precepts.
All you bodhisattvas who have resolved to attain enlightenment—
even those who have only just first resolved—
should likewise recite it.

For example, he exhorts others as well: "The Buddha has already attained perfection and yet still recites these precepts; how can you, who have not yet attained perfection, refrain from reciting them?
This applies even up to those at the stage of the ten types of *caryā-pratipannaka*.
The lower grade of the worthy;
the tenth, the nurtured;
the middle grade of the worthy.
The ten vajras,
the supreme sages,
and the ten stages.
This refers to the "Extremely Joyful" and so forth;
all bodhisattvas also recite this,
which collectively points back to the aforementioned numbers.
Therefore, the subsequent arises because of the preceding; because it was born from the preceding Buddhas that we recite this together.
Thus, the light of the precepts.
The essence of the precepts is like light that issues from the mouth;
the Buddha’s own mouth has spoken forth these precepts.
It exists because it has conditions and is not without cause.

"Conditions" refers to the teacher, the disciple, the ritual implements, and the formal procedure; "cause" refers to the verbal recitation of the phrases and the internal reception of the textual meaning that perfumes the seeds within.
Because these internal and external causes and conditions are complete, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) is finally established; therefore, it is said as such.
Radiant, radiant.
Because the precepts are manifold and the matters they prohibit and prevent are numerous, they are called "radiant.
They are not blue, yellow, red, white, or black.
Precept has as its essence the capacity for growth— arising from wholesome thoughts and preventing evil— which resides upon the seeds of volition perfumed by it;
it is not the five types of manifest color, nor is it form.
Because it lacks material obstruction,
it is not mind;
it is not the eight consciousnesses, nor the mental factors associated with them.
It is not existent,
because the nature of the precepts is not defiled;
it is not non-existent.
Prevention and restraint are not non-existent;
yet they are not the dharmas of cause and effect.

The term "dharma" applies to both [types of] precepts, though they are not the primary causal dharmas. The primary causal dharmas are the seeds of the four wisdoms; the precepts are not the primary [causal dharmas].
The fruit-dharmas and the dharmas of the true fruit are the two types of *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis) realized therein.
This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas;

if one traces back the myriad streams and thousand currents to their origin, they all emerge from this fountainhead. Through the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood, one ultimately achieves perfection.
The Buddha has no basis other than this precept;
it is the root of practicing the bodhisattva path.
Among the six perfections and myriad practices, the merit of the two benefits cannot be perfected without transcending this precept.
This is the root of all the sons of the Buddha in this great assembly.
By citing those who have already attained Buddhahood as examples for Bodhisattvas, it exhorts the assembly of beginner sons of the Buddha— the three stages of worthiness—
to realize that they must cultivate these precepts if they wish to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, the great assembly of sons of the Buddha should receive, uphold, read, recite, and study this well.
This is an exhortation to receive and study it, intending that they grasp its textual meaning and maintain it without forgetting;
by reading and reciting its words and studying its meaning thoroughly from beginning to end, one will finally attain the Buddha-way.
"Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively.
This is the Buddha’s command for the true disciples present to listen with careful discernment.
"If there are those who receive the Buddha's precepts..."
"Individuals" (*pudgala*) refers to those who are capable of receiving the precepts: the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a conventional person;
kings, princes, the hundred officials and ministers; bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; the eighteen Brahmā heavens and the sons of the six heavens of desire;
commoners, eunuchs, male and female libertines, slaves, the eight classes of spirits and deities, *vajra*-deities, and animals.
This includes everything up to and including emanated beings;
in total, these twenty categories encompass kings, ministers, the fourfold assembly, devas, humans, and the eight classes of supernatural beings—
anyone who possesses the Mahāyāna lineage, has resolved for bodhicitta, and seeks the fruit of Buddhahood is included therein.
Those who merely understand the words of the Dharma Master,
grasp the meaning of the text, and clearly comprehend the underlying principles,
and who fully receive the precepts, are all called those of the foremost purity.

Because it is pure through the observance of the precepts and the severance of hindrances by those of the two vehicles, it is called "the foremost. This refers to the provisional entity that receives the precepts.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddhas, speaking to the assembly of those who were the immediate recipients of the teaching.
There are ten grave *pratimokṣa* rules;
this refers collectively to the number of the ten grave precepts.
If one who has received the bodhisattva precepts does not recite these precepts, [they are not considered to have truly received them].
This refers to those who do not recite it; such persons are not bodhisattvas.

For one to be a bodhisattva, they must necessarily practice the two benefits [of self and others]; if one does not recite it, their practice for self-benefit is deficient, and they will likewise be unable to transmit it to others.
If one fails to bestow benefit upon others, both forms of benefit are deficient; therefore, such a person is not a bodhisattva, nor are they a seed of Buddhahood.

The seeds of the four wisdoms of a Buddha grow through the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*); thus, one attains Buddhahood. If one does not recite [the precepts], one will not practice them; if one does not practice them, [one cannot attain realization].
Thus, the lineage of the Buddhas would not increase; since it does not increase, one cannot attain Buddhahood, and for that reason [the teaching] is abandoned.
I also recite in this same manner.
Following the example of the Buddha’s own study and recitation, I exhort others to recite as well. The benefit of reciting the precepts is for the purpose of attaining Buddhahood.
All bodhisattvas have studied, all bodhisattvas shall study, and all bodhisattvas are now studying [this].
Having cited examples above, this serves as an exhortation to uphold [the precepts] below.
Thus, the characteristics of the bodhisattva-prātimokṣa have been briefly explained.
"Characteristics" (xiàng) refers to the marks of observance and transgression, the states of perception and sensation, or the physical forms and appearances;
it means "to correspond" or "to accord."
It is so. It must be so. One should study.
In practicing and studying,
one maintains a respectful mind;
in the mind of receiving instruction, one constantly gives rise to reverence.
"Receive and uphold it.
Receive, maintain, and preserve it so that neither the words nor the meaning are forgotten.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Added by the Council.
O Son of the Buddha!
Śākyamuni, wishing to proclaim the Great Precepts, addressed those present who were ready to receive them, instructing a portion of them to resolve their minds upon the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva precepts arise from the True Dharma; as a son of the Buddha, one is destined to succeed to the rank of a Buddha.
If one kills oneself, or personally commits the act of killing, [one violates these precepts].
To instruct others to kill,
and furthermore, to personally teach and exhort others to carry out killing— these two forms of killing pertain to all three karmas; as for the mental karma,
it applies to both oneself and others.
"Expedient means of praising killing" refers to two types of praise: either praising the person who kills or praising the method used to kill;

each of these two further divides into two—praising [the act] before it is committed to incite the killing, and praising it after it has been committed to cause delight. Because such skillful speech is called "good," it is termed "expedient means."
Seeing [the act] being committed, they rejoice;
seeing the killing, they comply and give rise to a mind of joy and delight, never feeling any revulsion toward that killing,
and so forth.
The instances of killing are so numerous that they cannot all be fully enumerated here,
for there is killing by means of incantations and killing through the power of sorcery.
The causes for killing pertain to the three poisons: killing for the sake of profit has greed as its cause; killing to avenge a grudge has hatred as its cause;
and killing due to ignorance of the distinction between sin and merit has delusion as its cause.
The conditions for killing (*vadhapratyaya*). All factors that constitute the union of agent and object, as well as those upon which they depend, are termed "conditions" (*pratyaya*).
The act of killing (*vadhadharma*).
Killing according to established rules;
the karma of killing;
that which is one's primary occupation or by which one makes a living.
One must not intentionally kill any living being whatsoever,
including those counted among the class of sentient beings.
This single phrase is excellent as it applies universally to all the aforementioned instances of killing mentioned together.

"This Bodhisattva" refers to the disciple who has previously received the precepts; having already received the precepts, one who practices both self-benefit and the benefit of others is further designated as a Bodhisattva.
One should give rise to a mind of constant compassion; that is,
one should appropriately generate a mind that removes suffering and bestows happiness, remaining unchanging,
as well as a mind of filial piety.
In the practice of a bodhisattva, one regards all sentient beings as always being like one's own parents; throughout successive lifetimes, there is no birth that has not been received from them,
and thus one employs skillful means to rescue and protect them.

When seeing sentient beings undergoing the hardships of birth or those whose lives are at its end, the Bodhisattva does not begrudge their own body or life, but rescues and protects all sentient beings.
To refrain from killing any living being and to protect the Dharma through compassion constitutes the precept of benefiting others; it is the rescue of those in peril.
This concentration ought to produce merit;
yet it instead brings about self-harm.

"Instead" (fǎn) means "to reverse" (fān). Since one does not rescue others from suffering and hardship, one is already not a Bodhisattva; now, moreover, one reverses this by bringing harm upon oneself—hence the saying.
On the contrary,
they indulge their own minds;
"indulge" means to let their own minds run wild and commit limitless acts of killing.
To kill for the sake of gratification,
and upon having killed, to feel a sense of exhilaration that accords with one's desires and mind— this is [the nature of such an act].
This identifies the perpetrator of the act of killing.
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva;

it is the formal definition of the offense. Here, "bodhisattva" distinguishes this from the *pārājika* offenses of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). *Pārājika* is translated here as "defeat" (*tashengchu*). First:

There are three consequences for such a downfall: first, one loses all share in the fruits of the path; second, one no longer dwells in common with others and is no longer counted among the ranks of the Sangha;
third, after casting off this body, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
Since compassion is the very foundation of a Bodhisattva, to now violate it constitutes a grave offense.
"O Disciples of the Buddha," [the Master] addressed those present,
concerning both self-theft and causing others to steal.
The two types of stealing and the three karmas are the same as before.
Regarding the preliminary effort (*upakrama*) of stealing: taking what is not given through unjust means, such as deceiving with measures and scales, or failing to repay loans and so forth.
Stealing by means of incantations:
using spells to cause spirits or deities to take [an object], or using the power of incantations to delude people's minds so that they relinquish [their property] for one to take it, etc.;
these are the causes of stealing.
It is not for one’s own benefit, but simply because one does not wish others to take it, so as not to cause them poverty;
anger serves as the cause. Apart from greed and anger, taking what is not given due to delusion can be understood by analogy with greed.
The conditions for theft (*steya-pratyaya*): both the subject who steals and the object stolen, as well as all auxiliary factors such as breaking through a wall, are the conditions.
This is the nature of theft (*steya-dharma*).
The method of stealing;
the karma of stealing;
that is, actually committing it or making it one's livelihood.
...and so forth,
surpassing all other spirits and deities.
Objects within a shrine have an owner;
they belong solely to that owner.
Regarding the property of bandits:
one who seizes back what was plundered by bandits,
as well as all other forms of wealth and goods.
They steal everything that can be possessed by ghosts,
down to a single needle or a single blade of grass;
these few examples serve to illustrate many more.
One must not intentionally steal.
Merely having the intent to steal—excluding cases where it arises unintentionally—and forming a firm resolve constitutes the offense of theft.
Furthermore, for a bodhisattva...
To restate the preceding: a son of the Buddha who has received the precept against stealing should give rise to the Buddha-nature;
because his mind accords with the principle of the Buddha, he harbors no intention to steal.
With a heart of filial piety,
one regards all sentient beings as having once been one's own parents in past lives; thus, by acting with such filial devotion, one certainly does not commit theft.
Compassion. It should arise fundamentally from the intent to rescue others from suffering and grant them happiness;
one should constantly assist all beings in generating merit and attaining joy.
When a Son of the Buddha sees those without merit, he teaches them to generate merit; when they have generated merit, he exhorts them to sever evil and cultivate the precepts.
When a Son of the Buddha sees those without happiness, he constantly practices bestowing happiness, supporting them with his mind so that they may obtain it.
Yet, on the contrary, they steal the wealth and property of others.
Since a Bodhisattva ought to practice giving but now fails to do so, this constitutes one fault;
furthermore, because they steal the property of others, they incur a grave offense—hence the phrase "on the contrary."
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
If a son of the Buddha engages in sexual misconduct himself or instructs others to do so—
whether through the two [physical] or all three types of action.
This refers to all women,

as it is stated thus because there is no distinction made between those who are close or distant, or beautiful or ugly. This being a precept for men, the corresponding rule for women should state "all men."
One must not intentionally engage in sexual misconduct.
This excludes cases involving force or lack of intent,
which are causes for such conduct.
The three poisons serve as the causes: it can be known that the defilement of greed is not actually affection, but rather a desire to humiliate others, which is caused by hatred;
this is shown externally, while delusion serves as the cause internally. These are the conditions for sexual misconduct.
The conditions for this are the harmonious union of persons, obscured by affection and desire, and so forth.
As for the practice of sexual intercourse, it is naturally conducive to such states.
Regarding the karma of sexual misconduct:
they take the actual commission of such acts as their primary pursuit,
even extending to female animals, goddesses, and female ghosts or spirits.
There are ten classes of beings— beasts, spirits, ghosts, humans, devas, mothers, daughters, sisters, and other six types of relatives— as stated in the *Chao* [Sutra],
extending even to those who engage in sexual misconduct through improper paths.
Worldly conventions differ from the fundamental form; thus, [certain] places are considered non-Dharma for monks, and all such places are considered non-Dharma because they are unreasonable.
This is collectively termed "non-Dharma.
Yet, for a Bodhisattva...

Because one immediately receives the teaching according to the occasion and practices both self-benefit and the benefit of others, one is called a Bodhisattva; thus, one should bestow the pure Dharma.
One should give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, for all sentient beings have been one's parents throughout many lifetimes.
To deliver all sentient beings:
the bodhisattva’s vows of practice consist of the vow to rescue those in suffering and the resolve to deliver them,
purifying the Dharma and bestowing it upon others.
He taught them the precepts, yet they instead obstructed hearing, contemplation, and cultivation; though they attained perfect realization and were entirely pure,
possessing every rule and regulation, they were nonetheless called "pure dharmas," while they in turn gave rise to all manner of human lust.
A Bodhisattva should practice giving in accordance with the pure Dharma and teach others to sever sexual desire;

yet now, being unable to teach them, he ceases to be a Bodhisattva and instead gives rise to thoughts of and engages in sexual misconduct toward all people. Therefore, it is said, "he conversely acts contrary to this. This is the general heading.
They engage in sexual misconduct with animals, even with their mothers, daughters, sisters, or other members of the six classes of kin;
this is a specific reference.
They are devoid of a heart of compassion.
It is appropriate that one should grant them happiness and extract their suffering; yet, by now initiating defiled conduct that causes them to fall, one lacks compassion.
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha utters false speech themselves, teaches others to utter false speech,
or— whether through speech and mind alone, or actually involving the body— deceitfully manifests different intentions or feigns joy and anger as skillful means to speak falsely.
Originally seeking wealth, they falsely proclaim misfortunes and blessings.
This false speech has the three poisons as its cause; for the sake of fame and profit, they agitate the hearts of others, remaining ignorant of sin and merit.
The conditions for false speech:
these are the factors upon which false speech depends.
The nature of false speech.
Adhering to rituals;
the karma of false speech;
and seeking profit through one's primary activities, meritorious works, or means of livelihood.
Furthermore, they do not see what they claim to see, nor do they see what they claim not to see;
they likewise hear, perceive, and know the eight types of false speech.
This constitutes verbal falsehood of body and mind.

The body conceives the thought of false speech while the mind constitutes the characteristic of false speech; furthermore, the body serves as the condition for false speech while the mind serves as its cause.
When cause and condition are explained together, they are all termed "false speech."
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva—
referring to the aforementioned son of the Buddha who has received the precepts and practices both self-benefit and benefit for others—
constantly generates right speech.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing constitute the eightfold right speech.
Right view:
since speech is not deviant, it invariably gives rise to right view.
It also gives rise to correct speech and correct view in all sentient beings;
with both self and others being correct, the two benefits are simultaneously accomplished,
and yet it further causes all sentient beings to arise.
One who possesses the correct capacity within oneself is then able to transform others; now, however, he acts contrary to this, and thus deserves his punishment.
This is "false speech," the speech of the eightfold wrong path.
Wrong view,
wrong and deluded seeking,
and wrong action.
Because one perceives what is wrong and because the three karmas are not upright, one gives rise to wrong karma;
this constitutes a pārājika offense for a bodhisattva.
O disciples of the Buddha!
The Buddha told the interlocutor, who was correctly addressing the issue of frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*): "If that is so, why does the scriptural passage discuss only the selling of liquor?

He replied: "In this case, we follow the sequence of the ten courses of action (*daśa-karmapatha*), where [the selling of liquor] properly falls under frivolous speech. Selling liquor is the cause of frivolous speech;
the scripture cites the cause to reveal the effect."
Selling alcohol oneself and teaching others to sell alcohol—
these two pertain to all three types of karma.
These constitute the cause of selling alcohol.
It also extends to the three poisons.
Regarding the conditions for selling alcohol:
the yeast, rice, and dregs.
The method of selling alcohol,
namely brewing and so forth;
the occupation of selling alcohol.
For the sake of obtaining livelihood and the means of subsistence from others, one generates much frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*) due to these causes and conditions.
No kind of intoxicant whatsoever may be sold.
The term "all [intoxicants]" encompasses many varieties, including rice wine, fruit wine, medicinal wine, as well as those that are dry or moist, clear or turbid.
"This is alcohol" refers to all the aforementioned types of alcohol that serve as the causal conditions for the arising of offenses.

One immediately incurs the offense of frivolous speech; furthermore, the arising of the three karmas, the ten transgressions, and the thirty-six faults—all these causes and conditions for committing offenses originate from this alcohol.
Yet, a Bodhisattva ought to engender the wisdom of clarity and penetration in all sentient beings.
Since it is called the Bodhisattva’s fundamental teaching for benefiting sentient beings, which employs the wisdoms of hearing, contemplation,
and cultivation of the Three Vehicles to give rise to the outflow-free wisdom of clear realization and decisive penetration,
how can one instead give rise to further birth?
To practice with wisdom while failing to guide sentient beings through that wisdom is already a fault;
because it gives rise to inverted views, it constitutes a grave offense.
For all sentient beings, such an inverted mind constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

If a disciple of the Buddha, when properly restraining harsh speech, asks: "What is the fault in speaking of another's transgressions? The answer is: To speak of the transgressions of a good person is necessarily the act of an evil person;
since an evil person has no virtuous words, to speak of the transgressions of a good person is itself harsh speech.
This passage describes the transgressions of lay and ordained bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs;

it pertains generally to the three types of action (trikarma), involving the internal mind as well as the outward movements of hands and body, and specifically belongs to the Mahāyāna while generally explaining the faults of the five vehicles.
It refers to teaching others to speak of their transgressions;
having spoken of one's own faults, one further uses skillful speech to instruct others to speak of the faults of those who practice the five vehicles.
The causes of transgressions:
the three poisons serve as the cause; speaking of faults for the sake of fame and profit has greed as its cause; desiring to harm others without seeking one's own benefit has hatred as its cause;
and being deluded regarding the retribution of good and evil has ignorance as its cause.
The conditions for transgression:
name, status, power, and long-standing evil habits from past lives;
and the phenomena of transgression.
Using skillful speech and rhetoric, they transgress the rules and commit sinful deeds;
their primary concern in their formal discourse is the act of speaking ill of others.
Yet when Bodhisattvas,
O Son of the Buddha, hear evil teachings, they give rise to goodness;
even upon hearing of externalists and wicked people, they do so.
Those outside the Buddha-dharma constantly harbor arrogance and envy, speaking of the faults within the Buddha-dharma;
they do so toward both the wicked people of the Two Vehicles and the Buddha-dharma itself.
Although the Two Vehicles are disciples of the Buddha, their respective paths—the Great and Small Vehicles—differ, and they likewise speak of the faults of the Mahāyāna.

To claim within the Buddha-dharma that there is what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya is impossible, for that which is called the Buddha-dharma can never be non-Dharma or non-Vinaya; yet now, one falsely asserts such things of the Buddha-dharma.
One should always give rise to a heart of compassion [toward such persons].
When a bodhisattva sees superior persons speaking ill of others and recognizes that the offense of slander is profound, they constantly give rise to a heart of compassion and pity,
and they teach and transform those wicked people.
Beholding all sentient beings as always being like an only son, the bodhisattva does not abandon even the wicked, but continues to teach and transform them.
To cause others to give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna;
to lead non-Buddhists to have faith in and turn toward the Buddha-dharma;

and to cause those following the three vehicles to turn their faith toward the Mahāyāna—if a bodhisattva, on the contrary, speaks of faults and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma himself, this constitutes a bodhisattva *pārājika* offense.

When a Bodhisattva, out of compassion, stops others from slandering [the Dharma] so as to benefit sentient beings and inspire faith in them, yet continues to slander even after being stopped, they are no longer a Bodhisattva;
because they then speak for themselves, it is said that they incur an offense by speaking against [the truth] on their own account.
If a disciple of the Buddha is strictly forbidden from double-tongued speech, why do the sutras speak of "self-praise and disparaging others"? The answer is that while these transgressions are many—
namely self-praise, disparaging others, double-tongued speech, divisive talk, and inciting strife between two parties— the sutras consolidate them into a single name.
Self-praise;
praising one's own virtues and disparaging others.
To slander the faults of others, or to falsely defame them when they have no faults—"to slander" means to break, to destroy;
it destroys the goodness of others, involving not only speech and mind but also the body, such as pointing with the hand, scolding, or reviling.
To fail to praise those who deserve praise, to praise those who should be slandered, or to both praise and slander indiscriminately—these merely conceal the virtues of others.
To praise oneself is to disparage others;
one also teaches others to praise themselves and disparage others,
instructing them to act as I do in disparaging and praising.

The cause for disparaging others consists of the three poisons. Specifically, self-praise combined with greed and anger serves to manifest the faults of others; disparaging others combined with greed serves to manifest one's own virtues.
Delusion is necessarily present as an auxiliary factor. Furthermore, praise and disparagement driven by fame and profit have greed as their cause.
Harming others, praising oneself, and disparaging others have hatred as their cause; if there were no delusion, one would certainly not praise or disparage.
Disparaging others is a condition, for those who praise or disparage must rely upon conditions.

To disparage another’s Dharma or another’s karma—this should be explained according to the previous interpretation. Even if there were faults or evils, a bodhisattva, for the sake of protecting their own roots of goodness and life, should not disparage or praise [others];
how much less so when [the faults] do not actually exist?
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should undergo all forms of praise and humiliation on behalf of all sentient beings;
without discriminating between enemies and kin, just as there are those who receive such insults, the bodhisattva should cause them to undergo that humiliation in their stead.
Evil deeds turn upon oneself.
Whatever actions cause harm or affliction to sentient beings are collectively termed "evil"; that which is evil is also loathsome, and such evil deeds are drawn back toward one's own person.
To give good things to others.
Whatever matters are pleasing to one's own heart and mind, if one relinquishes them to others, this is giving good and receiving good.
If, however, one extols one's own virtues, [this is not so].
It is appropriate to practice in secret, concealing one's own virtues while proclaiming the goodness of others; failing to do so is not a transgression.
However, to now personally extol one's own virtues is truly not the way of a Bodhisattva.
To conceal the good deeds of others and cause them to suffer defamation constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva.

If a Bodhisattva does not conceal their own acts of giving but only reveals their own virtues, they have already failed; to further conceal the good deeds of others increases their transgression, and thus they shall incur a grave offense.
O Sons of the Buddha!

Question: In the *Sūtra on the Proper Regulation of Greed*, why is it said that stinginess (*mātsarya*) is the answer? Answer: When the mind of greed is characterized by parsimony and does not relinquish, this is precisely the mind of stinginess;
or, because stinginess increases the sequence of the ten karmic paths, it is indeed greed itself.
Being stingy oneself;
through mental action,
teaching others to be stingy.
Vocal karma, as well as bodily and mental actions, involves the concealment and protection of objects; thus it pertains to all three types of karma.

Regarding the causes of stinginess (*mātsarya*): the three poisons serve as its cause. Retaining things for oneself and not giving them away has greed (*lobha*) as its cause; hating others and not relinquishing [possessions] has hatred (*dveṣa*) as its cause; and not [giving] has delusion (*moha*) as its cause.
One knows that the retribution for sins and merits has ignorance as its cause and stinginess as its condition.
Whether due to one's own current lack, past resentment, or things not being to one's liking, it is for these reasons that one makes chests sturdy and locks them with hard, tight bolts.
Hiding things away in deep burial is entirely due to the conditions provided by a stingy mind.
To be stingy with the Dharma is to guard and cherish it for one's own convenience.
The karma of stinginess is firm and not relinquished, or one is preoccupied with establishing a household livelihood;
yet, for a bodhisattva...
The text specifies that one should respond to those who are appropriate vessels by relieving their poverty and suffering;
whenever one sees any impoverished person coming to beg,
they are the sentient beings to be saved.
According to what each person requires,
he grants everything to all beggars, bestowing it upon them in accordance with their needs and desires.
Although he provides whatever is desired, even up to great and unspeakable pleasures,
if a bodhisattva— with a malicious mind, a mind of anger,
or because of past enmity— does not relinquish his anger, or fails to give for the sake of livelihood out of greed, this constitutes a malicious mind of hatred.
That person does not practice giving because anger constitutes an evil mind that is ignorant of the merit of giving; they do not practice giving because delusion constitutes an evil mind.
This extends to not giving even a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass.

Within the context of material giving, a small amount is cited by way of analogy to illustrate the great; thus it says, "even down to a needle or a blade of grass"—if one does not give even such a meager thing, how much less could one give more?
Furthermore, when there are those who seek the Dharma, one does not explain for them even a single word, a single verse, or a portion of the Dharma as small as a mote of dust.
This Dharma-giving consists of giving even a few verses and a small amount of the Dharma; since one is already stingy with so little, how could one possibly relinquish much?
To instead respond with verbal abuse and insults is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

A Bodhisattva ought to practice giving, yet now that they do not give, they are already termed "greatly stingy"; furthermore, because they respond with double the abuse and insults, this constitutes a grave transgression.
If a Buddha’s disciple is angry themselves and teaches others to be angry...
Second, the three types of action that harbor malice: one’s own mental action of anger, inciting others through verbal action, and displaying an angry countenance.
Regarding the causes of anger:

while the "three poisons" serve as the general cause, specifically regarding anger, it refers to both the seeds and the manifest states; furthermore, greed for fame, profit, and the like serves as its cause.
Disobedience and compliance, as well as external delusion, serve as the causes;
hatred serves as the condition.
When one encounters objects such as fame, profit, enemies, or the gathering of adversaries, hatred arises.
The phenomenon of anger;
the methods for generating anger;
and the karmic effects of anger.
The manifestation of anger and malice takes this as its function;
however, a bodhisattva should give rise to roots of goodness within all sentient beings,

causing those of the five castes to all resolve their minds to cultivate the practices of their respective vehicles and realize the fruits of their respective vehicles— these being the three roots of goodness.
This refers to non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, or the roots of goodness of the Three Vehicles;
these are matters free from contention.
The essence of the aforementioned roots of goodness is capable of harmonizing disputes and litigation.
Constantly give rise to a mind of compassion.
For a bodhisattva who benefits sentient beings, compassion is the foundation.
[Cultivate] a mind of filial piety and obedience.
Toward elders, one is like a parent; toward juniors, one is like a younger brother or sister. Above, one is filial;
below, one is compliant. Between enemies and kin, there is no distinction.

Yet, conversely, among all sentient beings, one gives rise to anger and malice, making no distinction between the honorable and the lowly, the noble and the base, the holy and the ordinary, nor between the good and the virtuous, but acts only with hatred.
It is because of anger that it is said thus.

Even toward non-sentient things, when the mind of hatred is fierce, encountering anything that offends one's feelings gives rise to the root of resentment; this is hatred directed toward the insentient.
They revile and insult them with harsh speech,
failing to restrain their verbal karma; furthermore,
they strike them with their hands and attack them with knives and staves.
The bodily karma is not patient;
the mental [karma] still does not cease.
When the mental karma is not patient—and thus all three types of karma are not patient—anger immediately arises.
When the person who previously provoked anger seeks repentance,
and before the Bodhisattva’s mind of resentment has subsided, that person comes to the Bodhisattva to confess their transgression and offers sincere words of apology and thanks.
When the person who was previously angry sees that the Bodhisattva’s mind is not violent or arrogant, they address him with kind words, saying:
"This was my fault; please do not hold me in contempt.
Yet, if their anger is still not resolved, [the Bodhisattva continues].
If a bodhisattva’s mind of anger has not yet been dissipated,
this constitutes a pārājika offense for that bodhisattva.
Even if they have properly performed repentance, because the anger still persists, it shall be considered a grave offense.
If, O sons of the Buddha, one were to properly restrain delusion by asking, "For what reason does the Sūtra say that slandering the Triple Gem and so forth? the answer is:
it is because, according to the sequence of the ten karmic paths, this is delusion; with delusion as the cause, the fruit of false views arises, whereby one slanders the Triple Gem.
They slander the Triple Gem themselves.

These sons of the Buddha, while relying upon the protection of the Triple Gem to seek the Way and advance in their practice, personally give rise to slander toward the Triple Gem and teach others to slander the Triple Gem.
To slander [the Dharma] oneself is an error; to further teach others to slander the Way is a transgression even more grave. These two types of slander also encompass the three karmas.

Regarding the causes of slander: the causes are likewise the three poisons. To slander for the sake of fame and profit has greed as its cause; to slander out of harboring resentment has hatred as its cause; and ignorance is [the cause of the third].
Delusion is the cause;
slander is the condition.
Status and rank—whether already attained or not yet attained—and resentment and so forth are all that which serves as the supporting conditions.
Slandering the Dharma;
being skillful in speech and reasoning;
and the karma of slandering.
They practice such deeds or take them as their primary pursuit;
yet when a Bodhisattva observes these non-Buddhists,
he considers all those who hold views outside the True Dharma to be collectively termed "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika).
As for "evil persons," this refers generally to all those who commit the ten non-virtuous actions;
even a single word of slander against the Buddha's voice [is sufficient].
That is to say, when a son of the Buddha hears heretics and evil persons slandering the words of the Buddha,
his heart is filled with such piercing pain that it is as if three hundred spears were piercing his heart.
Upon seeing or hearing external slander, the pain in his heart is as acute as being pierced by spears.
How much more so when one slanders with one's own mouth;
how much more so when one slanders both with mouth and body—how could this not be utterly painful?
Thus, one fails to give rise to faith.
They do not believe that the Three Jewels are the supreme field of merit for sentient beings;
they lack a heart of filial piety.
They do not believe that the Three Jewels are the supramundane Dharma-body parents, or else, due to slandering the Three Jewels, the calamity extends to their own parents.
Mother, if one instead assists evil people and those with false views to slander [the Dharma], this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
To assist the wicked in slandering is to incur a grave transgression; whereas to slander oneself, lack faith, or be unfilial is a lesser offense than assisting the wicked and the heterodox.
It is also manifold.
O virtuous practitioners who have well studied!
The Buddha addressed all the sons of the Buddha who are well able to cultivate and study the ten precepts as described above.
These are the ten *pratimokṣa* precepts of this bodhisattva;
they refer to the ten kinds of individual liberation vows (*prātimokṣa-śīla*).
One should train in them and must not transgress even a single one of them, even to the extent of a speck of dust.
The Buddha exhorted them that regarding each of the ten precepts, they must not violate even as much as a speck of dust; if this is so for a small amount, how much more so for a great deal?
How much more so, then, for violating all ten precepts in their entirety?
One must not violate even a small fraction of the minor precepts, let alone violate them in their entirety;
violating one or two constitutes an obstruction.
If there are those who have violated them, they shall be formally identified among those present who have transgressed these ten precepts.
One cannot manifest the arousal of the bodhicitta in this present body.
Since the arousal of the bodhicitta must rely upon the observance of the precepts, it will not arise here because of the deficiency of that condition due to the violation of the precepts;
furthermore, one loses the status of a king and the status of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
Just as one who wishes to succeed to the royal throne in a future life must first receive the bodhisattva precepts in this life— if they violate those precepts,
the cause for the fruit of the throne is lost;
likewise, the status of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī is also lost.

This is stated with reference to the renunciant bodhisattva; for the two groups of renunciants do not rely on outward appearance, but must possess the great precepts of a renunciant bodhisattva to truly constitute this status.
Furthermore, one loses the ten stages of initial departure,
which constitute the lower level of the stage of worthiness (*kṣānti*).
Then there are the ten stages of nurturing.
The ten stages of the Diamond-like Samādhi constitute the rank of the intermediate sages.
The ten Bhūmis constitute the rank of the superior sages.
The ten stages,
such as the Stage of Supreme Joy;
the Buddha-nature.
The principle realized and the wisdom that realizes it constitute the essence of the Buddha,
the eternally abiding sublime fruit;
they are the two types of transformation (āśraya-parāvṛtti), the immovable and uninterrupted, subtle and wondrous fruition.
Everything is lost.
This summarizes the aforementioned results:
one falls into the three evil realms.
The *Xiashan jing* (Sūtra on Lower Goodness) states that each of the ten courses of karmic action can be committed through three grades of mind:

namely, those committed with a superior grade of mind lead to rebirth in hell; those with a middling grade lead to rebirth as a hungry ghost; and those with an inferior grade lead to rebirth as an animal.
For two or three kalpas,
amidst the intermediate kalpas of increase and decrease,
they do not hear of their parents.
Although those born by transformation in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals possess an increase in delusion, they are no different from those who do not [hear] them—
or it may simply be because these are words that can only be disparaged— thus it is said that they have never heard the names of the Triple Gem.

The three miserable realms are places of suffering; alternatively, even if one is born among humans due to past evil karma, one may not encounter the Triple Gem, and thus it is said that "one has not heard its name.
For this reason, one must not commit any of these transgressions individually.
"Because," as stated above, "the offense of violating the precepts leads to rebirth in the three evil realms,
you must not violate even a single precept one by one. You, all you bodhisattvas..."
Having spoken these ten grave precepts, the Buddha addressed the assembly gathered at the Three Jewels:
"Those who have now studied, those who shall study, and those who have already studied—
since even the Bodhisattvas of the three periods who have already entered this stage still practice and train, how can you, O great assembly, [afford to neglect them]?"
One should not train otherwise.
These ten precepts are what one ought to train in;
this citation indicates that these ten precepts are precisely what should be studied.
One should uphold it with a reverent mind.

Since the precepts are the very foundation of the Buddha, one ought to honor, revere, and serve them; one must maintain them with a diligent heart and commit them to memory so as not to let them fall into ruin or be lost.
The eighty thousand chapters on majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) shall be explained in detail.
This sutra originally consisted of one hundred and twelve fascicles and sixty-one chapters;

now, this single chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi-dharmamukha*) in two fascicles has been extracted from that great compendium. Therefore, it is indicated that the extensive text is to be found as explained in that original teaching.
Also. Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra, Volume One;
Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra, Volume Two.
The Buddha told them:
"This is the addition to the compilation;
all the bodhisattvas shall speak."
These are indeed the words of the Buddha.
Having thus finished explaining the ten *pātimokkha* rules, this concludes the preceding section.
"O sons of the Buddha, these ten *pārājika* dharmas have already been explained," and so forth, up to the ten [rules] concerning the arrogant teachers.

The monastic community constantly hears the ten minor defilements regarding entering armies and so forth; the monastic community constantly hears the ten minor defilements regarding requiting resentment and so forth;
the monastic community constantly hears the nine minor defilements regarding rescuing those in peril and so forth;
and the monastic community constantly hears the nine minor defilements regarding teaching and admonishing and so forth.
The forty-eight minor precepts shall now be explained;
they follow immediately in the subsequent text.
The Buddha said:
These are the words of Śākyamuni, the Lord of Transformation.
"O Son of the Buddha":
the Buddha addresses the assembly being transformed at the stage of the Three Worthies (trayaḥ-puṇya-kṣetra), calling them "Sons of the Buddha" because they receive and uphold the Buddha’s words.
When one desires to receive the position of a king,
and intends to receive the position of a king in a future life, one must first, in this present life, diligently uphold the pure bodhisattva precepts.
When assuming the rank of a Wheel-Turning King,
even the four types of wheel-turning kings do not depart from this precept as their cause.
Likewise when officials of the hundred ranks receive their positions.
Because the civil and military officials, generals, and ministers are not uniform, they are called the "hundred officials" (bai guan); this is also based on this precept.
One should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
This phrase applies across the three preceding sections.
All ghosts and spirits protect the person of the king and the persons of his officials.
Because this precept serves as the cause for attaining the noble positions of kings and ministers, it brings about the protection of all ghosts and spirits;
thus, they rescue one from calamities and provide constant guardianship.
All Buddhas rejoice;
because by receiving these precepts one shall attain Buddhahood and act in accordance with the Buddhas' intentions, they rejoice.
It is not only the Buddhas who rejoice; bodhisattvas, devas, humans, non-humans, and others—all without exception rejoice.
Having already received the precepts,
once the reception of the precepts from the preceptor is completed,
one gives rise to a heart of filial obedience.
The Triple Gem is the supramundane parent; one should give rise to a heart of reverence, filial piety, obedience, and compliance, receiving and following their instructions.
Having received the precepts, one must necessarily maintain a mind of solemnity and respectfully protect them.
He saw the Elder,
the foremost among the assembly,
his preceptor.

This term, *upādhyāya*, means "one who has been approached for study," referring to the preceptor who provides instruction and receives the recitation of the Dharma; it is the one from whom one receives the precepts.
This term, *ācārya*, means "preceptor of conduct" (*vinaya-ācārya*).
A senior fellow student:
one who studies under the same teacher, is senior in age among those studying together,
and shares the same views.
They share the same aspiration for the Buddha-way,
practice together,
and jointly cultivate the deeds of self-benefit and benefiting others.
This refers back to what was stated above:
one should rise to welcome them, pay homage, and inquire after their well-being.
Regarding the five aforementioned classes of people who come from outside, one may welcome them; once they have stayed for two nights and depart, one must prostrate to them.
When they are ill, one must go to inquire after their health; when they are at ease, one should also inquire after their well-being morning and evening with reverence.
Yet the Bodhisattva,
pointing back to those sons of the Buddha who had previously received the precepts,
instead gave rise to a mind of arrogance.
One should have given rise to humility and reverence, yet instead one gives rise to self-reliance and a deluded mind;
one should have understood that the precepts worthy of honor are obtained from a teacher, yet instead one gives rise to a deluded mind and fails to know this.
Arrogance:
one should act with reverence toward those worthy of respect, yet instead gives rise to contempt for others.
Anger: [the mind of] hatred.
Being obscured by delusion, one is ignorant of those who should be honored;
consequently, one does not rise to welcome them or prostrate,
due to the influence of that prior delusion.
In each case, he made offerings that were not in accordance with the Dharma;
out of anger and pride,
he even sold his own body.

This indicates that while the matter is of the utmost gravity, it is not necessarily entirely impossible; if there were no material offerings available, one could sell oneself, or even offer one's kingdom,
cities, men, and women,
following the same principle.
The seven treasures refer to gold,
silver, and so forth. The hundred things refers to all manner of objects.
However, regarding the objects worthy of offering, they are collectively counted as one hundred in total,
which are then presented and provided as offerings.
He gives it to them;
indeed, he offers all his possessions and provides for them with complete and perfect facilities. If he were not to do so...
If one acts in such a manner and fails to provide offerings as described above, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the classification of this offense:

it is called "minor" in contrast to a grave offense; it is called a "defilement" because it pollutes pure conduct; and it is called an "offense" because it destroys virtue. As for "destroying," it means to ruin what is wholesome.
The Dharma does not arise for those who enter evil destinies by means of destruction.
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally drinks alcohol—
"intentionally" meaning constantly, specifically, that is, with a focused mind, habitually and perpetually drinking it— [he commits an offense].
Furthermore, the faults arising from alcohol are immeasurable.

This is shown precisely as the fault of drinking it: it is the gateway to manifold calamities, the root of afflictions, the cause for the dissipation of wealth, and the spread of ill repute, and so forth;
hence it is said to be "immeasurable."
If one passes a vessel of wine with one's own hand to another person so that they may drink it—
meaning that although one does not drink it oneself, one personally hands the wine over and instructs another to drink—
it results in being born without hands for five hundred lifetimes.
This is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*);
how much more so when one drinks it oneself?
This indicates that the transgression of drinking it oneself is greater than the former.
Furthermore, one must not teach any person or any sentient being to drink alcohol.
To teach others to drink alcohol inevitably harms their virtue and gives rise to evil in them; it is not the practice of a Bodhisattva.
If one intentionally drinks [alcohol] oneself or teaches others to drink it, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
This rule concludes the offenses incurred by both drinking for oneself and teaching others to drink.
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat...
Since you are called a Buddha’s disciple, compassion is your fundamental principle; you must not intentionally eat the flesh of sentient beings.
No meat whatsoever may be eaten.
That which is specifically prohibited and severed refers only to those types of meat that necessarily involve the taking of life.
It severs the seeds of the nature of great compassion.
This correctly demonstrates that the fault of eating meat arises because great compassion is the cause; one should therefore be called a Buddha-to-be.
The nature of great compassion is itself the seed, or it is by being nurtured through compassion that the inherently existing seed of bodhi gradually comes to fruition.
The Buddha is the seed of the nature of great compassion;
yet all sentient beings see him and depart.

The fulfillment of a Bodhisattva’s practice lies entirely in transforming and giving birth to beings; once beings have departed, one loses the external conditions for transformation, and it is certain that [the work] will not be accomplished.
The Buddha said:
"For this reason,
because of the preceding passage, and because there are faults in eating meat as previously mentioned."
All bodhisattvas—
whether lay or ordained, male or female—
must not eat the flesh of any sentient being.
One must not eat any kind of pure meat whatsoever.
Eating meat incurs immeasurable sins,
further shortening one's lifespan and causing many illnesses.
If one intentionally eats them, one commits a minor offense.
O disciples of the Buddha,
you must not consume fermented grain liquors or meat.
Regarding the consumption of the five pungent roots:
this is a general prohibition against eating them,
specifically garlic and leeks.
These are the mountain onion,
the *ci* onion,
and the *hu* onion.
Garlic, home-grown onions,
and asafoetida.
This encompasses all pungent, foul-smelling, and unclean substances.
These five kinds refer back to and specify the aforementioned five pungent herbs (*pañca-garadala*).
Among all foods, one must not eat these;
it is strictly enjoined that none of these five pungent herbs (pañca-garaka) may be consumed.
If one should intentionally eat them, one commits a minor offense (laghu-pāpaka).
If a Buddha’s disciple sees any sentient being,
with a mind intent on benefiting others, they should universally rescue and deliver them without partiality; if such beings have violated the precepts—
whether the eight, five, or ten precepts, or have breached their prohibitions— they should all be instructed to repent.
"Prohibitions" (*jin*) are also "precepts" (*jie*). The precepts of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are able to restrain the fourfold assembly from the ten evil deeds of the three karmas;
because one now violates these precepts, it is called "breaking the prohibitions.
This includes the seven heinous offenses (*saptātyaya*), the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakaṣṭa*), and all other transgressions against the precepts.
To summarize what has been said above:
one should instruct them in repentance.
For every single offense committed, one ought to provide instruction to them so that they may perform repentance.
Furthermore, for a bodhisattva not to teach repentance is a direct violation of the Buddha’s regulations for communal residence.
The second fault is that one who does not repent while living together must necessarily share in evil.
To share in the Sangha’s offerings while persisting in unrepentant evil violates the Buddha’s regulations; this is the third fault.
They perform the *poṣadha* together;
yet, failing to repent for their transgressions while entering the *poṣadha*, they merely follow worldly sentiments with their minds constrained by fame and profit—this is the fourth fault.
The entire community dwells together and recites the precepts.
If one lacks internal observance of the precepts yet does not expose their transgressions or instruct them to repent,
it is because they fear others will learn of their offenses and thereby lose their offerings.
One commits a minor offense (light defilement).
If a Buddha’s disciple sees a Mahayana Dharma Master—
meaning that the Buddha’s disciple, through the eyes, the mind, or the ears, perceives, knows, or hears of a Mahayana Dharma Master— [and fails to honor them, they commit an offense].
They are fellow students of the Mahāyāna;
they study under the same teacher and share the same view.
They tend toward the same great fruit;
they practice together;
they cultivate the same great conduct.
He came and entered the monastic quarters;
"the place where the monks reside" refers to within the monastery or a private residence.
The houses where people dwell are the places where lay bodhisattvas receive [guests] with respect. A "city" (nagara) signifies abundance;
it is that which abundantly receives the population and their goods.
A "village" (*yì*) refers to a district (*xiàn*); this is also a place where both monastics and laypeople receive visitors.
If someone comes from a hundred or a thousand *li*, [they are welcomed here].
He does not obstruct those who come from nearby or go to the furthest distances;
that is, he rises to welcome them when they arrive and escorts them when they depart.
When a Bodhisattva sees these four types of Mahāyāna practitioners coming, he rises to welcome them, and when they depart, he escorts them.
I prostrate.
Having not seen you for many days,
I offer this供养 (pūjā).
He resided there for a long time,
making offerings three times each day:
morning gruel at the hour of the Tiger (寅), midday meals at the hour of the Dragon (辰), and evening medicinal decoctions.
One consumes three *liang* of gold daily;

yet the kindness of entering the gate of Buddhism to escape the suffering of the triple world exceeds the kindness of one's parents' nursing— the latter being beyond measure— how much more so than those three *liang* of gold?
The food and drink consisted of a hundred flavors,
exquisitely refined to the utmost degree;
there were couches and seats.
Reclining and resting upon beds; preaching the Dharma and arranging seats;
providing medicine;
and whatever vehicles for travel may be required.
Serve the Dharma masters.
With the aforementioned items, provide for and support these four kinds of Dharma masters,
granting them everything they require.
One should only offer what is suitable for the ritual and fit for presentation.
One should constantly invite a Dharma Master to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day,
at each of these three times daily.
One should perform prostrations three times each day;
one should request the teaching three times, performing prostrations on all three occasions,
and never give rise to a mind of anger.
Whether much is said or little is said, one gives rise to neither anger nor a mind of resentment;
even when others speak in ways that contradict one's own feelings, one remains free from resentment and distress.
To preserve the Dharma, one should sacrifice one's body;
to seek even half a verse of the Dharma, one should give up one's life.
Failing to do so constitutes a minor offense.
Violating prohibitions constitutes an offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha is in any place,
the total number [of precepts] is indicated therein.
There is the teaching of the Dharma;
this refers to the teaching of the Tripiṭaka. Vinaya.
The Vinaya Piṭaka is specifically indicated here as "extinguishing," referring to the extinguishing of afflictions, karma, and so forth.
Regarding the Sūtras and Vinayas, according to this sūtra, the sūtra is itself the Vinaya.
In a large residence, at a place where the Dharma is preached,
or at any location accessible to both monastics and laypeople, one may preach the Dharma.
This applies to a bodhisattva who is newly trained.
To demonstrate that they are capable listeners,
they should hold scrolls of the Sūtras and Vinaya;
whether holding a Sūtra text or a Vinaya section, there must logically be a Śāstra, so they should respectfully carry the volumes of the Tripiṭaka.
[Place] the volume [in its case]. Upon reaching the Dharma Master’s location, listen to and receive his teachings, and inquire about them.
Once you have heard the Dharma, do not forget what you have received; reflect upon and practice it repeatedly, and whenever doubt arises, consult him immediately.
One should go to all places where the Dharma is preached—whether in mountain forests, under trees, on monastic grounds, or within rooms—and listen and receive it.
This indicates the proper place for listening.
If one does not go there to listen and receive it, one commits a minor offense (light dust-offense).
If one has not yet attained the Buddha’s intent, it is difficult for understanding and practice to arise; if one does not study and hear the Tripiṭaka, one will not know the path of cultivation.
Even at the cost of sacrificing one's life, one ought to seek it with devotion. To have a lecture being given and yet not listen—how could the loss be greater? Alas!
With nineteen years remaining in this life, and fire already emerging from within the water, how can it be saved? Unless there be some other great benefit.
Alternatively, if the other person is not equal to oneself, there is no offense in not going to listen.

If a disciple of the Buddha turns their mind away from the Mahāyāna, it should be stated according to the preceding rule: "One must not turn the mind away from the Mahāyāna," which is equivalent to correctly receiving the Mahāyāna.
The sūtras and vinaya are eternally abiding;

for they expound the two bases of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) that constitute the eternally abiding Buddha, which are attained through cultivation and progress based upon the sūtras and vinaya.
To say that these are not the word of the Buddha [is incorrect].
They slander the Mahāyāna, claiming it is not the Buddha’s word,
yet they accept and uphold the sūtras and vinaya of the two vehicles— the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The evil views of the śrāvakas and non-Buddhists,
the ninety-five heterodox speculations outside of principle,
and all prohibitive precepts.
This collectively subsumes the prohibitions and precepts of the two vehicles and non-Buddhist paths,
as well as the sūtras and vinayas of false views;

it also refers to those non-Buddhist sūtras and vinayas that contradict the principles of the three vehicles, or those sūtras and vinayas of the two vehicles that contradict the principles of the Mahāyāna.
"Wrong. This reiterates the preceding summary of the offense.
This constitutes a transgression of a minor offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha sees anyone who is ill—whether an enemy or a relative—he must provide universal relief; because he rescues all those he encounters who are sick, it is said "all."
One should constantly make offerings to them,
providing medicinal decoctions according to their illnesses and whatever they require at any time; or, by speaking the Dharma in accordance with their inclinations, one should gladden them,
no different from how one would treat the Buddha.
