One should make offerings to the sick with a mind like that of a Buddha, or contemplate that the sick person will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of caring for the sick is the foremost.
Although the seventh [type of] merit— [offering to] the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, parents, teachers, elders, the poor, the sick, and animals— is superior to the first,
if it concerns one's own parents or a parent who is ill, there is the grace of their nurturing and raising.
The master and his disciples:
when the master is ill, he possesses the virtue of providing instruction;
when the disciple is ill, [the same applies].
Those who possess the capacity to uphold and flourish the Triple Gem— these three aforementioned categories should have their ailments relieved.
As for those with impaired faculties,
they may lack one or more of the five faculties, such as the eye faculty and so forth.
Regarding the hundred kinds of illness and suffering,
he rescues each one as it arises,
nourishing them all until they are healed.
Among the hundred ailments, whichever one afflicts them, he immediately provides medical treatment so that they may recover and be at ease;
yet the bodhisattva, with a malicious mind,
instead regards those matters of illness with malice.
A mind of anger prevents the arising of compassion; a mind of resentment [does the same].
If there is a long-standing enmity or resentment,
or if one does not enter the monks' quarters—
due to these three mental states— one does not go to the place of the sick.
In cities, towns, wildernesses, mountain forests, or along roads—
anywhere where all people fall ill—
if one sees someone suffering from disease and fails to provide relief, one commits a minor offense of defilement.

If one does not rescue [others] due to a lack of compassion, one incurs the fault; however, if there is another great benefit, and one harbors no malice or resentment, it is not an offense even if one falls ill.
O Disciples of the Buddha, you must not store any weapons for combat, such as knives, staves, swords, bows, arrows, spears, or axes, nor any implements of war, nor any evil...
One must not store any instruments for killing living beings; indeed, anything that harms creatures is forbidden.
This intention seems quite broad, as even things such as fists and hands can harm living beings;
thus, "all" may be used here to refer to a limited category of such items.
Yet, even if a Bodhisattva were to have their own parents killed, they would not seek retribution; how much less so for killing any other sentient being. Regarding the phrase "even if" (*nai-zhi*):
it is an abbreviation that skips over other sūtras to reach the most weighty point—that there is no offense greater than that against one's parents.

Because parental kindness is profound, even if they are killed, the resentment is heavy; yet if one does not repay such resentment, how much more so regarding other beings? Therefore, one should practice loving-kindness and forbearance. This question is merely... [end of fragment].
If one stores these [weapons] but does not use them to kill living beings, what fault is there? The answer is: it causes others to revile and criticize one;

furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, one guards the mind, and upon seeing such instruments of killing, the intent to kill arises within. Once that intent to kill has arisen, one immediately incurs the guilt for the act.
If one intentionally hoards any weapons, such as knives or staves, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Such an act violates established regulations and invites calamity.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart; they shall be explained in detail within the following six chapters.
The concluding exhortation points to the extensive [teachings].
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, you must not, for the sake of gain and profit or out of an evil mind, harbor such intentions.
An evil mind consists of the three poisons; these three poisons are the root of all evils. For the sake of fame and profit, one gives rise to greed; once greed arises..."
Consequently, anger and delusion will surely follow.
To "serve as an envoy to communicate with other states" means to receive a mandate to act as a messenger to convey the state's communications.
When military arrays meet,
they deliberate on life and destiny, fix the timing for a decisive battle,
and raise armies to strike one another down.
"To mobilize" means to assemble a multitude; that is, to mobilize troops and engage in mutual warfare.
To kill immeasurable sentient beings—even though this involves killing others as well—is primarily the transgression of taking life.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva must not enter an army to come and go.
If one comes and goes for no reason, inviting suspicion, slander, and reproach, such conduct is already unacceptable;
how much more so when one intentionally acts as a traitor to the state?
If one intentionally orders the killing of many living beings,
or acts intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light垢罪).
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally traffics in free persons.
According to the preceding and following texts, it should be stated that one must not intentionally buy or sell "liangmin" (良人) and the like; "liang" (良) refers to those who are good and virtuous,
whereas "nu" (奴) and "bi" (婢) are designations for those who are lowly and inferior.
Regarding the six domestic animals—oxen, horses, dogs, sheep, pigs, and chickens—one should take these six types as the standard for all other livestock; it is in every case improper [to trade them].
One may, however, trade for coffins, boards, and timber at the market.
To sell wood for making coffins—
to trade in the implements for containing the dead—
is for a Bodhisattva to engage in selling such things that invites public censure and reproach.
If one intentionally commits this act oneself or instructs others to commit it, one incurs a minor offense (light defilement).
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders others for the sake of fame and profit;
or out of an evil mind harboring resentment from the past, manifests jealousy; or out of an evil mind, possesses both [jealousy and anger]—these constitute an evil mind.
With the three poisons of delusion as their cause, one may give rise to slander;
one slanders a virtuous person when there is no basis for it.
One falsely slanders a good and upright person who is ordinarily without fault.
A "virtuous person" (satpuruṣa) is one who cultivates the wholesome practices of the three vehicles.
A "Dharma-master" (dharmabhāṇaka)...
The teacher who expounds the Dharma and explains the Dharma;
the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the instructor (ācārya).
The Sangha refers to the great assembly within the hall;
the king refers to the sovereign.
Emperors,
nobles, and high ministers.
Regarding the offenses of the seven reversals and ten grave transgressions:
in relation to the aforementioned seven classes of persons, both types of slander are termed "reversal" and "grave" offenses;
this applies specifically to one's parents.

Abiding [in this practice], whether as a householder or one who has left the home life, there is nothing that does not take the physical body born of one's parents as the basis for upholding the precepts and practicing filial piety;
likewise with siblings,
who are born of the same parents.
Among the six types of kin—
brothers, sisters, wives, and children—
one should give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience.
The Venerable One receives with a heart of filial piety and respect; those of lower station receive with a heart of compliance.
With a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he bestows happiness upon those who lack it; with a heart of compassion (*karuṇā*), he seeks to rescue those who suffer.
Yet, on the contrary, they commit even greater acts of hostility and harm.
Since they fail to give rise to compassion and filiality toward their superiors and instead give rise to a harmful mind—this is why it says "on the contrary.
As for "falling into undesirable states": [it refers to those who]...
Because it causes one's parents and others to give rise to anger and resentment, leading them to fall into the evil realms, it is called "an undesirable place.
This constitutes a minor offense of defilement.
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind...
"By" means that which serves as the condition; "therefore" means the reason why. It is because an evil mind acts as the cause that one is set ablaze, emitting great flames to burn.
It can burn; it is that which burns forests, mountains, and wildernesses.
The Buddha prohibited [the use of fire] because it is the dwelling place of insects, beasts, ghosts, and spirits.

Setting fire [to forests] from the fourth month through the ninth month is prohibited because these six months are the period when insects and animals breed; however, in reality, one must not burn them during the other six months either,
as those creatures still depend upon them for their existence.
If one burns the houses and dwellings of others,
the residences of the common people,
or cities and towns.
The residences of kings and ministers,
monastic quarters,
and the dwellings of those who have left the household life.
The field and the wood pervade all people,
as well as ghosts and spirits.
Objects within burial mounds; objects within shrines and temples;
official property;
and items stored in the government treasuries.
All things that have an owner are merely the property of that owner;
one must not intentionally burn them.
This refers collectively to the aforementioned objects.
If one intentionally burns them, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
If a disciple of the Buddha [burns] another disciple of the Buddha...
Having received the Buddha’s teaching and succeeding to the Buddha’s position, one is from then on a disciple of the Buddha;
this identifies those who can transform others, including non-Buddhists, evil persons, the six types of relatives, and all spiritual friends.
All these are beings to be converted;
one should instruct each of them individually to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya,
as well as their textual expositions.
One should instruct them in the principles of meaning and logic,
causing them to understand the gateways of practice for advancing in the Mahāyāna,
and leading them to resolve upon bodhicitta.
To cause those who have not yet resolved their minds to do so:
the ten minds of departure, which are the lower stage of worthiness (*kṣānti*).
The ten minds of nurturing are the intermediate stage of worthiness;
the ten adamantine minds are the final stage.
Regarding "the superior sages":
among the thirty minds, this refers to the mental states of the three superior sage stages; in reality, there are forty-four minds.
Explain each one in its proper sequence,
from beginning to end, including the stages of preparation and enhancement,
as well as the ritual applications.
The procedural rules for the forty-four moments of mind— entering, abiding, and emerging— can be practiced; yet,
because the Bodhisattva possesses a malicious mind,
he conceives hatred toward the person being instructed, fearing that they might encroach upon his own interests.
Out of a mind of anger,
or because he had previously been treated with hostility and thus gave rise to resentment, he did not reveal the Great Teaching to him,
but instead arbitrarily taught the sūtras and vinaya of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas.
That [Great Vehicle] uses great roots to indirectly demonstrate the small teachings;
whereas for external paths, heterodox views, and treatises,

even using the Great Nature to demonstrate the Small is already inappropriate, let alone further teaching them heterodox doctrines— their fault is even deeper, and is therefore called "horizontal" (橫).
This constitutes a minor offense of defilement.
Since a Bodhisattva ought to practice the two benefits for self and others, now that both self and others are harmed and one has contravened the Buddha’s words, this [offense] corresponds to that.
Transgression.
If a Buddha’s disciple should, with a good heart—
“good” meaning wholesome— a mind corresponding to the eleven wholesome [dharmas], this is collectively termed a “good heart.”
Those who study the Mahāyāna originally,
by virtue of their great nature, first give rise to the cultivation of the Great [Vehicle],
as well as its majestic deportment, sūtras, and vinaya.
The definitive precepts to be expounded each possess the rules of conduct for walking, standing, sitting, and reclining;
these are extensively explained.
Through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one becomes widely learned and possesses great erudition, thereby practicing and realizing the underlying principles.
The meaning and flavor [of the teaching] cause the mind and spirit to become expansive, joyful, and serene; this above clarifies self-benefit.
Seeing later those newly initiated bodhisattvas...
Having first studied the sūtras and vinaya with the intent to benefit others, one should preach them when new students come seeking instruction.
There are those who travel from a hundred or even a thousand li to seek the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.
Furthermore, these two cases—one more proximate and one more remote—should also be explained;
they should be explained in accordance with the Dharma.
There is no room for irrational or groundless discourse; the essential point lies in receiving and practicing the words of the Buddha.
Regarding all ascetic practices:
when about to preach the Dharma, one first explains the suffering of asceticism. What is meant by the suffering of an ascetic?
It refers to such acts as burning the body, burning the arms, or burning the fingers.
He demonstrated that the essential purpose of practicing asceticism is to take the Dharma as one's priority, not sparing even body or life. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to cultivate samādhi, he may light a single lamp before an image of the Tathāgata, burn a finger joint, or apply burning incense to his own body."
I say that for such a person, all karmic debts from beginningless time are fully repaid by means of incense sticks.
If one does not offer one's body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, one is not a renunciant bodhisattva.
Now, since the Buddha’s grace is most profound and his spiritual power is inconceivable, if one does not act for this purpose, how can one become a Great Being?
One might ask: "The Buddha possesses great compassion and takes pity on all beings; yet now he causes them to suffer. How can this be called compassionate salvation? The answer is:
The Buddha’s original intent is to cause them to accomplish merit and virtue, not out of any harmful intent. Furthermore, it is feared that they would otherwise have to repay their past karmic debts.
Even unto hungry tigers, wolves, lions, and all hungry ghosts, one should sacrifice one's own body, flesh, hands, and feet to provide for them,
thereby enabling the practice of asceticism to bring salvation to all living beings.
Thereafter,
first explain the practice of asceticism so that when they engage in the practice, it may be taught to them in its proper sequence, one by one.
The six perfections and so forth are all taught in successive order.
For them, he teaches the True Dharma—
the supreme Dharma that is free from error.
It causes the mind to open and the wisdom-mind to arise; furthermore, it makes the precepts examined, the mind clear and distinct,
and the intellect liberated.
His consciousness is clear and distinct, being free from error in every detail; furthermore, because he has not forgotten what was heard,
contemplated, and cultivated, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and honor, invited him [to teach],
fearing that if he were to understand, it would encroach upon his own profit.
When one should have answered,
they did not answer; when asked about the Mahāyāna teachings, they should have responded accordingly, yet now they remain silent and instead explain the sūtras and vinaya in a distorted manner.
This is a perverted explanation regarding the three trainings and so forth.
The characters have no priority or sequence;
one may join the preceding with the following or join the following with the preceding.
To slander the Three Jewels by saying,
"The Buddha did not teach in this way," "The Dharma is not explained in this way," or "The Sangha does not transmit it in this way," but to speak all such things from one's own delusions,
constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
If a Buddha’s disciple, for the sake of their own food and drink,
uses money or goods to sustain their body;
For oneself, one utilizes all manner of things for the sake of wealth,
gain, and the necessities of food and clothing.
Fame and prestige:
the renown of noble power and the reputation for excellence.
Therefore, one draws near to kings, princes, ministers, and officials.
The reason for this is that the former refers to those who act out of a sense of righteousness as superior conditions and thus draw near;

the latter refers to those who seek profit and fame, for whom the Buddha does not permit proximity. However, if it is for the sake of upholding the Triple Gem and enabling its power to circulate, one may draw near.
Apart from these purposes, the four aforementioned matters are all collectively inappropriate.
"Relying on the creation of a physical form.
"Relying" means depending upon; it refers to depending upon one's power and authority to strike and beat others.
Beating with a staff to cause pain; striking in coordination to instill fear.
Begging: relying on others for support and soliciting alms.
Dragging and pulling.
If one begs from someone at first and does not receive [what is desired], one then demands it by dragging and pulling them to see a superior official,
seizing [the object] by force.
This is not the grasping of meanings,
nor of coins, goods,
wealth, or all manner of things.
To seek all manner of profit,
employing a hundred schemes and striving for these things through a hundred pursuits,
is called "evil seeking."
Greedily grasping,
seeking much,
and never satisfied in one's seeking.
To instruct others to seek [it],
to entrust it to those with power to seek it, to compel others to seek it, or to instruct them to seek it as I do—
all these are devoid of compassion.
They forcibly oppress and afflict others,
lacking any heart of filial piety;
thus they contravene the words of the Buddha above, and their calamity reaches their parents.
This summarizes and determines the offense;
one commits a minor secondary offense (light defilement).
If a disciple of the Buddha studies and recites the precepts,
they should instruct those who are ready according to their capacity,
practicing six times throughout the day and night.
During the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night,
one should uphold the bodhisattva precepts,
reciting and retaining them until they are mastered, and maintaining them with mindfulness so as not to forget.
To understand its meaning and principle;
"meaning" (*artha*) is itself the "principle" (*nīti*), both of which are what is explained by the recited phrases.
One must clearly comprehend the essential intent of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

The Buddha-nature is the nature of the nature of original practice; this nature is the equal true nature. To understand these two natures is to realize that the stages of awakening and realization differ in their sequence.
Yet, the Bodhisattva does not comprehend even a single phrase.
That is, verses consisting of four or five syllables per line;
a verse consists of four lines.
The causes and conditions of the precepts (*śīla-vinaya*).
The precepts themselves are the discipline (*vinaya*); the transmission of the precepts has compassion as its cause; receiving the precepts has the seed of the bodhicitta as its cause;
and the harmonious union of teacher and disciple, initiating the request for realization, constitutes the condition. To be ignorant of these is called "not understanding."
"Understanding.
This refers to one who falsely claims to understand;
in reality, they are utterly deluded, yet they feign and deceive by saying, "I understand this."
This is to deceive oneself;
knowing clearly that one's own mind does not understand, one will incur the offense of deceiving others,
and thus also deceives others.
Not understanding [the precepts] and yet instructing others is itself deceiving them.

Failing to understand each and every point, one reiterates the previous transgression of feigning understanding; thus, regarding the causes and conditions of the precepts, as well as the rules for receiving, studying, upholding, and violating them, one is entirely deluded.
Regarding all dharmas,
if one lacks the capacity to engage with the three categories, the four truths, and the six perfections,
yet— out of ignorance— acts as a teacher for others and confers the precepts upon them, they commit a minor offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind—
the three poisons constituting this evil mind—
sees a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts.
When a son of the Buddha sees a bhikṣu who upholds the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts,
holding an incense burner in his hand and carrying a hand-bell while walking in circumambulation to make offerings to the Buddha.
One practices the bodhisattva path;
the bodhisattvas of the three periods of time tread this path to attain buddhahood,
yet you instead incite strife between the two sides.

When a worthy person cultivates bodhicitta, there is nothing therein that is not like the two tusks of an elephant; yet they cause others to give rise to anger and poison by creating appearances and causing harm,
slandering and deceiving the worthy.
They engage in groundless slander and commit every kind of evil;
they perform all such wicked deeds.
This concludes the summary:
one commits a minor offense.
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of a heart of compassion—
since the Buddha achieves Buddhahood through compassion— exhorts others to cultivate a compassionate mind to save living beings and practice the act of releasing life.
In the performance of meritorious deeds, taking compassion as the essence, the practice of releasing living beings is the specific action.
"All men are my fathers":
if one wishes to cultivate a compassionate mind, one must engage in contemplative practice; the term "all" here encompasses every male being.
All women have been my mothers.
Since all these women are encompassed within that category, one must certainly regard them as parents; only when the thought of killing has utterly ceased may one release living beings.
This is because there is no birth in which I have not received life from them.
Because my own cycle of birth and death has been boundless since time without beginning, I have taken birth in all these places.
All sentient beings of the six realms have been my parents;
since they were all my parents, it is not permissible to take their lives or eat their flesh.
If one kills and eats [a being], one is killing and eating one's own parents;
if one kills and eats the parents of many lifetimes, why is there no offense of parricide? The answer is that because the lives are separated, the perception of them as one's parents is absent.
It is also because they kill my former body.
"Former" means old; my old body was a sentient being's form composed of the four great elements.
Since the bodies of others are likewise composed of the four great elements, to kill another's body is to kill my own former body.
"All earth and water were my former bodies; all fire and wind are my original essence.
This explains the aforementioned point.
Therefore, one should constantly practice the release of living beings.
Therefore, as explained previously, since beings of both sexes across the six realms are all one's own parents, one must constantly practice the release of living beings;
this constant practice of releasing life takes compassion as its fundamental basis.
In every life one takes birth;
in every place where one takes birth, one shall practice the release of living beings.
This is the eternally abiding Dharma.
This is the natural law and constant principle:
to teach others to release living beings.
To practice this oneself and to teach it to others constitutes the conduct that benefits both self and others.
If you see people of the world killing animals,
when they are about to strike down, you should instruct them so that it becomes difficult for them to carry out the blow; at such a time,
you should employ skillful means to rescue and protect them.

One should use kind words to instruct and transform them so that their minds are opened; only then can they be saved. If one speaks directly without success, it may instead bring harm upon oneself and fail to relieve their suffering and distress.
Regarding the pain of being killed,
he constantly taught and expounded upon the Bodhisattva precepts,
which are the very foundation for attaining Buddhahood.
To deliver sentient beings:
now, hearing the precepts and abstaining from killing to avoid the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms is precisely what constitutes deliverance.
This is especially so on the anniversary of the death of one's parents or siblings.
On the anniversary of one’s death or on the annual memorial day,
one should invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*—
that is, this very sutra— or to expound upon the entire Mahāyāna Vinaya-piṭaka.
May this merit support the deceased;
by reciting this merit for their sustenance,
may they be able to behold all Buddhas.
If one is among humans or devas, they will be reborn in a pure land where they may behold the various Buddhas;
if they are born among humans or devas,
even in obscure or perilous places, they will still attain existence as a human or deva.
If it were not so, then such dwelling would mean that for a lay or ordained bodhisattva, the merit as described above must assist their kin;
if it were not thus, [the merit would not reach them].
One commits a minor offense (āpatti) and incurs transgression by violating prohibitions.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart, as is extensively explained for each one in the "Chapter on the Extinction of Offenses."
The characteristics of the precepts.
A summary, an exhortation, and a detailed exposition.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha."
Addressing the person before one:
when met with anger, one should respond with anger;
this should be stated as "one must not respond to another's anger with anger," which constitutes mental patience (*manas-kṣānti*).
To repay a blow with a blow;
having been struck by an evil person, one must not harbor malice and instead strike back—this is patience regarding bodily action (*kāyakarma*).

Furthermore, it should be said that one must not repay abuse with abuse—this is patience regarding verbal action (*vākkarma*). When the three types of action are not requited, this is the true Buddha.
My son, if one has killed one's parents, siblings, or other members of the six classes of kin, one must not seek retribution.
This is because each person’s own past karma involved killing others; now that they have been mutilated by another, how can one retaliate in turn?
If the sovereign of a state is killed by another, one must not seek retribution.
Although he dwells upon the land of the king, drinks the water of the king, and protects the Triple Gem—thus possessing great kindness—the sovereign has invited this death through his own karma;
therefore, it is not permissible to retaliate.
Killing in retribution for what was done to one's parents does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety.

If one’s parents are those who have bestowed kindness upon one in the present life, all sentient beings are one’s parents from previous lives; thus, they are those who have bestowed kindness in the past.
To kill them is to act contrary to the Way of Filial Piety. If a parent is killed, it is only right that one should cultivate goodness to provide posthumous support for them.
This is said because they would otherwise return to commit acts of killing.
Furthermore, they do not even keep slaves, nor do they beat, strike, or revile them;
since beating and reviling cause suffering and are neither compassionate nor beneficial, it is said that they do not keep them.
Every day, one gives rise to the three types of karma.
First harboring anger toward servants and slaves, one is able to give rise to the three karmas of body and speech by beating and reviling them;
the verbal offenses are immeasurable.
Vocal karma is particularly predominant;
how much more so, then, for intentionally committing the seven heinous crimes?
Even the commission of offenses through the three karmas toward inferior objects such as slaves and servants is not fit to be committed, let alone the grave sins of the seven reversals.

It may be permitted for a lay bodhisattva who is a king to act [in this way], provided that he protects the Triple Gem and the people and seeks to pacify disorder; however, for a renunciant bodhisattva, it is not permitted.
This is killing.
To seek revenge without compassion is not the way of one who has left the household life; seeking revenge is contrary to compassion.
As for those who seek retribution even among their six close relatives:
since one cannot even bear to repay one's parents, it is certainly improper to seek retribution from one's six close relatives.
To do so constitutes a minor offense (light dust-offense).
Regarding the offense of violating prohibitions and failing to exercise forbearance:
if a disciple of the Buddha has initially left the household life,
the formal regulations for those who have left the home are established concurrently with the admonitions for those who remain at home.
He has not yet attained any understanding.
Although he calls himself a son of the Buddha, he ought to practice the Mahāyāna; yet he has not at all heard or seen the principles of the Mahāyāna teachings.
Nevertheless, he relies on his own cleverness and intelligence.
In his time as a layman, he had studied poetry and the classics, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence;
perhaps relying on his noble status,
he had formerly served as a royal minister.
Regarding age: whether it be secular years or monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇerī*),
one might rely on the prestige of a prominent clan.
In India, the Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas were, in the high antiquity of this land, officials who possessed great wealth and noble lineages;
"noble lineage" (gāomén) and "high and distant reputation" (ménwàng gāoyuǎn) may be considered synonymous with "great clan and noble lineage" (dàxìng gāomén).
Great liberation.
Worldly liberation has remainder.
Great merit.
Abounding in money and silk;
possessing an abundance of the seven treasures;
and having worldly wealth in great profusion.
"By means of this arrogance.

Yet they do not consult or receive the sutras and vinaya from learned Dharma masters;
this is because they rely on themselves and disparage others.
As for those Dharma masters:
Those designated as objects of contempt include those of low birth,
such as the Vaiśyas and Śūdras of India, or the poor and humble classes of this land.
Young in years;
his secular age and monastic seniority are not yet sufficient.
Of humble origin.
Of lowly lineage and weak constitution,
impoverished,
with a home consisting of nothing but four walls.
Though they lack the various faculties— that is,
they are deficient in the eye and other faculties—
they nonetheless truly possess virtues.
He fully possesses the three trainings and the three types of wisdom;
he understands all the sūtras and vinayas.

To disparage others who possess understanding while claiming oneself to be free from ignorance—despite having already manifested the complete mastery of what those of virtue study—is the transgression of pride.
When this pride exists, other forms of pride arise accordingly.

Now, when a newly initiated bodhisattva addresses someone who has not yet understood, and since that person is designated as "one who does not understand," they must certainly seek instruction. At the time of seeking the Dharma, one must...
Abandon arrogance.
Do not examine the lineage of the Dharma teacher;
do not consider whether the Dharma teacher’s lineage is lowly or inferior, but observe only that the Buddha-dharma is the excellent rule for advancing on the Path.

If there is one who can expound the profound meaning of the Sage’s spiritual paradigm and untie the knots of doubt, thereby benefiting me, I shall devote my whole heart to honoring them and pay no mind to their other faults.
Whether the Dharma Master is good or bad is not my concern; I shall regard the Dharma Master as I would the Buddha while observing his preaching of the Dharma.
If one does not come to consult and receive the Dharma Master regarding the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
this constitutes a minor offense (*āpatti*) because the meaning of the Mahāyāna is superior to that of other vehicles.
Violating the regulations constitutes an offense, except in cases such as illness or other hardships.
If a disciple of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—
this clearly indicates the time for receiving the precepts— it is revealed that when the Buddha was still in the world, there was no self-administered ordination.
With a sincere heart,
one intends to rescue others from suffering and bestow happiness,
employing a mind of altruism when receiving the bodhisattva precepts.
This [method] applies to both self-benefit and benefit for others at all times after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
one receives the precepts by making a vow before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* explains the ritual procedures in detail.
One should perform repentance before the Buddha for seven days.
The *Buddhanāmasūtra* states that within a single seven-day period, one should perform repentance before an image of the Buddha during the six periods of day and night;
thereby, one shall behold auspicious signs.
As will be explained below regarding the Buddha coming to touch one’s crown with his hand and so forth,
one immediately obtains the precepts;
having extinguished transgressions and become pure, one then obtains the precepts.
If one does not obtain a favorable sign within seven days,
and no favorable sign is obtained even within that period, one must not stop; rather,
one must seek with renewed devotion for two weeks, three weeks, or even up to a year.
Because the obstructions have varying degrees of thickness and the duration of time varies, it is limited solely by the appearance of signs; furthermore, it is not fixed to exactly one year.
One must simply seek auspicious signs.
Having made the vow to receive the precepts oneself, no signs are known;
once an auspicious sign has been obtained,
one should acquire any one sign among those various signs.
One may then receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.

Although this is merely a symbolic representation, one must generate a sense of profound reverence, as if standing before the actual image, to express one's sincerity, offer prayers, and perform repentance;
only after reciting the threefold *karmavācanā* for self-ordination does one truly obtain the precepts.
If one does not obtain a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*), one cannot receive the precepts even before an image of the Buddha;
for if there were no sign to manifest it, who would know that the precepts have been obtained?
However, when receiving the Bodhisattva precepts before a Dharma Master in person, it is not necessary to see a favorable sign.
Why is this? Because these Dharma masters have transmitted it from teacher to teacher, there is no need for auspicious signs;
thus, by receiving the precepts before a Dharma master, one immediately obtains them, for by generating a mind of profound respect, one thereby attains the precepts.

This refers to receiving the precepts from a teacher; the headings, indications, explanations, and conclusions can be understood accordingly. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the ritual procedures in detail.
If there is no capable preceptor within a thousand li, one may receive the precepts through self-vow before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, provided that one perceives auspicious signs.

In each of the eight directions, such is the case: to have [the precepts] yet not receive them is to be arrogant toward others; to seek them from afar when they do not exist is to fear falling into self-deception.
Therefore, it is said thus: one must necessarily see the signs and form the connection to constitute receiving the precepts for oneself.
If a Dharma master relies on his own understanding of the sutras, vinaya, and Mahayana precepts,
and out of self-conceit regarding his wisdom,
forms close friendships with kings, crown princes, and high officials.
They associate with those of high status as friends;
yet when newly initiated bodhisattvas come to inquire about the meaning of the sūtras or the meaning of the vinaya,
these newly initiated ones come seeking such meanings.
If one does not answer questions with due care, respect, or kindness because of a frivolous mind, a haughty mind, or an evil mind, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
This offense is incurred through these three evil states of mind.
O Disciples of the Buddha, if there are the Buddha’s sutras and vinaya...
"Excluding external teachings" refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma;
"the Mahāyāna Dharma" excludes the Hīnayāna Dharma.
Right view arises based on the true Dharma;
it is the state of correctness.
The true essence of reality revealed by the True Dharma is the Dharmakāya of the True Dharma;
it encompasses all three bodies, including the Dharmakāya of conditioned and unconditioned meritorious qualities.
Yet they are unable to apply themselves diligently to study and cultivation;
regarding the aforementioned dharmas, they neither hear nor contemplate them, and thus the three types of wisdom do not arise.
Consequently, they abandon the seven treasures.
"Abandoning the precious treasure of the True Dharma"—this phrase may belong to the following section.
It refers to "inverting" by studying false views instead;
because one has not studied the True Dharma well and thus failed to increase in virtue, yet now studies what is false, it is called "inversion. False views are... [text ends]
In general, the two vehicles—
the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— are not beneficial [to others]; therefore, they do not accord with the Mahāyāna, and their disparagement of it is termed "heresy."
The non-Buddhist paths number ninety-six;
these are the secular scriptures.
These are the Nine Classics and the Three Histories.
Abhidharma— here translated as "Counter-Dharma"—
refers to the treatises of the Hīnayāna.
Miscellaneous Treatise (*Saṃkīrṇa-śāstra*).

This is what is meant by severing the Buddha-nature.

It is through hearing, reflection, and cultivation that the seeds of Buddhahood arise; now, because one studies erroneously, the conditions for these seeds are lacking and they do not increase—this is called "severance."
Regarding the causes and conditions for obstructing the Path:
since the Path consists of the manifestation of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), it does not arise through false study;
nor is it the practice of the Bodhisattva path.
This is said because those who now follow heterodox studies abandon both [their own] benefit and the benefit of others.
If one intentionally practices such things, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
However, if one has the remaining strength to assist the True Dharma by taming those difficult to tame, it is not prohibited to study all five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

O sons of the Buddha, after the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa,
this precept shall serve as the master for settling disputes at such times.
He acts as a master of the Dharma,
for he possesses mastery through his excellent knowledge of the passages and obstacles within the teachings of the Tripitaka;
he acts as a master of the monastic quarters.
The head of the monastery and the master of instruction are those who know how to perform offerings and worship.
The Master of Seated Meditation was well-versed in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, possessing clear understanding of the eight meditative attainments (*aṣṭa-samāpatti*).
The Master of Conduct and Movement...
The leaders who travel abroad with their followers each attain mastery according to what they preside over;
therefore, this clarifies how those who harmonize disputes during the Semblance Dharma and Final Dharma periods after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.

As described above, each of the five leaders occupies their respective position, well-acquainted with the rules of conduct; they proceed and retreat according to established regulations and bring about peace and happiness.
They skillfully reconcile disputes and litigation.
Having become the leader and being honored by the assembly, he shall mediate and exhort those who have disputes and litigation so that they may comply with the teachings.
He shall properly guard the property of the Triple Gem;
the property of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha each has its own designated destination and must not be used interchangeably.
Do not use things without measure.
Each has its proper standard; use them according to their appropriate application, as if they were one's own.
One must not treat the property of the Three Jewels as one's own, using it at will when needed; rather, one should cherish the property of the Three Jewels as if it were one's own.
To instead disrupt the community and fail to harmonize it—when one is oneself unworthy of veneration yet further disturbs the assembly—how can such a person be called a leader of the community?
Regarding strife:
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explicitly teaches that there are six roots of strife capable of giving rise to all forms of conflict:
(1) mutual opposition resulting in the commission of undesirable acts; (2) concealing one's various evils and being unwilling to disclose them; (3) [regarding] equality...
Among these types, there are four ways in which one receives the retribution of excessive gain for oneself: (1) mutually deceiving others regarding robes and other requisites;

(2) frequently committing transgressions of the three karmas and violating the training rules; (3) holding inverted views and attachments regarding the Dharma and its meaning; and (4) possessing four further factors that sever the root.
First, physical, verbal, and mental actions motivated by a mind of loving-kindness can sever the first two [categories of faults].
Second, by equally receiving offerings and sustenance, one can sever the third and fourth [fetters]; third, by equally pursuing ethical discipline (*śīla*), one can sever the fifth;
fourth, by equally pursuing right view, one can sever the sixth.
As for those who recklessly use the property of the Triple Gem:
To designate the five masters without following the rules regarding location and purpose, and to employ them arbitrarily,
constitutes a minor offense (light dust-offense).
If a disciple of the Buddha has previously resided within a monastic dwelling...
In a place where there is no designated presiding authority, those who have resided there first are considered the masters.
When they later see visiting bodhisattva bhikṣus arrive,
they collectively designate them as "guests who have come."
He entered a monastic compound,
the dwelling place of an ordained bodhisattva,
whether it be within a house, a city, or the residence of a king.
The dwelling place of a lay bodhisattva,
even down to the location for the summer retreat (varṣā),
should not be too small according to where one dwells during the retreat.
Furthermore, within great assemblies—
whether at places where the Dharma is preached or at places where vegetarian feasts (*zhāihuì*) are held— these five locations, though accessible to both monastics and laypeople,
are primarily for the reception of the Sangha; therefore, the Sūtra speaks of being "within the monastic quarters" (*saṃghārāma*).
The resident monks should welcome those who come and see them off when they depart.
Those who arrive first at the aforementioned five locations should immediately welcome those who follow and see them off as they leave,
thereby demonstrating freedom from the stinginess of attachment to one's dwelling place.
Food and drink constitute offerings.

To provide food when one is hungry and to provide drink when one is thirsty is "offering" (*pūjā*); to advance wealth and advance practice is "nourishment" (*upastambha*). "Offering" refers to that which is presented; "nourishment" refers to the resources by which one is sustained.
Dwellings; bedding and furniture when the Sangha resides there.
Sleeping mats;
rope beds and wooden beds;
offerings for the time of sitting in meditation.
One should provide for every matter;
whatever is required shall be supplied in accordance with proper ritual.
If one lacks the necessary items, one should even sell oneself or one's children.
This indicates that because he established these practices with the utmost sincerity, they were not necessarily entirely non-existent.
Whatever was required for his needs, he provided it all;
as for what was essential, he did not fail him.

If a donor comes to invite the assembly of monks or visiting monks for whom there is a share of offerings, the monastery steward should assign the visiting monks to receive the invitation in due order.
The inviter does not distinguish between resident and visiting monks; once the visiting monks have arrived among the assembly, they should accordingly receive their portion.
Because a portion of the offerings and gains should be received through a formal sequence of appointment,
the resident monks alone accepted the invitation without appointing visiting monks.
Since the host did not invite the entire Saṃgha and did not state that he was inviting only the residents, yet they now accepted it exclusively, this constitutes a transgression.
This is a transgression.
The master of the monastic quarters incurs immeasurable sin.
To accept [the offerings] alone is greed; not to appoint [a replacement] is anger; there must necessarily be delusion—since these three poisons are all present, immeasurable sin is incurred.
Karma arises from this;
there is no difference from animals.
Merely craving wealth and food makes one's retribution equal to that of an animal, for such a person thinks only of water and grass.
He is not a śramaṇa;
he does not cease his evil mind;
he is not of the Śākya lineage.
This violates the words of the Buddha;
if one intentionally acts thus, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
O Sons of the Buddha, under no circumstances shall you accept special invitations for offerings and allow them to enter your own possession.
It is not prohibited for the donor to specifically designate a benefit for an individual member of the assembly;
however, such offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions.
Since the donor has no intention of inviting a specific group, the assembly generally comprises those from the ten directions, treating ordinary and noble alike.
Furthermore, by separately accepting invitations and taking the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself,
one not only incurs the offense of accepting separate invitations, but additionally commits the transgression of misappropriating the goods belonging to the eight fields of merit.
The property of all Buddhas, sages, individual teachers, parents, and the sick—
these five categories of objects in total— must not be taken for one's own personal use.
To use them for oneself constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
One should contemplate the principles of gain and loss, of fault and lack of fault, and of what should be employed and what should not be employed.
If there are, O Sons of the Buddha, ordained bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, and all donors—
These are people who, within the secular world, honor what is good and cultivate merit.
When they invite the Sangha as a field of merit to seek their aspirations,
these three types are shown as those who invite the Sangha to seek merit.
One should enter the monastic quarters and inquire of the administrative officers;
the Hall-Attendant (Upadhivārika) and the Ritual Master (Karmadāna) shall know the sequence.
If one now wishes to invite [the monks] according to their order:
If one who is capable of making the invitation is admonished, they will immediately obtain the presence of the worthy and holy Sangha of the ten directions.
Although the order of invitation may involve ordinary monks, one still obtains the merit of the worthy and holy ones; for when the mind is free from obstruction, one is equal to the worthy.
Because they are noble, they are subsumed within the Sangha of the ten directions; because their minds are impartial, they accord with the Buddha-mind.
Yet worldly people invite them separately;
worldly people, with the minds of ordinary beings, make such distinctions in their invitations.
Five hundred arhats,
the noble monks of the Hīnayāna,
and the bodhisattva saṃgha.
Although the noble monks of the Mahāyāna thus obtain vast merit,
it does not equal that of a single ordinary monk according to the monastic order;
the benefit and merit obtained by inviting a single ordinary monk according to the monastic order with a mind of equanimity is superior.
Because of the merit of [inviting] more than five hundred noble monks, if one’s mind is without discrimination, the merit obtained should be equal.
If one specifically invites individual monks,
one must specify the individuals being invited.
This is the dharma of the non-Buddhists.
The ritual protocols of the non-Buddhists include a method for separate invitations;
the Seven Buddhas have no such method for separate invitations.
Because the Buddha Vipaśyin did not originally possess these dharmas,
they do not accord with the way of filial piety and contravene the Buddha’s mind.
If one intentionally invites the Sangha separately, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). However,
if it is due to the power of a king or a minister, or if it does not follow personal favoritism but is for the sake of honoring virtue to achieve great benefit,
or if the regular sequence of invitations to the Sangha has already been completed, then there is no offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind—
that is, with the three poisons as the basis for that evil mind— takes this evil mind as the cause and gives rise to the thirteen subsequent evil dharmas for the sake of gain and support.
These are the conditions upon which they rely:
trafficking in the sexual favors of men and women; preparing their own food by hand, grinding and pounding it themselves;

practicing physiognomy on men and women, interpreting dreams for good or ill fortune, and determining whether a child will be male or female; performing incantations and crafts; training hawks; and compounding hundreds of kinds of poisons.
Various poisons, such as snake venom, gold and silver poisons—
where gold and silver possess poison or where poison is made to take on the appearance of gold and silver—
and *gū* (malevolent sorcery) poisons.
These are the evil dharmas that have been proscribed;
they are entirely devoid of compassion and filial piety.
These aforementioned evil dharmas harm sentient beings and contravene reason.
If one intentionally commits such an act, one incurs a minor offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind— driven by greed,
anger, and delusion— [acts in this way...]
They themselves slander the Triple Gem,
yet rely on the protection of the Triple Gem to seek wealth and profit,
feigning intimacy and attachment.
Outwardly manifesting refuge while inwardly plotting evil,
they verbally profess emptiness;
their mouths comply with the Triple Gem while constantly discoursing on the principle of emptiness.
Their conduct exists within the realm of existence.
Their actions contradict their words; though they speak with good intent, they plot evil deeds.
They act as intermediaries for laypeople, facilitating relations between men and women.
Although this person has left the household life, their mind harbors no thoughts of evil; yet, for the sake of wealth or profit, they act as a matchmaker,
conveying the intentions of men to women and the intentions of women to men,
engaging in sexual intercourse.
Mating also occurs through the union of two intermediaries;
this creates various fetters and attachments,
whereby one has been unable to attain liberation from beginningless time until now within the cycle of birth and death.
Regarding the six days of purification (*upoṣadha*):

among the five precepts, there are six days of purification each month—the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth—on which it is fitting to cultivate goodness; yet now one instead commits evil.
During the three months of the long fast—
namely the first, fifth, and ninth months—
one commits the sins of killing and stealing.
The six fast days and the three months are originally for laypeople (*avadātavasana*) to cultivate goodness; now, they instead practice evil deeds.
Those who break the fasts and violate the precepts—none of their various evils fail to stem from this breaking of fasts and violation of precepts.
One commits a minor offense (light defilement). These are the offenses established by the precepts;
these ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart, as explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts."
Exhortation to Broaden One’s Understanding.
Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra, Middle Volume.
Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra, Lower Volume.
The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha, after my parinirvāṇa,
such evils did not exist when the Buddha was in the world or during the first millennium of the True Dharma;
it is only in this degenerate age that they appear."
Precisely at this time, when the five turbidities are rampant during the age of the semblance dharma,
if one sees those of external paths who are deluded,
frantic, and ignorant, yet harbor hatred and jealousy toward the Buddha-dharma and commit such evil deeds.
All evil persons,
those who commit the ten non-virtuous actions,
and bandits.
This is also why evil persons who increase their wealth through robbery are further designated by this name.
They sell images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and parents;
they sell images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and world-appearing parents, and they also sell their own biological parents.
The selling of the sutras and vinaya is extremely common;
so too is the selling of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
The former refers to the sale of physical images; this refers to the sale of living persons.
It also refers to the sale of bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment].
When those who have first resolved to seek Buddhahood encounter such evil factions, they are sold.
Or, being compelled by official service,
they may owe goods to the government and sell themselves for money to pay the debt,
becoming slaves to anyone.
Those who sell designated objects have a specific purpose for doing so;
yet, when a Bodhisattva observes this,
they see before them the act of selling sacred images as if they were common worldly goods.
One should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness,
taking pity on those being sold who will surely undergo sorrow and suffering,
and employ skillful means to rescue and protect them.
Using skillful speech and excellent means of transformation, they correctly sell [the images] at the time of sale and protect them when there is a desire to sell.

Everywhere they teach and transform others to acquire funds to redeem Buddha and Bodhisattva images, as well as all scriptures and Vinaya texts belonging to Bhikṣus, Bhikṣuṇīs, and those who have resolved their minds toward Bodhisattvahood.
This clarifies what is protected by the teachings.
If one does not redeem [the transgressor], one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
This constitutes a formal offense for violating prohibitions.
If a Buddha’s disciple does not store swords, staves, bows, or arrows—
whereas the previous precept prohibited their storage, this precept prohibits their storage and sale— there is no grave offense in failing to respond. Furthermore,
they must not engage in selling with light scales or small measures, nor use official authority to seize the property of others, nor harbor malice by binding or destroying them.
Success. Family estate.

Because these various dharmas invite public slander, censure, and disapproval, and because they do not constitute a formal restraint (saṃvara), both the one who provides sustenance and the one who is sustained each incur half a transgression.
