If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind or two unwholesome minds...
One contemplates the fighting of all men and women alike.
Men and women may be categorized into four types:
those who fight in military arrays, soldiers and generals, bandits, and others.
When engaged in martial contests of equal skill, one must not vie with force nor risk one's life; one should observe this with the eye of the supreme precept.
Furthermore, one must not listen to the sound of blowing conch shells or other sea shells.
The drum:
it is sounding; it is movement. As soon as it is moved, it sounds.
The horn.
Its shape is curved like a horn;
it is a lute with seven strings.
The se has twenty-five strings;
the zheng.
It resembles a thirteen-stringed lute;
it has a single hole like a flute.
The *konghou* (harp-lute) has twenty-four strings. Song.
The sound of singing is *jiào*.
*Jiào* refers to the *jiàozi* (a type of wind instrument).
"Ji" (技) refers to artistry;
it is the sound of music.
However, because the two objects of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and sound (śabda) predominate,
it is thus; one must not play with dice,
which refers to the coordination of the four numbers.
Go (weiqi):
Emperor Yao used it to instruct his ignorant sons.
Pāsaka (Borasa xi).
In the Western Regions, there is a military game in which two players each deploy twenty or more elephants or horses on a board;
they vie for control of the main thoroughfares from afar, considering such mastery to be victory.
This is *tanqi*.
A board made of stone with a surface of jade or similar materials, its four corners raised, was commonly used by palace officials,
men, and women for the game of *liùbó* (six-in-hand).
This refers to the game of *shuanglu* (backgammon).
Regarding "hitting the ball" (*paiqiu*): this refers to playing by striking, hitting, tossing up, or tossing down the ball.
Stone-throwing:

this refers to playing with large stones by either dragging them along or tossing them; in common parlance, this is called "dragging the *dǔ*. Pitch-pot: [the art of throwing arrows into a small vessel].
The neck of the jar is one chi and two cun high, and its belly is five cun deep; twelve counting-sticks are used, representing the twelve months.
Throwing them beyond three steps is called "pitching the jar" (*touhu*).
There are eight paths for the sticks to follow.
The eight lines constitute the path; because the chess pieces and others follow along these paths, it is called "leading the path" (qiāndào), which refers to the eight paths.
This is the "moving city."
The ritual for walking the city walls is merely the play of children.
As for the "claw-mirror":

originally one uses a single mirror, but later one applies medicinal ointment to the fingernails, performs the ritual methods and incantations upon the mirror, and then one will see auspicious signs within the mirror.
Among the "inauspicious" and so forth,
"shī" (蓍) is the opposite of "shì" (式).
Grass.
It originates from low-lying, damp lands in the southeast; if it grows within a tortoise shell, this grass possesses spiritual power.
Where this grass grows, floating clouds appear above it.
Regarding the willow branch:
on the fifth day of the fifth month at noon, go beneath a willow tree and look upward for one that has broken itself.

Carve a human figure from this willow branch and place it in a quiet room. Offer sacrifices and recite incantations over it; it possesses spiritual efficacy, and by questioning it, one may know the fortune or misfortune of others.
"Bowl" (pōyú):
"Bowl" refers to a vessel; "basin" (yú) refers to a shallow dish. By means of a spell for consecrating vessels, one listens to the speech of others to know matters of good and ill fortune.
Using a skull for divination,
one can know good and bad fortune; if one seeks wealth and profit, one may then recite mantras to cause the person's heart to tremble,
and so forth.
They perform divination and soothsaying.

Regarding the four aforementioned matters, these do not apply; they belong exclusively to the fifth category. Divining by heating tortoise shells is called *bu* (divination), while manipulating the *shichang* stalks is called *shi* (soothsaying).

The practice of manipulating the *shichang* grass is a method of divination; furthermore, mirror-divination and soothsaying exist in this region, whereas divination using willow branches and the like exists in the West.
These belong to the state.
One must not engage in activities such as serving as a messenger for thieves or bandits.
These seventeen items are evil arts practiced by commoners, non-Buddhists, and wicked people; the Buddha has prohibited them.
If one fails to act, the two benefits are deficient;
if one does not perform each [of these duties], or performs them for improper reasons, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
If one attempts to transform sentient beings through "commonality" (samānārthatā) but fails, all others likewise incur offenses.
If a disciple of the Buddha upholds the prohibitive precepts,
their mind shall always protect and assist them in maintaining correctness and abiding in restraint; they shall be cautious and frugal in guarding against faults and preventing evil,
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
These are the four modes of deportment.
There are six periods of time throughout the day and night;
that is, three periods each for the daytime and the nighttime.
Read according to the original;
recite.
"Contrary to the root" refers to this bodhisattva precept.
It is like a vajra,
for the mind it sustains is firm and indestructible;
it is like one wearing a life-preserving float while wishing to cross the great ocean.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is extensive,
as is the *Grass-Tie Bhikṣu* story;
the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on Ornamentation) is also extensive.
One constantly gives rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna;
because one believes in the Mahāyāna teachings, principles, practices, and fruits,
one knows for oneself that one is a Buddha who is not yet perfected.
Because one has faith in the Mahāyāna, this is the beginning of the "great nature" (mahattva), and one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
All Buddhas are those who have already become Buddhas,
for they have relied upon the teachings to understand the principles, practiced accordingly, and realized the great fruit.
One must resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

Once faith has been established, one must desire to achieve it for oneself; one must necessarily give rise to the Great Bodhicitta, never allowing it to depart from the mind for even a single thought-moment.
There is no retrogression.
If one gives rise to even a single thought of the two vehicles or of non-Buddhists,
the small can obstruct the great, and the false can obstruct the correct.
One commits a minor offense.
If a Buddha-son, he should always give rise to all vows;
this is a general injunction for all Buddha-sons to always give rise to vows. From cause to fruition, as the various practices are extensive, so too must his vows be.
"Not one" is the general heading.
Filial piety toward one's parents is the first vow.
The preceptor,
the two vows,
and the Triple Gem.
The two characters for filial piety and obedience run through these three vows.
The fourth vow is: "May I obtain a good teacher and fellow students."
A virtuous friend and spiritual mentor—
may these five vows include the three characters "obtain" (得) as a thread running through them—
constantly instruct me in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.
Add the word "vow" (praṇidhāna) to the six [perfections] above.
[These constitute] the ten stages of setting out (daśa-prasthāna) and the seven noble ones (saptārya).
Ten nurtures,
eight vows,
and ten vajras.
The nine vows,
the ten stages,
and the ten vows.
May I attain understanding and practice according to the Dharma.
This concludes the explanation of the forty mental states above.
Firmly upholding the Buddha’s precepts, I would rather sacrifice my body and life than let them depart from my mind for even a single thought-moment.
All sons of the Buddha should constantly give rise to these ten kinds of great vows, with their minds never regressing.
If any bodhisattva does not give rise to these vows, they commit a minor offense.
To violate these regulations constitutes an offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha, having made the ten great vows,
then makes the vows of the ten precepts inferior [to them], [he commits an offense].
One upholds the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha.
Upholding the precepts serves as the causal practice, while making vows serves as the auxiliary practice; when these practices support one another, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
One should make this vow, saying:
The preceding marks the expression of the vow; what follows is the formal wording of the aspiration.
"I would rather cast this body into a great pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of knives than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
The sūtras and vinayas of all Buddhas state that to engage in sexual misconduct is to destroy the sūtras and vinayas, whereas to refrain from such conduct is not to destroy them.
Furthermore, one who commits impure acts with any woman may make this vow:
Beyond his previous vows, he made another vow:
"I would rather have my body encircled on all sides by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh than, with a body that has broken the precepts,
accept any clothing from a faithful donor."
Because he formerly gave robes with pure faith, he obtained skin as pure and golden in color;
now that he has broken the precepts, he does not produce such superior merit and cannot receive offerings of faith, and thus he makes this vow.

Furthermore, they make this vow: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and great flowing fierce fires with this mouth for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever use a mouth that has broken the precepts to eat the food of a hundred flavors offered by faithful donors."
By giving food with pure faith, one obtains longevity, eloquence, peace and happiness, wondrous complexion, and the full endowment of heroic strength and vigor.
By giving drink, one obtains the eternal departure from all thirst of afflictions and the full endowment thereof.
To be free from the four faults of speech is able to generate such merit; now that you have committed these four transgressions of speech, may you [be purified].

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather lie with this body upon a floor of hot iron within a great net of fierce flames than ever receive a hundred kinds of beds and seats from a faithful donor with a precept-violating body."

With pure faith, one originally prays for the supreme state that transcends the mundane; yet, having personally committed three transgressions of bodily karma, one cannot generate the merit of "defeat" (parājika) in others—this is my wish for you.

Furthermore, he made this vow: "I would rather endure three hundred spear thrusts with this body for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever receive the hundred-flavored medicines and provisions from faithful donors with a body that has broken the precepts."
By giving medicine to the sick, one should obtain the perfect nectar of the deathless, the wondrous medicine free from old age, illness, and death, lacking nothing;
yet since this merit does not arise now because my body has committed these three transgressions, I pray thus.

Furthermore, he made this vow: "I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever again receive with a body of broken precepts the various kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, and fields offered out of faith by a donor."
By virtue of having given houses and dwellings as gifts, one shall become a shelter, a home, a refuge, a resort, a haven, and a destination for all sentient beings, lacking nothing;
by virtue of having given gardens, groves, fields, and lands as gifts, one obtains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and samādhi;
therefore, the three unwholesome actions of the body [of the donor] are now difficult to surpass even by such superior merit.
Thus he made this vow: "I pray that it may be so.

Furthermore, I make this vow: 'I would rather have this body of mine, from head to foot, smashed with an iron hammer until it is like fine dust, than ever receive the respectful prostrations and offerings of a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts.'"
Bending the body and humbling the mind to pay reverent homage to the Triple Gem can evoke the merit of the "unseen crown" (*anavalokitamūrdha*), which is a primary retribution;
since this merit is difficult to produce even when one practices the three modes of conduct oneself, the vow is thus expressed.

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather have my two eyes gouged out with hundreds of thousands of hot iron knives and spears than ever look upon the beautiful forms of others with a mind that violates the precepts.
By giving various excellent requisites as gifts, he attains the perfection of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Since there is no dharma that is not fully perfected, if one now breaks the precepts and regards the dust-like color of what other donors have given as insignificant, this merit will not arise;
therefore, one should establish a vow.
Furthermore, one should make this vow: "I would rather have my ears pierced all over with hundreds of thousands of iron awls for the duration of one kalpa or two kalpas."
I never, even with a mind of broken precepts, listened to pleasant sounds.

By bestowing various kinds of music and chanting the wondrous and sublime voices of the Triple Gem, I obtained the Tathāgata’s divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), which can perceive all subtle and exquisite sounds.
Now that I have broken my precepts, this merit will not arise; therefore, I pray as follows:
Furthermore,
he made this vow: "I would rather have my nose cut off by a hundred thousand blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts,
greedily smell various fragrances."
Because one has given powdered incense and ground incense as offerings, one shall obtain pure precepts, extensive learning, and all *samādhis*.
Because one has practiced the noble conduct of applying incense, one shall obtain a body that is universally fragrant and pure.
Because it is difficult for the merit of noble conduct to arise when one’s own mind violates the precepts, you now establish this vow.

He further made this vow: "I would rather have my tongue severed by hundreds of thousands of sharp blades than ever, with a mind that has broken the precepts, consume the hundred-flavored pure food of others.
Now, he merely takes the flavors tasted by the tongue among the five sensory objects, which differ from what the third Buddha previously spoke of regarding the gift of superior flavors.
One who [maintains purity] shall experience the supreme flavor of ambrosia and attain the mark of a great man;
among all flavors, they will always obtain the most excellent, ultimate flavor. Since the merit of the supreme flavor of precept-breaking does not arise now, I therefore establish this vow.
He further made this vow: "I would rather have my body hacked to pieces with a sharp axe than, with a mind that violates the precepts, crave pleasant tactile sensations.

These refer to the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) among the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); because they are exquisite, agreeable, pleasing, and gratifying to the mind, they are called "pleasant tactile sensations" (*sukha-spraṣṭavya*).
By giving such things as clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions, merit arises, as explained above;
however, since it is now difficult for merit to arise from those who have broken the precepts, one establishes this vow.
Again, he made this vow: "May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood.
This is the thirteenth vow: to universally benefit the infinite sentient beings of the Dharma-realm and to collectively fulfill the vow for unexcelled Bodhi.
If a bodhisattva does not make these vows, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
This is a transgression against the established regulations; all bodhisattvas must collectively make the aforementioned thirteen vows.
If a Buddha’s disciple, they should constantly practice *dhūta* during two periods:
the two seasons of spring and autumn.
The correct term is *dhūta*, which means "to discard. There are twelve kinds of *dhūta* practices, each possessing ten types of superior merits and functions as described in the *Dvādaśadhūta-sūtra*.
Regarding the ten aspects of the practice of constant sitting (*naiṣadyika*), they are:
first, not craving the pleasure of the body; second, not craving the pleasure of sleep; third, not craving the pleasure of bedding; fourth, having no bedding...

At that time, there were ten benefits: first, one is free from the suffering of being attached to fine seats; second, the five [hindrances] do not accompany one; third, one’s desires are few; fourth, it is easy to obtain seats for meditation; fifth, it is easy to read and recite the scriptures;

sixth, the hindrance of sleep is slight; seventh, the body is light and easy to rouse; eighth, the mind has little craving for seeking seats, bedding, or clothing; ninth, [the mind is] focused on the Dharma; tenth, [one is] free from the affliction of attachment to material things.
He sat in meditation throughout both winter and summer;
he did not emerge even during the most extreme cold or heat, and fearing that many insects and ants would be harmed by the summer heat,
he entered the summer retreat.
The text for seeking the noble path and observing the summer retreat is extensive.
One should regularly use *yāṣṭika* (willow branches), also known as tooth-sticks; the following lists eighteen matters.
Soap powder can remove impurities and cleanse the mouth and hands.
The three robes.
The five-strip robe, the seven-strip robe, and the great robe (saṃghāṭī)—the robes of the field of merit—must always be kept with one.
The *kundi* (Sanskrit; here translated as "pure vessel") is used to hold water for purifying the hands.
The almsbowl (pātra)—
its full name is pātrā, which here means "an appropriate vessel.
The sitting mat (niṣīdana).
Having properly spread out his seat and paid homage to the Buddha and his mendicant’s staff,
he concentrated his mind without distraction to ward off dangers such as tigers.
Incense burner:
for burning incense of faith.
Water strainer: for filtering water.
One should immediately use a water filter, for fear of consuming insects;
there are also hand towels,
face towels, and foot towels, which must be kept separate according to their respective functions.
A knife: four inches in length, used for cutting fingernails, tailoring garments, and so forth.
A pair of tongs.
The fire-mirror is made of copper; by facing it toward the sun, one obtains fire for burning incense, preparing food, and so forth.
The tweezers are for extracting thorns and removing hair.
A rope bed;
sitting in meditation and practicing *śamatha-vipaśyanā* wherever one may be.
Sūtra.
One must examine the Buddha’s intention to collect the mind and eliminate distraction.
Regarding the Vinaya,
since one must know the rules for maintaining and violating precepts, there ought logically to be a treatise that elucidates the training in wisdom.
Buddha images.
By contemplating these images, one may come to know the true Buddha.
Bodhisattva images.

One should always regard those who have advanced in practice as virtuous friends; therefore, these eighteen items, which together constitute the conditions for practicing *dhūta* and progressing on the Path, must be kept constantly by one's side.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva practices *dhūta*, [these are required].
This refers to the two previous periods,
as well as the period of traveling abroad to pay homage and pursue studies.
Wherever one comes from,
there must be a place from which one departs;
whether it be a hundred li or a thousand li.
By citing these two numbers, it is implied that all other items—whether distant or near, coming or going—are likewise composed of these substances.
These eighteen kinds of objects constantly follow the body;
this refers to the time of traveling abroad.
Regarding the dhūta [practices]:
the following two periods are for wearing [the robes] according to one's person.
From the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the [fifteenth day of the tenth month].
Of these five items, eighteen kinds of objects are always to accompany the body during two periods of time.
However, for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as prescribed in the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras, certain requisites must invariably accompany the person at all times, regardless of the specific occasion.
Just as a bird has two wings,
so too are time and objects; without wings, a bird cannot soar high, and a bodhisattva deficient in these cannot travel far.
If on the day of the *poṣadha*, there should be a monk who has come after a dispute, the Buddha instructed that the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) be adjusted accordingly:

if it is known he will arrive on the fourteenth day, one should recite them before the thirteenth; if it is known he will arrive on the fifteenth, one should recite them on the fourteenth; or else one may not recite them at all, or follow his arrival.
On whatever day the disputes are extinguished, one should immediately speak [the precepts].
A newly initiated bodhisattva should recite the Dharma-precepts of the Buddhas during the *poṣadha* every half-month.

When reciting the precepts, if one performs the *poṣadha* alone before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, that single person shall recite them; if there are two or three people, they should do so together.
Even if there are as many as a hundred thousand people, there shall be only one person who recites; the reciter sits on a high seat while the listeners sit on lower seats.
Each person dons the nine-striped, seven-striped, or five-striped *kāṣāya* robe.

In the Sanskrit language this is called *poṣadha*, which is translated here as "Pure Abiding" (*jìngzhù*), or simply "Purity" (*jìng*). This is because through confession, the vessel of one's own body becomes pure.

"Purity of Abiding" (Jingzhu) is also called "Nurturing" (Changyang), meaning to nurture the pure mind; it is also called "Harmonizing the Great Assembly," meaning to harmonize with all Buddhas in their activities.

If there are four or more people, one performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). If there are three people, each cultivates the proper ritual demeanor and further says:
"Two Venerable Sirs, please attend to me with a single mind. Today is the fifteenth day of the month, and I, [Name], shall recite the precepts."
If two people are facing each other, they should proceed as described above; if it is a single person, they should mentally contemplate and verbally recite:
"Today is the fifteenth day for the Sangha’s recitation of the precepts; I, [Name], am pure. This should be stated three times for each.
The procedures for entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*) are each performed according to the Dharma;
this is the text for entering the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*).
This applies when one is practicing the dhūta ascetic practices.
When a bodhisattva practices the twelve kinds of dhūta ascetic virtues,
he must not enter difficult places;
this is the general designation of difficult places.
If there are national calamities, an evil king, uneven terrain, dense vegetation, lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, wind,
or the perils of bandits on the road, or venomous snakes;
This is a separate enumeration of the eight difficulties (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa).
One cannot enter any of these difficult places.
This concludes the eight locations mentioned above.
If one practices the dhūta austerities or even observes the summer retreat (varṣā), one must not enter any such dangerous places.
One who wanders abroad must not enter them, nor may one enter during the summer retreat.
If one intentionally enters them, one commits a minor offense (duṣkṛta).
To violate these regulations constitutes an offense.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha, you should sit according to the proper sequence of the Dharma.
Since you are called a "disciple of the Buddha," you must know that the correct Dharma and the ritual order of etiquette ought to accord with the law; this is the general heading.
This refers to the sequence.
Those who have received the precepts first sit in front, while those who have received them later sit behind.
This precisely clarifies the order of precedence.
Regardless of age— whether they be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, nobles, kings, princes, or even eunuchs and slaves—
those who have received the precepts first shall sit in front, while those who have received the precepts later shall sit in order behind them.
This specifically indicates that Bodhisattvas must sit according to their respective order based on the protocols of the fourfold assembly, without allowing any confusion or disorder.
Do not be like the foolish outsiders who sit without precedence or sequence— whether old or young— like soldiers or slaves.
Regarding this Dharma,

the heterodox are foolish and dull, truly ignorant of ritual propriety; as soldiers and slaves who are fierce and base, they find it difficult to distinguish between the honorable and the lowly, and thus there is no established order.
In my Buddha-dharma, those who come first sit first, and those who come later sit later.
Because the Buddha-dharma has its regulations, one establishes one's own correctness according to this sequence.
If a bodhisattva sits out of accordance with the proper sequence, they commit a minor offense.
Violating the prohibitions incurs offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha constantly teaches and transforms others,
being able to personally advance in goodness and diminish [the faults of] those they transform, such a person is called a Bodhisattva.
All sentient beings are those to be transformed; thus,
one establishes monasteries.
It is a place for the peaceful dwelling of the Sangha;
a site where Buddha-stupas are erected amidst mountains, forests, gardens, and fields;
and a location for the practice of the Way.
Places for sitting in meditation during the winter and summer retreats—
deep chambers and quiet rooms removed from noisy and cluttered environments—
should be established in all locations where practitioners walk the Path.
However, wherever one enters to practice the path of cultivation, one should honor and maintain it so that it remains pure and elegant.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings without distinction between enemy and kin.
To expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas clarifies the proper conduct of a bodhisattva. Because the bodhisattva possesses great faculties, they expound the Mahāyāna.
[This applies even] in cases of illness.
When all sentient beings suffer from illness, one should preach the Sūtras and the Vinaya for them to rescue them.
In times of national calamity or the threat of bandits,
one should likewise rescue them as described above.
On the day of the passing of one’s parents, brothers, preceptors, or teachers, as well as during the third week and up to the seventh week,
one should read, recite, and expound upon Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas at all assemblies for the observance of fasts and the seeking of merit.

Regarding the initial day of death, or the anniversary of death each year—which is the *jichén* (taboo day)—one begins with the first seven-day period, up through the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh seven-day periods.
Question: If one merely lectures on the sutras for the deceased, that will suffice; why is it necessary to observe these seven-day periods? Answer:
Within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the being undergoes death once every seven days. It is essential [to provide support during these intervals].
It is said thus because one receives birth through the merit of the sutras serving as sustenance for illness.
"Coming and going to manage one's livelihood" has the meaning of providing for one's life; those who seek profit do so mostly for the sake of sustaining their lives.
When the five perils arise— being burned by great fires, swept away by great floods, blown about by black winds, shipwrecks upon rivers and great oceans,
or the danger of rākṣasas.
Furthermore, one should read, recite, and expound upon this sutra and its vinaya,
causing each person to read, recite, and expound this precept-sutra; for this sutra is itself the vinaya,
extending even to all karmic retributions for transgressions.
To summarize the gravity of these matters, this sutra explains them collectively:
the three evil realms are precisely the three paths of suffering.
The seven heinous offenses,
karmic obstructions,
and the eight difficulties; being bound by handcuffs, fetters, stocks, and shackles upon their bodies.
These are all karmic obstacles (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
Having much lust, much anger, and much delusion are afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Those with many illnesses and those hindered by karmic retribution should all read, recite, and expound upon this sutra and its vinaya.
These three obstacles can likewise be extinguished by reciting this sutra.
If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not do so, they commit a minor offense (light impurity) and violate a prohibition,
thereby incurring a karmic penalty.
These nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind; they shall be explained in detail within the Chapter on the Brahma-Mandala.
This is the summary and exhortation pointing toward the detailed exposition.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, when bestowing the precepts upon others..."
This refers to the occasion when one seeks to receive the precepts;
at that time, one must not exercise discrimination.
For the Buddha is truly able to bestow [the precepts] and universally save all with a compassionate heart.
"All. This is a general enumeration of those being excluded:
kings, princes, ministers, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, laywomen, lecherous men, and lecherous women.

Women, the eighteen Brahmā deities, the six classes of desire-realm devas, those without sexual organs, those with dual organs, eunuchs, slaves, and all ghosts and spirits are all capable of receiving the precepts.

This is a specific demonstration that there are seventeen categories of vessels for the precepts; however, they must understand the language and be able to comprehend the meaning of the texts in order [to receive them].
One who is capable of receiving the precepts but does not understand the language is not a fit vessel for the precepts.
One should instruct them regarding the *kāṣāya* robe they wear;
this is because those who have left the household life receive the precepts in robes of improper color.
All [garments] are dyed with a discolored hue;
by altering the original white color, they contravene the mind of attachment and thus accord with the Path.
In accordance with the path of practice one cultivates, one must wear robes of appropriate color and abandon emotional attachments.
All dyed garments— whether blue, yellow, red, black, or purple— as well as all bedding and requisites, must be entirely dyed in a discolored hue.
This clearly explains the practice of wearing dyed robes.
All garments worn on the body must be colored;
with the exception of the *kāṣāya*, all other garments must likewise have their original white color altered. Aside from white, all other colors are [permissible].
It is called "altering the color" because it alters the original white color.
In all lands, whatever clothing people wear, a bhikṣu must ensure that his attire differs from that of the laity.
Regardless of which country or region one may be in, it is sufficient that one’s appearance differs from that of the local common dress.
When wishing to receive the precepts, one should announce to the preceptor: "There is a person seeking the precepts who wishes to receive them from the preceptor."
The preceptor should ask:
"The preceptor asks you:
'In this present life, have you not committed any of the seven heinous offenses?'"
Because it is impossible to know [the offenses] from such a remote past, one asks only about the seven grave obstacles present in the current life;
thus, such a person is not a fit vessel for the precepts. Therefore, when intending to confer the precepts, one first inquires regarding their transgressions.
A Bodhisattva Dharma Master must not confer the precepts upon a person who has committed the seven heinous offenses in this present life.
"Admonition" refers to the precept-bestowing master.

The seven heinous offenses are: shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an ācārya, causing a schism in the Saṃgha that obstructs the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and killing an arhat.
This enumerates the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*).
If one possesses all seven prohibitions, one cannot receive the precepts in this very life;
this is the reason why it is determined that such a person should not receive them.
All other persons may fully receive the precepts;
with the exception of those who have committed the seven heinous offenses, others who understand the words of the preceptor may receive the precepts.
This is the dharma for those who have left the household life.
The rules of ritual procedure:
one does not prostrate before kings, nor does one prostrate before parents;
these are the rules for those who have left the household life.
That one's six relatives do not show respect is also a sense of not performing prostrations.
That ghosts and spirits do not pay homage means that there are those who come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Dharma, simply because they understand the Dharma Master’s words.
However, the conclusion following the word "but" (但) establishes that one must certainly bestow the precepts without making any distinctions.
If a Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, does not immediately bestow the precepts upon all sentient beings,
they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
If a disciple of the Buddha teaches others to give rise to faith,
they must take that initial faith as the foundation for benefiting others, as the primary basis for entering the Dharma, and as the foremost gateway to transcending toward the Path of the Sages.
When a bodhisattva acts as a teacher who provides instruction to others,
this refers specifically to one capable of teaching; such a person,
upon seeing someone wishing to receive the precepts, [should act accordingly].
When one sees someone coming to request the precepts,
one should instruct them to invite two masters; thus,
one instructs the person seeking the precepts to make the invitation.
Upādhyāya refers to the invisible teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata; Ācārya...
"I myself am the visible teacher.
Regarding the two teachers, one should ask as follows:
"The first teacher" refers to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the *ācārya*; the second teacher is the one who asks. If the Buddha were in the world, it would be the Buddha’s awakening.

Śāriputra, after the present Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, you should ask the teachers of the six heretical schools: "Is the preceptor who transmits the precepts the upādhyāya, or is the karmavācanā master the ācārya?
This is intended to correspond to the passage in the sūtras concerning the six masters.
"Do you have the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)? If these offenses are manifest in this present life, the preceptor should not confer the precepts upon you;
if you do not have the seven obstructing offenses, you may receive the precepts.
This is the method for inquiring regarding obstructing offenses.
If there are those who commit the ten grave offenses—
the ten *pārājika* transgressions—
they should be instructed to perform repentance.
Since heavy offenses reside within you, they will inevitably obstruct the Noble Path; therefore, you must perform repentance.

Before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, this instructor shall teach you the ritual procedures so that you may, before the sacred image, with utmost sincerity and profound remorse, repent for your transgressions.
Reproach.
Six times throughout the day and night, recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
This is the manner of performing repentance; by reciting the precepts, one recalls and recognizes the characteristics of transgressions.
With utmost sincerity and earnest urgency,
he prostrated before the thousand Buddhas of the three periods of time.
With a reverent and devout mind, one prostrates before three thousand Buddhas throughout three kalpas.
To "attain the vision of auspicious signs" is the general description; these are, that is to say, signs of good fortune.
Whether it be seven days, two or three weeks, or even up to one year—these are the time limits for repentance.
This is because the obstructions of each individual vary, being either thick or thin, distant or near.
One must see auspicious signs;
one's limit is simply the seeing of such signs.
"Auspicious signs" refers to the Buddha coming to touch one’s head, seeing light, seeing flowers, and various other extraordinary phenomena.
The characteristics of what is seen in clarity are of many kinds, as explained in other sutras.
One thereby attains the extinction of transgressions;
because the obstructions are exhausted, the manifestation of these signs results in the extinction of transgressions.
If there are no auspicious signs, it is because the precepts have no form or characteristics and cannot be known; for this reason, it is said thus.
Although one performs repentance, it is of no benefit.
Because precepts are manifested through signs, and that which is signless cannot manifest the perfection of the precepts;
such a person, even in their present body, does not obtain the precepts,
nor do they attain the perfection of their former precepts.
One may then receive the precepts with increased intensity;

this merely causes the precepts to be further augmented, strengthened, and nourished, though they have not yet reached full perfection. One must receive them again in order to achieve the complete, formless, and manifest precepts.
If one commits any of the forty-eight minor precepts, the offense is extinguished through confession before another person.
One should stand before a Buddha image and address the other person face-to-face, saying: "Venerable Bhikṣu [Name], I have committed such-and-such an offense;
I now confess it to you, O Virtuous One. I pray that you will take pity on me and remember that I am pure, so that this offense may be extinguished. (Recite three times.)

The previous statement regarding the formal admonition by the Saṃgha says: "You must deeply repent for yourself and not commit [the offense] again hereafter. [The candidate] replies: "How could that be possible?

It is not the same as the seven *ānantarya* (obstructive) offenses. This is explained by way of contrast; since the characteristics of the aforementioned seven *ānantarya* offenses are such that they can also be extinguished, it is said "it is not the same. One should further say: "Nor is it..."
The ten grave precepts are the same [as those for laypeople]. However,
regarding the "instructor" (śikṣācārya), the Buddha spoke of the teacher capable of providing instruction.
Within this Dharma,
one should thoroughly understand each of the characteristics of the light and heavy offenses among the three aforementioned categories.
To thoroughly understand the gravity or lightness [of offenses], to know that light offenses— whether with signs or without signs— are extinguished or not,
and to realize according to reality and in accordance with the Dharma what is expressed by the teachings, is called "excellent understanding.
This applies even if one does not understand the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas.
This refers to those who are deluded regarding the teachings.
Because they do not understand the characteristics of right and wrong— whether grave or light—
concerning the seven prohibitions, the ten major precepts, and the forty-eight minor precepts mentioned previously.
Not understanding the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya),
and not knowing the principle of the truly supreme truth as it is expounded; this is the stage of the nature of the cultivated seeds (śrutavāsanā-bīja).
The ten faiths nurture the nature and encompass the ten abidings and ten practices.
The nature of the lineage (*gotra*) is the indestructible nature;
it is the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) and the nature of the path (*mārga-gotra*).
The ten stages,
the nature of the True Dharma,
and the state of Buddhahood do not explain the characteristics of the subduing and abandoning of afflictions throughout the five positions.
Regarding the various degrees of meditative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*),
this clarifies the extent of practice within the five stages and the entry into and emergence from the ten factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*).
Although the four dhyānas possess eighteen factors without confusion, they actually consist of only ten: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, samādhi, adhyātmasaṃprasāda, upekṣā, smṛti, and prajñā.

The remaining [eight] are the suffering, pleasure, equanimity, and mindfulness experienced during the process of emerging from and entering into the dhyānas; thus, each of the four dhyānas possesses a varying number of factors.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
they do not understand the rules for the progression of all contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-caryā*),
nor do they individually grasp the essential meaning within these dharmas.
In summary, because they do not understand the ten factors within the five stages,
bodhisattvas become greedy for gain and profit for the sake of offerings and remuneration.
For the sake of fame and reputation,
they falsely claim to be able to explain [the teachings];
this is a wicked pursuit.
Seeking unrighteously and with force;
seeking excessively;
and seeking without satiety.
Disciples who crave profit;
disciples who are greedily attached to fame and gain,
yet falsely pretend to understand all the sutras and vinayas.
To be inwardly ignorant while outwardly manifesting the appearance of understanding is to deceive oneself;
it is to conceal one's own mind and remain unaware of one's own lack of comprehension.
Furthermore, to deceive others—
meaning that one who lacks understanding yet misleads others is deceiving them—
one who bestows the precepts upon another commits a secondary offense (light defilement).
If a disciple of the Buddha, for the sake of profit and gain, should [speak] before one who has not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts—
even if that person belongs to a great clan— because they have not yet resolved upon the Great Mind nor do they yet believe in the Great Precepts.
In the presence of non-Buddhist heretics and evil persons who slander the Mahāyāna,
one shall proclaim these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas.
The Buddhas upon the thousand petals, or the three thousand Buddhas of the three periods of time, all preach these precepts.
One must not preach them before those with wrong views,
nor should one slander them.
Except for the king.
Because the king possesses the power to either harm or benefit the Buddha-dharma, he must be told [the truth] when it is necessary;
all others are not permitted to speak [of such matters].

For ordinary people, one should not preach; however, for high ministers, it may be preached. One may also preach to those with the power to admonish the king regarding what benefits or harms the Buddha-dharma.
As for these evil persons, they do not receive the Buddha’s precepts.
This phrase runs through what follows:
they are called "animals" (tiryagyoni),
for their folly is as extreme as that of animals.
Life after life they shall not see the Triple Gem;
they will inevitably fall into ruin, for by not seeing them and failing to honor or behold them, they are as if they do not exist at all—
like wood or stone, devoid of mind.
Those who do not understand the fruits of karma and yet hold them accountable are like those of external paths and heterodox views; they are no different from wooden stumps.
This explains why it is said that there are eight reasons [for their failure], which refers precisely to the eightfold sūtra passage.
As for the Bodhisattva preaching the seven Buddha-teachings on the precepts before such evil persons:
in truth, these precepts have been taught by the sands-of-the-Ganges Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time—those who have already taught, those yet to teach, and those teaching now;
it is merely out of proximity that he speaks of "seven" here.
One commits a minor offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha has left the household life with faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, yet gives rise to the intention to violate these sacred precepts—
this clearly refers to a person who violates the precepts.
One must not accept the offerings of any donors.
This is because if one were to divide a single hair into a hundred thousand parts, even taking away just one part would diminish the donor's merit;
it is like sowing seeds in salt-encrusted soil where, despite the planting, no sprouts or fruit will grow.
Furthermore, one may not walk upon the ground of the king’s realm nor drink from the king’s waters.
Of the sevenfold merit derived from observing the precepts, the king receives two parts;
now that you have broken the precepts and possess no such merit, you must pay the king’s tax by walking upon his land and drinking from his waters.
Five thousand great ghosts constantly obstructed his path, crying out, "Great thief!
You who receive offerings without observing the precepts gain no merit for others; it is like stealing another's property.
Furthermore, whenever he entered a room, a city, or a house, the ghosts would constantly sweep away his footprints.
When the deity who protects those whose precepts are perfect becomes enraged at one who has broken them,
all people of the world will revile him, saying, "He is a thief within the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, all the devas, nāgas, and spirits who possess the divine eye will see the monk who violates the precepts as he approaches and call him a thief.
When they come or go, it is said that "the thief has gone.
All sentient beings do not wish to see them;
including those among devas and humans, none desire to behold them.
A person who violates the precepts is no different from an animal;
though rebuked as being like an animal, they think only of their food, being deluded and lacking awareness or discernment,
no different from a block of wood.
Furthermore, they are like wood or stone— stolid, obstructive, and devoid of cognition.
If one intentionally violates the right precepts, then for each instance of transgression,
whether minor or grave, against those right precepts, [the consequence follows].
One commits a minor offense;
by intentionally disparaging [the teachings], one incurs sin that destroys the body.
Therefore, O Sons of the Buddha, you should always maintain a single mind.
The sons of the Buddha cultivate goodness without permitting negligence; they advance in goodness without distraction, cultivating the mind without interruption.
They receive and uphold its text, grasping and maintaining it without forgetfulness.
"Reciting and chanting":
to read according to the original text is called "reading," and to recite from memory is called "chanting.
This refers to the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas.
Regarding the great practice of benefiting both self and others:
one might flay one's skin to make paper, draw blood for ink, use marrow as water, and break one's bones for pens to transcribe the Buddha’s precepts.
This merely expresses their supreme importance; however, protecting and upholding the Buddha’s precepts does not necessarily require using [one’s own body] to be fit for writing them.
Paper made from bamboo bark,
mulberry bark, and so forth.
Grain paper refers to the *zhù* and *gòu* trees. Silk,
plain cloth, bamboo, and silk-bamboo scrolls [are other materials].
Steam-bamboo tablets can be split and spread out like paper;
they should all be used for writing and kept. These are precisely suitable for writing upon.
One should always use caskets made of the seven treasures, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels to contain the scrolls of the sutras and vinayas.
One must strictly uphold the Buddha’s precepts;
if one fails to make offerings in accordance with the Dharma, [the consequences will follow].
Based on what was stated above, this is called acting in accordance with the Dharma; now, because it is not in accordance with the Dharma, one shall receive its retribution.
One commits a minor offense (light dust-offense) and a crime of violating regulations.
If a disciple of the Buddha constantly gives rise to the mind of great compassion—
since if compassion does not arise, there is no means by which to transform sentient beings—
and should enter all cities, towns, houses, and dwellings.
In the places where he travels to transform others,
he sees all sentient beings;
those whom he transforms through his own cultivation of the Great Practice are those who pass through the five vehicles.
One should proclaim: "All you sentient beings, you should all receive [the precepts].

Although one cannot ensure that everyone actually receives them through this formal exhortation, one universally transforms their aspirational mind so that they may receive them, and further causes them to know that the precepts are worthy of being received.
The three refuges and ten precepts firmly establish this gradual transformation; causing one to receive the remaining precepts is the cause for the Mahāyāna precepts.
If one sees oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, or any other domestic animals...

It is not that they do not understand human speech or are unable to generate the resolve for enlightenment; rather, this statement is made based on the fact that the Bodhisattva’s compassion is impartial.
Furthermore, there are certain classes of beings such as nāgas who, having come from among humans or devas at the beginning of a kalpa, all speak in human language.
One should mentally reflect and speak these words aloud:
"With a heart moved by compassion, as if addressing you with these words, my intent is to awaken you and establish the distant causal conditions for your future.
You, who are an animal, shall now give rise to the bodhicitta."

The *Dharmapada* states that five hundred monkeys, imitating arhats by erecting a stupa and performing prostrations morning and evening, encountered a mountain torrent and were swept away all at once;
they were immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The same applies to five hundred white rabbits.
All of these were animals who gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva enters all places— mountains, rivers, forests, and fields— they cause all sentient beings therein to resolve upon bodhicitta;
this clarifies the locations where they transform others.
If this bodhisattva does not give rise to the mind to teach and transform sentient beings,
failing to transform them and thus lacking the practice of benefiting others through the arousal of the bodhicitta,
they commit a minor offense.
If a disciple of the Buddha constantly practices teaching and transformation,
they should follow the teachings to transform others, causing them to attain progress and penetration through the principles of cultivation and abandonment; thus,
they should give rise to a heart of great compassion.
If compassion does not arise, it is difficult to transform those whose conduct is difficult to transform; this is the cause for transforming their conduct.
One enters the households of donors to cultivate the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Noble families:
the households of dukes, ministers, and those of high station;
among all such assemblies.
The two assemblies, the four assemblies, and the eight classes of beings constitute the audience for whom the Dharma is preached.
One must not stand while preaching the Dharma to laypeople; rather, the Dharma-preacher bhikṣu should sit upon a high seat before the assembly of laypeople.
He must not stand on the ground while preaching the Dharma to the four assemblies.
This demonstrates the proper protocol for preaching the Dharma.
When preaching, the Dharma master shall sit upon a high seat, provided with offerings of incense and flowers, while the fourfold assembly of listeners sits on lower seats,
as if serving their parents with filial piety or honoring the instructions of a teacher.
This concerns the matter of reverence in speaking and listening. For example,
it is like the fire-worshipping Brahmins,
such as the three Kāśyapas, who daily perform their rites of worship to the fire deity at the three times of the day.
If one who preaches the Dharma does not preach in accordance with the Dharma,
but clarifies only the verbal karma while neglecting the bodily and mental karmas,
they commit a minor offense.
If there are sons of the Buddha who receive the Buddha’s precepts with a mind of faith—
since a mind of faith is the cause for receiving the precepts, and without it one would certainly be unwilling to receive them—
whether they be kings, crown princes, officials of the hundred ranks, or disciples of the fourfold assembly.
These seven classes of people are all those who have received the Buddha’s precepts with faith;

yet, relying on their own noble status, they destroy the Buddha-dharma and its precepts by openly establishing restrictive regulations that forbid my fourfold assembly of disciples from leaving the household life to practice the Way,
and likewise prohibit the creation of images, stūpas, sūtras, and vinaya texts.

This means to rely on one's own noble status to destroy the Dharma. Even if the fourfold assembly lacks the power to restrain the Dharma themselves, if they rely upon and entrust themselves to the first three [assemblies], they likewise destroy the Dharma.
The first three can only restrain the latter four; thus, both the restrainer and the restrained are as described in the sutras.

This is the sin of destroying the Triple Gem; yet if a bodhisattva intentionally acts as one who destroys the Dharma—such as by ordaining evil persons, manufacturing images for sale, and so forth—they commit a secondary offense (light defilement).
Apart from such cases involving the control of evil people, the manufacture of images, sales, and the like, all other instances constitute the sin of destroying the Triple Gem.
If a disciple of the Buddha does not leave the household life with a good heart—
"good" meaning wholesome, while "not good" refers to the three poisons, among which greed is predominant—
then they do so for the sake of fame and profit.

This was indeed the doing of an evil mind; it was because he sought to attract a high reputation for himself and gain offerings that he preached the Dharma and precepts of the Seven Buddhas before the king and his ministers.
When a bhikṣu comes and explains the轻重 (light and heavy) precepts to the king and his ministers,
and those ministers understand and recognize what the bhikṣu has transgressed, they shall then punish him accordingly.

"Imposed. This refers to cases where Buddhist bhikṣus have violated the precepts; because they are required only to perform repentance and are subject to punishment according to secular law, it is called "imposed."
Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and bodhisattva disciples—
including both those who are householders and those who have left the home life—
engage in activities that constitute bondage.
This causes them to report [the matter] so that they may be punished with whips and fetters, or it causes them to regress from the Path.
It is like the worms within a lion’s body devouring the lion’s own flesh.
The *Saptasvapna Sūtra* and the *Siṃhamṛtyu Sūtra* state that for many days after a lion dies, the various beasts still harbor fear and do not dare [to approach].
After many days had passed, worms naturally arose within his body and devoured the lion’s flesh until it was gone.
This was not something that external paths or celestial Māras could destroy;

rather, it was because of the transgressions incurred by one who violates the Dharma and precepts, which must be returned to their original source. Thus it was during the time of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
The Path’s power of subduing is like that of a lion roaming fearlessly while the various beasts crouch in hiding;
the teachings left behind after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa are like the body of a dead lion, which for many days the various beasts fear and dare not approach.
Thus, for one thousand seven hundred years within and without the Buddha’s True Dharma, no heterodox practitioners, devas, or Māras have been able to destroy it.
The analogy of worms arising within a lion’s body after many days and consuming its own flesh until it is entirely gone signifies that one thousand seven hundred years after [the Buddha's passing],
the disciples of the Buddha will break the precepts and engage in evil conduct, thereby destroying the Buddhist teachings themselves;
it is not the path of Māra that can destroy them.
"If one receives the Buddha's precepts"—
this refers specifically to the person receiving the precepts—
who should protect the Buddha's precepts.
Having received the Buddha’s precepts and being called a son of the Buddha, one must practice in accordance with the teachings and protect the Buddha’s precepts.
One should do so as if thinking of an only child—
just as compassionate parents constantly remember their only child in every thought-moment.
Just as one serves one's parents,
or as a filial child serves and supports their parents with a mind that never departs from them,
when one hears heretics or evil persons slandering the Buddha’s precepts with malicious words, it is as if three hundred spears were piercing one's heart and a thousand [spears] piercing one's chest.
Whether one's body is struck by knives, cudgels, or staffs, there is no difference between these;
it would be better to enter hell for a hundred kalpas than to ever hear the sound of a single evil word that breaks the Buddha’s precepts.
This analogy establishes the resolve to protect the precepts.
How much more so when one personally violates the Buddha’s precepts?
Merely hearing the sound of someone breaking the precepts causes such pain that it is unbearable; how much more so for one who breaks them oneself—how could the heart not be deeply moved?
They teach others the causes and conditions for destroying the Dharma.
Since they themselves do not practice the two benefits [of self and others], this is already a fault; now that they further practice the two types of destruction, they shall incur grave offenses.
Moreover, they lack a heart of filial piety and obedience.
Because of destroying the Dharma, one ruins the Three Jewels; because of ruining the Three Jewels, one brings calamity upon one's parents.
If one acts intentionally in this way, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
This is subsumed under the sin of destroying the Dharma.
These nine precepts should be studied and respectfully upheld.
Having enumerated them, I exhort you to maintain them.
O sons of the Buddha, these forty-eight minor precepts have been received and maintained by you; they were already studied by the Bodhisattvas of the past.
"Bodhisattvas of the future should study as the bodhisattvas of the present are now studying.
