The following section concludes with an exhortation for the circulation [of this teaching]. Having finished expounding these ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, the Buddha addressed the assembly of the three classes of worthy ones (*trayaḥ-pudgalāḥ*) who were present as his audience, commanding them to listen attentively so that they might wholeheartedly practice and uphold them.
These ten grave and forty-eight light precepts enumerate the number of precept articles previously explained by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

It does not mean that the three eons (*tri-kalpa*) are designated as the three periods of time; rather, the past being boundless, the future being inexhaustible, and the present period—all are recited in the same manner. Therefore, it says below:
"What has been recited, what shall be recited, and what is being recited now—I too now recite in this same way."
I, Śākyamuni Buddha, now recite this together with all the Buddhas.
You, the entire great assembly,
are collectively addressed and informed by this indication to those present before you.
Whether it be kings, princes, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, or laywomen—
these are the seven distinct categories enumerated.
Those who receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts.
Among these seven categories, there are those who have never before received this precept and do not currently uphold it;
such persons should receive, maintain, recite, explain, copy, and protect it.
Among the ten types of Dharma-practice, these constitute five of the most excellent practices.
The Sutra on the Permanence of Buddha-nature and the Precepts.
It is only through the upholding, reciting, and reading of this sutra that one can realize the truth of the permanence of Buddha-nature;
furthermore, because this sutra can express and manifest the truth of the permanence of Buddha-nature, Buddha-nature is itself permanent, and Buddha-nature is eternally constant.
This scroll of the Precepts for Abiding shall circulate among all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Because it is received, upheld, and transmitted from one to another as previously described, it pervades the three periods of time.
Transformations succeed one another without ceasing;
lamps pass on from one to another without ending.
Thus, one shall behold a thousand Buddhas.
By upholding the precepts, one attains entry into the second bhūmi and beholds Vairocana Buddha upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal,

as well as the one thousand great transformation bodies of the Buddha upon that same thousand-petaled lotus pedestal; furthermore, by upholding the precepts, one beholds the Buddhas of the three kalpas and the three thousand worlds,
as stated in the sutras in general.
Buddha after Buddha hands it down.
The Buddhas extend their hands of teaching through compassion; sentient beings develop the aspiration for enlightenment, taking faith as their own hand.

When these two hands meet in accord, they draw forth sentient beings, leading them to become Buddhas who in turn transform other sentient beings. Thus, sentient beings continue to become Buddhas and continue to transform others.
Because they are born [in such states], it is said that "Buddha after Buddha extends a helping hand.
Life after life, they do not fall into the evil realms or the eight difficulties;
they maintain the precepts, and their minds are virtuous.
I am constantly reborn among humans and devas.
By the power of upholding the precepts, I draw near to birth as a human or deva; through the three stages of worthiness and the ten bhūmis, I shall ultimately attain Buddhahood.
I am now here beneath this tree.
The minor transformation-body Śākyamuni Buddha sat here beneath this Bodhi tree and proclaimed these precepts in brief.
This single-fascicle scripture on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is like a single hair-tip within the Dharma-gate of the Ineffable.
Agreed. Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment as precepts,
I shall speak of them based on their immediate application.
"You all should single-mindedly study the Prātimokṣa and joyfully practice it.
This clarifies that the great assembly receives it with faith and practices accordingly,
as is explained in detail for each point within the "Exhortation to Study" section of the *Animitta-devaputra-parivarta*.
This clarifies a forward reference to the extensive text. The preface to this sutra states: "This sutra originally consisted of one hundred and twelve fascicles and sixty-one chapters;
it is now indicated that [the relevant passage] is spoken within the 'Chapter on the Heavenly Kings' therein."
Regarding the "three thousand scholars" who were seated and listening at that time:

the commentary points out that there were three thousand listeners who had already attained the stages (*bhūmi*), and another three thousand who were still prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*). Furthermore, among those currently studying, there were those who had already studied, those currently studying, and those not yet having studied.
Now, when Kumārajīva recited the precepts, there were three thousand scholars who recited along with him; thus, it is simply called "the three thousand scholars."
The following section consists of two parts: the translator’s exhortation to encourage its circulation and the concluding verses.
First, regarding the prose: the translator describes how his disciples received and upheld the text with great joy.
When Master Kumārajīva recited this "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground," there were three thousand scholars in the thatched hall who received it from the Dharma Master.
Because they had studied the sutras, vinayas, and śāstras translated by him, they had never heard this "Chapter on the Mind-Ground Precepts" recited by the Dharma Master;
hearing it for the first time and finding it profoundly marvelous, they all gave rise to joy.
It is heard that the Buddha himself recited this;
thus, the three thousand scholars personally heard the Master of Dharma orally recite the brief text of the *Buddha-nature Precepts Sūtra*.
Each person held [the teaching] upon the crown of their head with hearts full of joy, receiving and upholding it;
the three thousand individuals each received it upon their crowns, prostrated, looked up with reverence, and were so filled with delight that they leaped for joy.
They internalized the meaning of the text without omission or forgetfulness, maintaining an uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness to manifest the utmost intensity of their devotion.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha finished expounding the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Precepts within the Chapter on the Mind-Ground Dharma-Door of Vairocana Buddha in the World of the Superior Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury.
This is the section where Kumārajīva, while reciting this sutra, based himself on its extensive version to briefly outline its essential framework;
he separately recited these passages of scripture to supplement the original text and further illuminate its beauty, encouraging their circulation.
The preceding paragraph concludes the previous section by stating: "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [emerged] from the world-system of the Lotus Treasury."
Having returned to the world of Jambudvīpa at the foot of the tree,
he preached the Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground as taught by Vairocana Buddha in the Lotus Treasury World of the Source.
The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis also speak thus.
This concludes the preceding passage; the remaining thousands of billions of Śākyamunis are likewise identical and without distinction.
From the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara,
continuing from the preceding text: emerging from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of the Void of Essential Nature,
he then sat upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays-King Throne and, in the Hall of Sublime Light, spoke of the ten world-oceans, up to the tenth [ocean].
The Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground, as taught by Vairocana Buddha in the Lotus-Pedestal Treasury World regarding my own origin,
was preached in the palace of the Heavenly King Īśvara;
it has now reached this place beneath the Bodhi tree.
The preceding text concludes by stating: "Furthermore, descending from the palace of the Heavenly King to Jambudvīpa, etc.
This is the section on the Ten Abodes Preaching the Dharma.
The preceding text concludes by stating: "Seated upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne, he preached concerning the ten world-oceans, up to..."

In the "Chapter on the Teaching of the Mind-Ground Dharma-Door in the Palace of Śiva," it is likewise for all bodhisattvas and the inexpressibly vast assembly to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain its meaning.

This concludes the preceding text; although the concluding passage is brief—summarizing the "Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground" taught for all sentient beings, ordinary people, and those shrouded in the darkness of ignorance on this stage—it fully summarizes the general outline of what precedes it.
"Billions of worlds" refers to the locations where the aforementioned large and small transformation bodies preach the Dharma and manifest birth.
"The Lotus Treasury World" (Padmakośa-lokadhātu).
This refers to the place where Samantabhadra preached the Dharma.
Regarding "worlds as numerous as motes of dust," the number of the first two types of worlds is equal to the number of motes of dust.
"The heart-treasury of all Buddhas" refers to the preceding fifty-four minds, which are able to encompass the virtues of a Buddha;
thus, they are the "earth-treasury."
"Refers to the myriad virtues of the ten stages (bhūmis) that give rise to the state of Buddhahood.

The 'Treasury of Precepts' (śīlaskandha) encompasses the merit of the untainted (anāsrava) states of the worthy and the sage, namely the aforementioned ten grave precepts and forty-eight light precepts."
"Furthermore,
the 'Treasury of Immeasurable Practices and Vows' refers to the aforementioned six perfections, myriad practices such as those for nurturing virtue, and the four great vows."
The Buddha-nature of cause and effect is the eternally abiding treasury.
"Cause" refers to the six perfections; "effect" refers to the three bodies (trikāya). The practice of the Buddha-nature continues without interruption.
The principle-Buddha-nature is immutably and eternally abiding. Both [aspects] encompass cause and effect, and both possess the meaning of containing and giving birth.
As each and every Buddha has finished expounding the immeasurable treasury of all dharmas,
and because what is spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time is identical, it is said that "the *tathatā* is finished," which carries the meaning of completion.
The hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas have each, for the sake of sentient beings in their respective realms, fully concluded this chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
All sentient beings throughout the hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds received, upheld, rejoiced in, and practiced it.

This collectively refers to the transformed sentient beings in those realms who, having each heard the aforementioned Dharma-gate of the Ground of the Mind, all together received, upheld, cultivated, studied, and joyfully practiced it.
The preceding text merely concerned the formal hearing of the ten stages and four [aspects].
The reason for rejoicing in the eighteen minor precepts is that by hearing this single fascicle of the sutra, one attains total penetration;
thus, the joy is not redundant. To explain this further:
if one opens the mind broadly...
The fifty-four minds,
the stages,
and the ten stages.
The various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are as explained in the "Chapter on the Seven Practices" of the *Buddhāvatamsaka-rāja-sūtra*.

"Characteristics" refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), the aspect of practice (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*), and the formal appearance (*ākāra-lakṣaṇa*). From the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*) through the five stages—such as the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) and the stage of application (*prayoga*)—each has its own distinct essential nature, practice, and formal appearance.
Since what was stated above is not exhaustive, this refers back to that [text] for further explanation.

"One with clear understanding and strong patience and wisdom" refers to a person of clear intelligence who, in the face of circumstances, possesses the great power to definitively discern right from wrong and to choose between the superior and the inferior.
One who is able to uphold such Dharma must,
by virtue of the strength of their prior patience and wisdom, be capable of reverently maintaining these ten grave precepts and forty-eight minor precepts.
"Until one attains the Buddha-way, how can one obtain the five kinds of benefits?
This means that as clarified previously, from the initial reception and upholding of such precepts until reaching the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*),
although one has not yet attained the Buddha-way, one will gradually and securely obtain the five kinds of meritorious benefits.
First, the Buddhas of the ten directions take pity on and constantly protect one;
by maintaining the purity of the precepts and acting in accordance with the Buddha’s mind, they perpetually bestow their protective mindfulness, so that Māras find no opportunity.
This is the benefit of being protected and mindful of by all Buddhas.
Second, at the time of death, one possesses the benefit of a joyful mind through right view;

knowing that one's precepts are complete, one will certainly be reborn in a good realm and shall behold the Buddhas. Thus, at the time of death, possessing the precepts brings joy to the mind—this is the benefit.
Third, the place of birth for successive lifetimes: it serves as the pure spiritual friend and fellow-born benefactor for bodhisattvas.
Fourth, the accumulation of merit: the perfection of ethical discipline is fully accomplished.
Because of the observance of precepts, all virtues arise; as one’s merit becomes perfected and one is able to reach the other shore, it is called the "Perfection of Precepts" (*śīla-pāramitā*).
"Perfection" (*pāramitā*) means "to cross over," and the accomplishment of the virtue of precepts is the benefit.

Fifth, regarding future lives: through the perfection of natural precepts, merit, and wisdom in this present life by virtue of maintaining the precepts now, one will achieve the accomplishment of natural precepts in every successive birth in future lives;
even if one does not encounter virtuous friends in those subsequent births, there will naturally be natural precepts capable of bringing about detachment from all [defilements].
The precept against evil generates the benefits of merit and wisdom.
This is the sphere of the Buddha’s practice;
by relying on this precept, one attains Buddhahood. Therefore, this chapter on the precepts is the sphere of the Buddha’s practice.
The wise person skillfully reflects and exhorts those with wisdom to contemplate that by means of this precept, one attains Buddhahood; they do not harbor the notion of a self.
Those among the various classes of non-Buddhists who are attached to signs are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Those who cannot believe in this Dharma are those who lack faith in these ten grave and forty-eight light precepts;
they have extinguished [the roots of goodness] and seek only personal realization.
Those of the two vehicles with fixed natures delight in entering nirvana without remainder and grasping at various forms of quiescence;

furthermore, they are not a locus for planting seeds, because such persons lacking the [Mahāyāna] nature are incapable of hearing this Dharma of the precepts, and thus no seed is planted. Although their spiritual lineage is not [of the Mahāyāna], [the teaching is still given].
Although [the path] is newly born, it grows by means of this precept.

When the seeds of the four wisdoms—the sprouts of bodhi—reach the stage of application (*prayoga*), they are about to give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*); this is called the "sprout of bodhi. Upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), [it flourishes].
The initial arising of the untainted [state] is called the sprout of bodhi; reaching the path of liberation is called the fruit of bodhi.
Now, taking this sprout, its radiance illuminates the world.
That is, the fruit of bodhi becomes the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), whose light of wisdom illuminates both internally and externally;
one should observe this with stillness.
These two lines complete the text of the preceding four lines. If a person wishes to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, they must contemplate [the truth].
The true mark of all phenomena (dharmas) is precisely their true nature;
it is neither born nor extinguished,
and this praise of the Dharma-body is free from the four marks.
Neither eternal nor annihilated,
the manifested Dharma-body is free from the two attachments to permanence and annihilation;
it is neither identical nor different.

Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal and pervades every single thing, it is said not to be "one"; because its essence is quiescent, profound, true, and constant, without differentiation, it is also not "different.
It neither comes nor goes.
Since it fundamentally has no coming, when could there be a going?
Thus, within this single mind,
one focuses on the preceding observing mind as it concentrates exclusively and without distraction upon the true nature of the object of observation.
Through skillful means and diligent adornment,
one must further extensively cultivate the myriad practices of the six perfections before being able to realize full perfection;
this is what a bodhisattva ought to do.
This is the practice of the two benefits.

One should study these stages in successive order because they preclude the notion of attaining Buddhahood instantaneously; thus, one practices and studies them sequentially throughout the five stages.
Regarding those in training and those beyond training,
those who have previously trained in morality, concentration, and wisdom, and those who have not yet trained in morality, concentration, and wisdom—
because they possess the nature of the Mahāyāna, they will certainly train in it now, even if they have not yet done so.
Do not give rise to discriminative thoughts,
nor harbor conceit on account of your lack of study;
this is called the first path.
The mind dwells in non-discrimination and right contemplation;
this is also called Mahāyāna, which here is translated as the "Great Vehicle.
A practitioner of the Bodhisattva path possesses a non-discriminative mind that is free from the notions of enemy and friend.
The *Buddhatva-śāstra* states that there are three kinds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*): first, craving; second, egoism; and third, various views.
Since the Tathāgata has completely extinguished these, they serve as the three fundamental roots [of affliction].

All of this arises from the cessation of the three causes of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); through the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the contemplative realization of ultimate truth, they are all completely extinguished.
This is the *sarvajñā* (omniscience) of the Buddhas.
This so-called "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*) is an alternative name for *prajñā*.
All the wisdom of the Buddhas emerges from this very source; it all flows forth from the truly pure *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, "all you sons of the Buddha"—

the two characters "therefore" (is gu) arise because they depend on the preceding text; since one attains wisdom by observing reality through the prior observance of precepts and thereby achieves Buddhahood,
the sons of the Buddha are thus exhorted.
One should arouse great courage,
observing that the realization of the fruits [of the path] does not arise from indolence;
thus, one should protect and uphold the pure precepts of all Buddhas as if they were a bright pearl.

Knowing that the fruit of the former Buddhas was attained through the cause of upholding the precepts, one should be exhorted to diligence in guarding the precepts as if they were a bright pearl—that is, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
All bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in this; those of the future shall likewise train.
Those who now study this are likewise studying it throughout the three periods of time;
this is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity.
This demonstrates that there is no one who can attain Buddhahood without upholding these precepts.
The "Holy Lord" (Śāstṛ) refers to the Great Sage (Mahāmuni), who is uniquely honored throughout the three realms; thus he is called the Lord. Now, this Holy Lord constantly praises these [precepts].
Regarding the precepts:
I have explained them in accordance with [the teachings],
which is to say that Kumārajīva, conforming to worldly conventions, praised and proclaimed them as being in accord with the Buddha’s intention.
The accumulation of merit is immeasurable;
through recitation, exposition, and circulation, many are transformed toward goodness. Thus, the arising of this mass of merit is likewise immeasurable.
Dedicate it to all sentient beings, that they may together advance toward omniscience.
I dedicate the merit accumulated from this transmission and recitation to all sentient beings, that they may together attain the Buddha-way.
May those who hear this Dharma swiftly attain the Buddha-way.
(End of Fascicle Lower of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra Commentary*)
Above, it is to extend and broaden the national destiny; below, it is to universally deliver all sentient beings.

In the summer of the *gengwu* year of the Great Age of the August Radiance of Longqing, there were certain practitioners, including Hui Cheng and Yin Zhu, who, desiring to propagate the transmission of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* to benefit future students, solicited donations to carve the woodblocks for its circulation. There is a preface by Shi Wu.
Could anyone who does not possess a profound yearning for the spirit of the Buddhas and patriarchs achieve such a state? For those students of later generations with resolute aspirations who,
upon reading this Sūtra of Precepts, suddenly cause the flower of the Bodhicitta to blossom, how could the merit of their teaching ever be fully enumerated?
